Sports.title: Grealish could have been Everton’s poster boy of a new era. Now his career is in limbo
Sports.content:
For the biggest game in Manchester City’s history, Jack Grealish was given a starting berth while Phil Foden, Julián Alvarez and Riyad Mahrez were on the bench. Grealish played the full 90 minutes of the Champions League triumph against Inter because Pep Guardiola had the greatest faith in the attacking midfielder, but three years on he is at risk of being yesterday’s man.

That trust dwindled, not helped by injuries, and Grealish made only 17 Premier League starts over the next two seasons under Guardiola. City wanted him to leave in the summer of 2025, and Everton provided the solution, taking him on loan and borrowing him again for this season. Six Everton appearances into this campaign he was left out of the squad for Thursday’s Carabao Cup win against Newcastle after missing training on Monday. Everton went public with the fact that there had been “a breach of club discipline”.

Grealish is 31 and has 39 England caps. He is supposed to be a senior player but his career has involved far too many indiscretions. Breaking lockdown rules, a driving ban and more than once becoming a viral sensation for being pictured inebriated out and about have painted an unwanted picture. Learning from mistakes is part of life but Grealish’s indiscipline is apparently not dwindling with age. Guardiola warned him over his behaviour, dropping him in 2021 for a match against Newcastle after he and Foden arrived for training worse for wear.

Grealish is aware of his flaws, which is a starting point, but dealing with them is a separate matter. “People go: ‘He likes to go out, he likes to party,’ and I do,” Grealish told Sky Sports last year. “I want to be able to live my life and enjoy myself but obviously there’s a time and a place to do that. Sometimes, I’ll be honest with you, I probably haven’t picked the right times.”

Initially at Everton it seemed Grealish could be the poster boy of a new era. There were winners against Crystal Palace and Bournemouth by early December of last year and he had accumulated six assists in 20 Premier League appearances before his season was ended in mid-January by a foot injury. Grealish had been inconsistent, though. He has not played more than 28 league games in a season since 2019-20 at Aston Villa, which should concern him.

There were reservations at Everton about taking Grealish back this summer but Iliman Ndiaye’s sale to City made it a pragmatic move to fill the void. Grealish had carried out pre-season under Enzo Maresca, who gave him chances in the Community Shield and on the opening day against Bournemouth. The Italian had time for him but the unlikely redemption arc at City was soon quashed. Maresca showed affection for Grealish on Friday, saying: “I still think that he’s a good boy, big heart.”

View image in fullscreen David Moyes was terse on the subject of Jack Grealish and seems unlikely to recommend keeping him beyond the length of his current loan. Photograph: Tony McArdle/Everton FC/Getty Images

At his best, Grealish is a wonderful player, a carefree spirit when dribbling with his socks around his ankles. In full flow, he gets fans up off their seats, makes and takes goalscoring chances and forces opponents to foul him, but those moments have been fleeting for far too long. The next seven months are crucial to Grealish’s career; he is at an age where he could play at the top for years but his status is declining rapidly. He is a £100m City signing and treble winner but those are past glories. Grealish needs to prove he has the respect for himself and for Everton to want more.

Grealish’s contract at City concludes at the end of the season, so there is plenty of incentive for him to show he is capable of shining in the Premier League and inspiring Everton to the cup win they crave. Instead, his career is in limbo. David Moyes was terse on the subject of Grealish on Thursday and seems unlikely to recommend keeping him beyond his loan. The Everton manager is working with a very small squad, so losing a senior player for avoidable reasons will surely frustrate and irritate him.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In an industry where the public is kept at arm’s length, Grealish is very approachable, happy to sign autographs for longer than his peers, eager to do the charity elements that come with playing for major clubs and known for his personal touch when others are businesslike. When entering and leaving Hill Dickinson Stadium, Grealish is mobbed, such is his popularity. He embraces it, posing for selfies with anyone who demands one, channelling a lot of positive energy into others, but he needs to find the self-awareness to do the same for himself.

“With me, I’m a big confidence player – I want to feel loved,” Grealish once said. He will not be feeling that from Moyes any time soon without radical change.

Sports.title: ‘We are not in Disneyland’: Arteta warns Dowman of Arsenal’s demands
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has warned Max Dowman that he “is not in Disneyland” and must learn from his red card against Fleetwood after Arsenal’s appeal against his three-match suspension was rejected.

The 16-year-old became the youngest player ever to be sent off in the League Cup on Tuesday as the Premier League champions crashed out to the League Two side Fleetwood. Arteta said he was “very disappointed” that the Football Association rejected the appeal against his red card and felt Dowman was lucky not to suffer a broken foot from “reckless tackles”.

But despite describing his reaction as “minimal”, the Arsenal manager revealed he had spoken to Dowman this week to underline his responsibilities after he was also sent off this month playing for England Under 19s.

“I’ve done it, so I try to prevent that [in future]. That’s why I’m so protective of these things and especially with young players, because we have made those mistakes. You know how much you can get punished and how much it can change what happens next, and it’s not the first time, so obviously we need to put an end to it very, very quickly,” Arteta said.

Arteta said he had not seen the criticism of his angry reaction to Dowman’s red card, when he appeared to aim a few choice words towards the forward as he headed down the tunnel. But he defended his actions after warning Dowman he was likely to be targeted before the game. “It’s something that we discussed just before we went out, because it’s not the first time that happened,” he said.

“For me, it was the best reaction ever to be able to be who I am. You want to see the reaction of his teammates? When they have to play with 10, you want to see that? That’s the level, and that’s the reaction. But the reaction when I don’t win, you know what the reaction is? I’m pissed off, big time.

“So we need to be ready for that. This is the environment and this is the reality. Otherwise, we are in Disneyland. We are not in Disneyland. We are in the Premier League at this level and we look after him so much that you cannot imagine. But at the same time, we’re going to demand [from] him like anybody else because he needs to earn the right to play.”

Dowman will be suspended for Sunday’s trip to Liverpool and the games against Hull and Newcastle, while Noni Madueke faces a late test to see if he has recovered from an ankle problem that kept him out of the game against Fleetwood. Arteta also revealed that Bukayo Saka is not expected back until at least after the international break as Arsenal await more news on his thigh injury.

Arteta said they had “put every argument on the table” in an attempt to clear Dowman’s name but to no avail. “Very disappointed,” he said. “Especially with the reckless tackles that he received, and then his reaction is minimal in relation to the action.

“I think you have to read the context of the player, the age, and what happened previously. It could have been really bad. And we are lucky today that he hasn’t had a broken foot. That’s clear.”

Sports.title: Are Liverpool in the title race? Their match against Arsenal will tell us a lot
Sports.content:
Every Liverpool win this season seems to come with an asterisk. Yes, they beat Brentford, but Brentford had a man sent off. Yes they beat Villarreal, but they conceded three. On Sunday, against Brighton the asterisks finally ran out. Liverpool beat the Premier League’s top scorers 2-0, kept a clean sheet against a side that had scored 23 goals in their first seven games, and won a league match at home for the first time since April.

Liverpool have won their last five games – including knocking Chelsea out of the Carabao Cup at Anfield on penalties – and are fourth in the Premier League, but there is still the sense that nobody quite trusts what they are watching. Liverpool remain a work in progress, with questions about their ability to create enough chances and break down stubborn opponents. Arsenal’s visit to Anfield this weekend will give us an indication of how much they have progressed under Andoni Iraola.

Given Liverpool’s spending and squad, this fixture should be seen as a title race six-pointer. Signing three attacking players for more than £100m – Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak – brings with it a certain level of expectation. The league table hardly dismisses their case for a title charge. Liverpool are fourth, a point behind Brighton and six adrift of Manchester City and Arsenal. A win at home on Sunday would put them just three points behind the champions. And they have been impressive in the Champions League, winning all three of their games so far to sit third in the 36-team table.

Since the 3-0 home defeat to Manchester City at the start of October, Liverpool have scored 15 goals in five games. Even that defeat at City comes with context. The game was goalless until Ryan Gravenberch’s red card changed it. It is a strong foundation, though cautious Liverpool fans – who have been watching the performances as closely as the results – will tell you there is still plenty to fix.

The fact we are discussing fixes rather than fundamental flaws is, in itself, a sign of how far Liverpool have come since May. In the last days of Arne Slot’s time in charge, their problems could not be solved by moving one piece on a tactics board. They had lost their identity and intensity. The tidy possession, early goals and sharp counterattacks that underpinned their title win disappeared – and Jürgen Klopp’s high-intensity press was long gone. Slot cycled through a 4-2-3-1, a diamond, a 4-5-1 and a back five without finding a system that worked consistently.

With a lack of identity came a struggle to balance an expensively assembled attack with a functioning defence. They conceded 53 goals in the league last season – their highest total since the 1993–94 season, when they had Bruce Grobbelaar in goal. They lost their resilience, too, conceding eight goals after the 90th minute. And they took just five points from losing positions compared with 19 the previous season. By the end of Slot’s time in charge they looked devoid of confidence and conviction.

View image in fullscreen Liverpool conceded 53 goals in the Premier League last season – their highest total since 1993-94. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/Reuters

Those fundamental flaws no longer exist under Iraola. There is a recognisable identity again: a pressing, transition-hungry side designed to win the ball high and feed Alexander Isak, who has six league goals – second only to Erling Haaland in the race for the Premier League golden boot.

Liverpool have kept clean sheets in half of their league games this season, which suggests the balance has returned too. The team presses from the front, confident to commit numbers forward with a settled back line of Ronald Araújo, Virgil van Dijk, Jérémy Jacquet and Milos Kerkez behind them. Araújo has turned the right-back position from a weakness to a strength, bringing some much-needed defensive prowess. And Barcola’s work rate means Iraola can use the attacking talent at his disposal without leaving the defence too exposed.

The fight has returned as well. Twice in the last fortnight, against Brentford and Villarreal, they have fallen behind and won. In fact, Liverpool have already picked up five points from losing positions in the Premier League – as many as they managed in the whole of last season. They are yet to drop a point from a winning position.

So, why are there doubts? The most obvious issue is their lack of goals. Liverpool have scored just 11 goals in their eight league games; eight teams have scored more – Brighton have scored more than twice as many goals as Liverpool. The underlying numbers are also a worry for Liverpool. They have only created six big chances – the second worst tally in the division after Coventry. To put that in some context, Manchester City have created 28 big chances, while Bournemouth, Everton and Brighton have all created 20.

View image in fullscreen Liverpool fans are still waiting for Wirtz to have a real impact for the team. Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty Images

Part of the explanation lies with the way opponents line up against Liverpool. They face a low block more than most sides in the Premier League and rarely face teams that are willing to play out from the back against them. For a side that is built to break at pace and wants to win the ball high up the pitch, there has been a noticeable lack of room to run into. Only one of their 11 fast breaks this season has produced a goal.

The other issue is that, while Isak is scoring, their attack has not yet clicked in the league. Florian Wirtz perhaps symbolises the problem best. He produces plenty of chances but rarely the decisive pass. He has, however, provided two Premier League assists for Víctor Muñoz goals this season and also one for Barcola in the Champions League.

Arsenal will prove an interesting test on Sunday as Liverpool will not face the problem of breaking down a low block. The champions will probably push high at Anfield and try to play in the Liverpool half. That will leave space behind, exactly what Iraola’s side have been missing.

Six months ago, the question was whether Liverpool could solve their fundamental problems. They are a team again: organised, intense and more resilient than in Slot’s last season. Results have been impressive so far but questions remain, namely whether Iraola can establish his high-pressing, transition-heavy approach against sides that play low blocks and still create chances at the rate of title challengers.

This is an article by WhoScored

Sports.title: Putellas provides mindset change as London City bid to upstage champions
Sports.content:
As Martin Semmens, the London City Lionesses chief executive, sits down is his office he looks like the cat that got the cream. He says he has just learned that the club’s Instagram page has generated 34m hits since Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d’Or on Monday evening, and it is only Thursday afternoon. On Sunday, two clubs with seven of the top 30 players in the Ballon d’Or rankings will go head-to-head when Manchester City visit Hayes Lane, Bromley. It is, Semmens, says, “awesome for the WSL”.

From the outside, it can feel slightly surreal. The independent women’s club, owned by the businesswoman Michele Kang, are third in the top flight, two‑and‑a‑half years after finishing eighth in tier two, and Semmens believes signing the world’s best player has helped change the mindset of everyone at the club.

“Her impact on our commercial business is extraordinary,” he says. “From a leadership point of view, she allows us to start thinking about really winning. The environment today feels like it can beat Man City on Sunday and that’s a lot down to her.”

He acknowledges that Putellas, a World Cup winner with Spain and four-time European champion with Barcelona, and her brand – she has more Instagram followers (3.7m) than a men’s club the size of Porto, for example – were pivotal in helping the club secure what they claim is the largest front-of-shirt sponsorship deal in the women’s game, with Nike. The club say it is worth more than the new NWSL franchise Atlanta’s sponsorship of $4m (£3m) a year.

“It’s insanely big,” Semmens says. “Our view on how to run this business, rightly or wrongly, was to invest first, invest in the everything to make it awesome, and then the commercial deal will be big. The other way, of: ‘Let’s sit back, let’s grow a fanbase, let’s wait for the money to come’ – we don’t have the patience for that. Michele’s vision was: ‘I’m going to invest now to prove that we can bring these deals in.’ That deal allows us to kick forward, it allows us to keep investing in players and infrastructure, because without it, we’re just burning Michele’s money, which is not the plan.”

Even with Kang’s money, signing a player who had been loyal to Barcelona for 14 years was never going to be straightforward. Semmens, the former Southampton chief executive, says: “The conversation went: ‘Wait until I’ve finished winning a Champions League with Barcelona and then we’ll have a conversation,’ which we loved and we respected, but we always had a feeling she would come.

View image in fullscreen Alexia Putellas has provided a huge commercial lift to the club. Photograph: Alex Ferrelly/Sports Press Photo/Shutterstock

“I think she had bought into four or five significant things. One, that we are independent, we’re a women’s-first environment. [Two] there’s a lot of power in coming to London, as a city. The WSL is important – people see WSL as the growth brand. And, after that, Michele had an unbelievably massive impact [on Putellas’s decision]. Alexia said to me: ‘Well, she said she was going to do all this stuff and she’s done it. So I want to be part of that.’ And then also, it allows her to have a legacy in the future – she will grow this club to a point where she’s creating a pathway for the next young players to come through in London.”

There are questions facing the club in relation to how much they have been spending and eyebrows were raised – to put it mildly – around the rest of the league when London City recorded an operating loss of more than 10 times their revenue for the 2024-25 season, when they won promotion as second-tier champions. Since then salary cap rules have been introduced in the WSL, stating no club’s player wage bill can exceed the following figures combined: 80% of revenue, plus up to £4m or a further 25% of revenue (whichever is higher).

View image in fullscreen Alexia Putellas’s arrival has undoubtedly put London City Lionesses on the map. Photograph: Nina Farooqi/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

Last season, when London City finished sixth, the league’s handbook said no punishments would be dished out for any breaches of that cap for that campaign only. From this term, points deductions could apply, which is one reason why it was imperative to increase commercial revenues. But were they within the rules last term?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“We are 100% within the rules, we will always be,” Semmens says. “It’s so important to Michele.” He says the “goal of the business” is to be profitable within five years and likens last year’s investments to a “start-up fund”: “The [salary cap] rules were set up with a clear understanding that they wouldn’t come until this year. The handbook is 100% clear. We want to see investment coming into the women’s game. Anything that kind of restricts positive and good investment obviously worries [me] but there is a need for rules and we’re 100% fine with that. We are super-transparent. We can reassure the fans that we are financially viable, sustainable, and we’ve made serious investments over the last two years to be profitable and successful in the future.”

Another question facing the club, particularly given their league position, is whether they would be eligible to compete in the Women’s Champions League, given Kang also owns the record eight-time European champions OL Lyonnes in France. Semmens says in reference to Uefa’s multi-club ownership rules: “One hundred per cent, it can be resolved. We will continue to argue the case that you should be able to [invest into multiple clubs] to see the women’s game accelerated.“It’s not about exchanging players like the men’s game. It’s not about one club dominating and the other being a feeder club. It’s a different model but we fully understand and respect the rules. Therefore, we will set ourselves up in a way where we’re allowed to and can compete in Europe together. There are clear rules, clear precedents in the men’s game and clear things you can do to allow both teams to flourish. We’re fully aware of that and we’ll comply with the rules.”

London City are three points off Chelsea and Manchester City, and Semmens says the aim is to “build a squad that is consistently in the top three”. He is looking forward to Sunday. “This is probably the No 1 game in the women’s game in the world this weekend,” he says. “That’s what we want to be: on the map.”

Sports.title: Football Daily | Newcastle’s Jaissle wants to scream while Grealish leaves Moyes speechless
Sports.content:
JACK AND JAISSLE, TUMBLING DOWN

While it is customary for fans of top-flight clubs with delusions of grandeur to cope with Fizzy Cup exits by pretending the competition is beneath them, this is no longer an option that is open to supporters of Newcastle United. Winning the trophy sponsored by a low-calorie, fruit-flavoured energy drink brand from Thailand may only rank fifth in the domestic pecking order behind the Premier League, FA Cup and both transfer windows, but nobody will ever forget how much it meant to hundreds of thousands of overjoyed Geordies when their team did exactly that the season before last to end a trophy drought dating back to the Jurassic era. And with a quarter-final trip to the tough-tackling League Two bullyboys of Fleetwood up for grabs during their match against serial trophy-dodgers Everton last night, the travelling Toon Army must have fancied their chances of being in the shake-up again.

Sadly, it was not to be and a season that could charitably be described as “mixed” hit another hole in the road as Matthias Jaissle – the German head coach, who Newcastle CEO David Hopkinson famously introduced as “a rock star” – masterminded another extremely tepid performance that smacked more of a half-hearted sound check at Trillians Rock Bar than his compatriots the Scorpions headlining the Wacken metal festival. “Well what do you think?” asked Jaissle of one reporter who questioned how much of Newcastle’s 3-1 defeat was down to avoidable errors. “And this is what is shocking and is frustrating as well and therefore I probably need to scream more. But that’s part of the game, you need to avoid these mistakes, be more mature, more clinical in these situations.” On the plus side, Jaissle and his gaffe-prone players will have their first chance to either put this debacle behind them, or plunge their fans into existential meltdown on Monday night when they play Everton again.

While David Moyes’s side have a quarter-final against Fleetwood that simultaneously looks extremely winnable and losable, last night’s victory was overshadowed by the absence of Jack Grealish, who was dropped for a breach of club discipline. The on-loan winger is reported to have missed training without explanation on Monday, with one paper reporting his no-show left his manager “incandescent” with rage.

“You probably know I am not going to give any details [about what happened],” whispered Moyes before the game. “It is a club decision and I support it. It is something I don’t want to speak about too much.” While Moyes was understandably reticent when it comes to discussing the circumstances surrounding his player’s absence from training, assorted pundits haven’t been so coy and have – correctly or incorrectly – linked Everton’s disciplinary action against Grealish with the player’s fabled fondness for a night out on the tiles. Whatever the reason behind his ill discipline, it is fair to say the 31-year-old is in danger of leaving a once great future far behind him and has clearly let his team down. “The one thing about Everton is that they have got real good values,” parped Moyes after last night’s win. Here’s hoping that, if required, those values extend to protecting their occasionally wayward own.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“It had been like one year and a couple of months and I still can’t walk on the stairs like a normal guy. I have to play football, so in my head I’m not going to give up, but I have to think that if this doesn’t work out, what do I do? I went to a physio in Sweden. He was able to change my nervous system and then it felt different. When I did the exercises, I said, ‘I don’t have pain, like this hurt yesterday. Why is this not hurting today?’ Then I did the next exercise and said, ‘this is not hurting,’ and I went into the room to my wife. And I told her, ‘it’s over, we’re going to do this’. From the minute I went into the room, it was better. There was still pain but it was different. Now I had control of my leg and then that is when the grind started that summer. I started to play football and it got better every day. I was limping and everything, but it was different now. I got much stronger in a short time and I went from ‘this guy will not play football any more’ to playing really good football in just a couple of weeks” – Dejan Kulusevski on how he was able to return to playing with Tottenham after a 17-month injury layoff left him fearing the end of his football career.

View image in fullscreen Dejan Kulusevski comes on for Spurs after a very, very, very long time out. Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

double quotation mark I clearly remember the first time I laughed out hard and loud, as a 12-year-old, reading Three Men in a Boat by Jerome K Jerome. Tonight, 50 years later, after a stretch of horrendous bad years and months (and for my mental health, I exclude the struggles of Tottenham), I read the Football Daily column. Its is often quite witty, but this time, reading about some penalty kick gone awry … I know, I have a simplistic sense of humour, but I laughed so hard and cried at the same time, that my family wondered what happened. Thanks for a cathartic experience. Words” – L Json.

double quotation mark As a Spurs supporter who saw my first game at White Hart Lane when I was five years old – almost eight decades ago – I can only express my relief that attention has drifted away from the continual ridicule of my team. The fact that a certain club that should return to south of the Thames managed to lose at Highbury (ironically), that lot from down Kings Road and Manchester United are all hogging the headlines for all the wrong reasons just makes life sweeter. It’s time for my second nap of the day now, so I’ll sign off” – Stewart McGuinness.

Sports.title: The academy system needs a refresh but now is the time for Carrick to trust in youth | David Pleat
Sports.content:
Watching Manchester United succumb meekly against Como and Bournemouth brought to mind questions and comparisons with yesteryear. Two of United’s most famous eras were built around their youth players: the Busby Babes and the Class of ’92. Could this be a moment for Michael Carrick to give their most talented academy products a meaningful chance?

In February 2025 I saw United beat Arsenal 3-2 in the FA Youth Cup at the Emirates Stadium. Jack and Tyler Fletcher did well for United and so did Harry Amass, a signing from Watford. Max Dowman, a generational talent, starred for Arsenal.

Not one of that United team has established themselves in the first team. Amass, a left-back, has two substitute appearances this season. The winger Shea Lacey, part of the same under-18s squad, has come on four times and got a Carabao Cup start.

Supporters, not least at Old Trafford, like players from the academy. The two United youth products who are regulars, Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford, are well established. I look at some of the club’s big signings and wonder: do they see themselves as real Manchester United players? With youth-team products you get spirit and identity – a deep pride in the shirt. That isn’t enough but to really assess them they need a proper chance.

You have to give a player a minimum of three starts in a row to see whether they have the potential to be a regular. Some players at United and elsewhere get an occasional Carabao Cup start and that’s it.

It is interesting that JJ Gabriel, a highly rated 16-year-old at United, and his advisers appear to think he could be better off elsewhere. Other young English players have made similar moves. Noni Madueke, for instance, left Tottenham for PSV at 16, got games and came back to sign for Chelsea, then Arsenal.

This is a wider issue than what is going on at United. The purpose of a youth system should be to produce players for the senior team – not to be a trading post, a way of raising funds to buy often mediocre players from abroad.

Tottenham have brought through internationals including Sol Campbell, Ledley King, Harry Kane and Andros Townsend over the past 30 years or so. This season their only homegrown player with a Premier League appearance is Mikey Moore, and he was sent back on loan – this time to Cologne – in August.

The loan system can be beneficial – look at Kane. I saw him at Leyton Orient on his first loan from Spurs and wasn’t sure he had the pace for the highest level. When he came back injured from a loan at Norwich, his rehab work, including weights in the gym, left him feeling fitter and quicker.

It got to a point where Tim Sherwood, Tottenham’s technical coordinator, was banging on the door for Kane to get a first-team chance. He got it, took it and this week won the Ballon d’Or.

Often as an academy player you need a sympathetic manager and strong advocate. Three players Spurs acquired for their academy were sold this summer: Alfie Devine to Preston and Will Lankshear and Ashley Phillips to Middlesbrough. Were they not deserving of an opportunity?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Will Lankshear moved to Middlesbrough from Tottenham this summer and is currently the Championship’s top scorer. Photograph: Aidan Hunter/Action Plus/Shutterstock

Liverpool have fielded a scouser every season since 1892 but named a 25-man Premier League squad in August without a player born in the city. They do have young English players and two – Rio Ngumoha and Trey Nyoni – have started non‑Carabao Cup ties this season, but looking across the Premier League I worry our national team talent pool is being eroded.

The academy system needs refreshing. Principally, under-21 football should be scrapped. There are 18-year-olds retained only so clubs have a big enough squad to support the one player who could become a diamond. A boy should be released at latest 18. Those who stay should be in the first team or on loan.

Young players need the competitiveness of senior football as soon as possible. Academy football is tidy and highly technical but has little resemblance to the frenetic, physical senior game. It also doesn’t test whether a boy has the mentality to cope in a tough dressing room where older players don’t want you taking their place.As a young player at Nottingham Forest I dribbled in training past an older teammate who warned: “Do that again, son, and I’ll break your leg.” It’s not like that any more but you need a certain character.

Too many over-18s are released from Premier League academies and want an EFL club without having the CV for that. Can they cope physically? Can they be trusted by a manager who has a short time to do well or faces the sack?

Top managers are also under pressure to win and so can be reluctant to give youth a chance. As a minimum they should be watching academy games when they can and asking: “Who have you got who could become a first-team regular?” Some managers separate themselves from the academy as if it’s another club.

Carrick watching United’s under‑21s this week showed he does take an interest. Now is his moment to be brave.

Sports.title: Fifa to miss equal Women’s World Cup prize money ambition set by Infantino
Sports.content:
Fifa is to fall short of gender equality with the prize money on offer at next year’s Women’s World Cup, despite making a record $15bn (£11.2bn) in revenue from this summer’s men’s tournament.

Gianni Infantino, the Fifa president, said in 2023 that the organisation’s ambition was to have equality for the prize pot for 2027, saying: “Fifa is stepping up with actions, not just with words.” There had, therefore, been widespread hope across the women’s game that 2027’s prize pot would match the men’s on at least a per-team basis.

There were 48 teams at the men’s event and 32 women’s teams will participate in Brazil next summer, so a women’s pot two-thirds the size of the men’s $655m would have been regarded as parity, but it is understood the women’s prize money will be about a third of the men’s.

That does mark a substantial increase. Some sources with knowledge of the extensive negotiations that have taken place in recent weeks are privately praising the rise, but one senior female source described the news as a “huge missed open goal” by Fifa. No decision is expected to be confirmed until December’s Fifa council meeting.

Sky News, which revealed that Fifa would not match the men’s prize fund, has reported that the women’s pot is being targeted to double from $110m in 2023 to $220m, which would be a more than seven-fold increase on the 2019 women’s finals in France. Fifa prize money to the men’s teams this year included $50m for the winners, Spain.

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino in Auckland in October 2022 for the draw for the 2023 Women’s World Cup. Photograph: Shane Wenzlick/Reuters

Senior Fifa officials are understood to have spoken to some leading female players to outline its wider investments in the women’s game and explain the decision, which is believed to be related to the commercial income the 2027 event will generate.

Infantino has previously criticised broadcasters for not paying more for the television rights for the women’s tournament, which in 2023 reached 933 million viewers on linear television and 895 million on streaming platforms, according to Fifa. The final between England and Spain in Sydney had a global live audience of 67 million and reached 222 million people overall, Fifa said.

Fifa did not comment when contacted by the Guardian but sources at the governing body said there would be further enhancements to the women’s club benefits programme and additional money ringfenced for the players who take part in the tournament.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It was confirmed this month that 2027’s Women’s World Cup teams will receive the same preparation money from Fifa as those who played at the men’s tournament. The preparation money has been more than doubled to $2.5m each.

Every player will be guaranteed business class or chartered flights, and their own hotel room rather than having to share, which Fifa says brings the provisions in line with the men’s World Cup.

Sports.title: ‘There’s a new chapter to write’: Le Bris upbeat as Sunderland eye Coventry reunion
Sports.content:
Twenty seconds of stoppage time remained when Enzo Le Fée picked up the ball and kissed it before taking a corner. As intended, the Frenchman’s perfect, right-footed delivery dropped into the corridor of uncertainty that leaves goalkeepers torn between leaving their line or standing firm.

It also dipped at the right moment for Dan Ballard to power a header in off the crossbar. Extra time in the 2025 Championship playoff semi-final second leg was almost over and Sunderland had secured a 1-1 draw that consigned Coventry to a 3-2 aggregate defeat.

As an outpouring of the loudest, most raucous emotion imaginable left the Stadium of Light feeling as if it was literally shaking, Régis Le Bris momentarily looked bewildered. By the time joyous comprehension began spreading across the Sunderland manager’s face, Frank Lampard was already a study in misery. Sunderland were on their way to Wembley, leaving Coventry in the Championship for another year.

Le Bris always believed that, at heart, football managers must be storytellers, and, suddenly, he had created the most compelling narrative of his career.

His players bought into his vision to such an extent that, having beaten Sheffield United in the playoff final, they finished seventh in the Premier League last season, qualifying for the Europa League.

Everything went so well it appeared almost a fantasy but now this magic carpet ride looks in peril of ending. Much hinges on whether Sunderland can secure only their second league win of the season at Lampard’s 19th-placed, finally promoted, Coventry on Saturday.

“There’s always a new story and a new chapter to write,” said Le Bris. “This game will be an exciting one with our intention to be us, show up with our identity, our pillars, our foundations and, after that, the game will be the game. Coventry have won twice in the Premier League so they are competitive. The Premier League is a new chapter for them but they are still efficient.”

Perhaps overstretched by the demands of European football, Sunderland have proved alarmingly inefficient at times this season. So much so that Nordi Mukiele, the former Paris Saint-Germain defender, recently accused his teammates of turning “arrogant”.

Clear the air dressing-room talks ensued and Le Bris seemed much happier after last Sunday’s 0-0 home draw with Leeds. “We saw Sunderland on the pitch today,” said the 50-year-old. “We showed we want to embrace the challenge. We were ourselves.”

A manager arguably let down by this summer’s recruitment refuses to fret about a demanding itinerary that, given Wednesday night’s 3-2 Carabao Cup win against Brentford, has just become even more congested.

“You won’t hear me complaining about this new journey, the busy schedule,” said Le Bris. “This is exactly where we want to be, with the opportunity to play regularly in Europe, to be competing in the Premier League and the domestic cups too.

“It’s demanding, but it creates the conditions to get better, to evolve and to be more proactive.”

If his attempts to introduce a more attacking style this season have produced mixed results, Sunderland’s manager has been hampered by the club’s failure to sign a long-coveted right winger, and a Premier League-ready striker capable of competing with Wilson Isidor as Brian Brobbey’s understudy. Recent injuries to Brobbey and Isidor have exposed a glaring lack of cover in this department.

While Florent Ghisolfi, Sunderland’s director of football, presided over some brilliantly radical recruitment immediately after promotion, backroom churn at the Stadium of Light has seen two previously key transfer market experts leave in the past year.

The formerly influential sporting director, Kristjaan Speakman, departed amicably once it became apparent there was too much overlap with Ghisolfi’s role. Stuart Harvey, the head of player recruitment, also left by “mutual consent”.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen ‘Sunderland’s story is important and something we’ve analysed,’ Frank Lampard said in August. ‘To see how they played last season gives us inspiration.’ Photograph: Ryan Browne/Shutterstock

Now the technical director at Stoke, Harvey was very highly regarded, with his intelligent use of data said to have played a significant part as he and Speakman helped lift Sunderland from League One to the top tier.

Ghisolfi, recruited from Roma, has an exceptional European contacts book and remains much admired. Yet in the case of Kevin Danso, a Tottenham loanee defender who will sign permanently next summer, his decision to prioritise height and power this summer has possibly proved questionable. Although an excellent character off the pitch, Danso has made some worrying individual errors as Sunderland have struggled in the absence of the hamstrung Ballard.

Paradoxically, the team’s one relatively diminutive summer signing – the £30m former Lyon winger Malick Fofana – has struggled to make an impact on the left. That said, a much-improved Carabao Cup performance against Brentford hinted of better things to come from the 21-year-old Belgium international.

The richly talented Le Fée remains integral to Le Bris’s plans, but constructing the right framework to bring out the best in a playmaker reportedly close to a senior France call-up has proved tricky at times.

It does not help that Granit Xhaka has not quite been his usual imperious self this season. Maybe at 34, age is catching up with the defensive midfielder, and perhaps Switzerland’s World Cup journey took his toll on the international captain? Certainly Xhaka’s recent suspension from the Switzerland squad after his admission of purchasing a fake Covid vaccination certificate has been an unwelcome distraction.

Le Bris, now working with a new set-piece coach, could do with having Xhaka back to his best at Coventry, and is also hoping Mukiele recovers from a minor throat injury to start.

There is a certain irony that, in August, Lampard described the Wearsiders as a post-promotion role model. “Sunderland’s story is important and something we’ve analysed,” he said. “To see how they played last season gives us inspiration.

“But now it is up to us to write that story for ourselves.”

Sports.title: Bruno Fernandes has 'TARNISHED' his Man United legacy after his public criticism of Michael Carrick - and peace talks might be 'papering over the cracks', warns Alan Shearer
Sports.content:
Bruno Fernandes has 'TARNISHED' his Man United legacy after his public criticism of Michael Carrick - and peace talks might be 'papering over the cracks', warns Alan Shearer

Alan Shearer has claimed that Bruno Fernandes has 'tarnished' his Manchester United legacy following his fallout with Michael Carrick over the last couple of weeks.

The Red Devils captain raised eyebrows when he questioned his manager's tactics after their side's 4-1 defeat by Como in the Champions League, and was subsequently left out of the team for their later loss against Bournemouth.

He spoke out just a matter of days after Lisandro Martinez had questioned United's activity behind the scenes, and left his United future in doubt.

That's according to all-time Premier League leading scorer Shearer, who claimed Fernandes' previous success is now marred.

'Fernandes is going to have to go out and perform, which he hasn't done for large parts this season,' Shearer told Betfair. 'I know he's been Man United’s go-to player for a long time now, he's been their best player, but it's no way for the captain to behave.

'He owes the manager a performance, he owes the club a performance, and he owes the fans a performance.'

Bruno Fernandes (right) has 'tarnished' his Manchester United legacy after criticising Michael Carrick (left), according to Alan Shearer

He added: 'I think he has tarnished his legacy at the club. I think the reaction that you saw at the end of the game against Bournemouth last week was pretty telling whose side the fans are on and it's Michael Carrick's, not Bruno Fernandes’, despite what he's done for the club.

'Whether that was part of him speaking to the manager and thinking, woah, I have got this wrong here. I don't know.'

Fernandes and Carrick held clear-the-air talks after the 3-0 Bournemouth loss, and many expect the midfielder to return to the side this weekend against Chelsea.

But it's unclear what will follow. Shearer, meanwhile, isn't convinced all is well.

'Fernandes and Carrick’s peace talks could’ve and probably should’ve happened before the game last week,' he added. 'Then there might not have been as much noise.

'Are they just papering over the cracks? I've been in a situation myself where I've not really got on with the manager in terms of Ruud Gullit and I guess you'd have to be on the inside to know what's really going on, but it would seem strange for him saying what he said, being left out and then being reinstated and then walking out as captain this week.

'It's not a good look, is it? It's pretty chaotic.'

Shearer suggested that crisis talks between Carrick and Fernandes may be 'papering over the cracks' amid the side's struggles

Old Trafford bosses decided not to sack Carrick with United in 16th place in the Premier League table, one point clear of the relegation zone.

The 45-year-old still faces a battle to improve results and performances and convince his employers that he remains the right person for the job.

Sources confirmed that Carrick has been given a second chance, and said that everyone is focused on showing a response on the pitch at Stamford Bridge following United’s worst start to a league season in 40 years.

The United boss was left in limbo after chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox held crisis talks on Monday with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and co-chairmen Joel and Avram Glazer.

The first indications that Carrick had earned a reprieve came shortly before 8am on Tuesday when he arrived at Carrington dressed in a club tracksuit and oversaw training as the players returned after a day off.

He had also turned up at the training ground on Monday but was there to watch United’s Under-21s play in a behind-closed-doors game against Hull City alongside his No2 Steve Holland and Under-18s coach Darren Fletcher. He stayed for three hours before leaving with his son Jacey, a member of United’s Under-18s.

Sports.title: 'We're not in Disneyland!': Mikel Arteta fires warning at Arsenal wonderboy Max Dowman, 16, after red card - and says it's not his first offence... as he admits Fleetwood loss left him 'p***ed off'
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has told 16-year-old Max Dowman 'we are not in Disneyland' as he insists his age does not give him a free pass following his red card against Fleetwood.

Dowman was sent off in the 86th minute of Arsenal's shock Carabao Cup defeat by Fleetwood on Tuesday after kicking out in retaliation to a challenge by Harrison Neal.

It was the second time he has been sent off this this month, having also seen red while representing England's Under-19s.

After the club's appeal was rejected by the FA, Dowman will now miss Arsenal's Premier League matches against Liverpool, Hull City and Newcastle.

As the teenager left the field, manager Mikel Arteta gave him a scathing look and uttered a few words to the attacker, understood to be: 'Get to the changing room, Max.'

And on Friday he suggested Dowman should have kept his cool under provocation.

Arsenal star Max Dowman (second from right) looks shocked after the referee shows him a red card at Fleetwood Town

Manager Mikel Arteta has words with the distraught youngster as he leaves the field

Arteta said: ‘I haven't seen the reaction to my reaction. But you have to understand the context, the relationship that I have with him and what we discussed just before we went out.

‘You want to always have the best reaction, the beautiful one. But do you want to see the reaction of his team-mates when they have to play with the 10 men, you want to see that? What do you expect?

‘I don't know. Or the England (Under 16) ones, they are his age, 16, the same. What is their reaction?

‘Whether it’s right or wrong, that's the reaction. And the reaction when I don't win, you know what is? I’m p***** off big time.

‘We have to be ready for that, this is the environment and this is the reality. Otherwise we are in Disneyland. We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League at this level.

‘We look after him so much that you cannot imagine, and at the same time we are going to be demanding that anybody continues to earn the right to play. Otherwise what are the rest of the boys going to tell me? It needs to be fair, that's all.’

He further explained that his touchline reaction was borne out of frustration having told Dowman to not react to such a scenario before the game.

‘I thought we discussed that before the game,’ the Spaniard said. ‘It was related to what could happen. Not only the red, but the 10 seconds before, the way he (Dowman) comes to receive the ball, what kind of ball that is, and after that if he gets tackled, what happens next. Exactly that.’

Arteta revealed he had spoken with Dowman about the incident. 'I had a talk with him yesterday,' he said. 'No issue at all. I've done it, so I try to prevent that.

'That's why I'm so protective of these things, and especially with young players, because we have made those mistakes. And you know how much you can get punished and how much it can change what happens next.'

On the FA’s decision to reject the Gunners’ red card appeal, he said: ‘Very disappointed, to be fair. Especially with the reckless tackles that he received, and then his reaction is minimal in relation to the action.

‘(We’re) disappointed that it's not been overturned after looking at the action back.

‘We have put every argument on the table to make a case for it. Not only the action, but when you look back at it in slow motion, the previous action and Max's action, it's clear that obviously we have a very different opinion.

‘And on top of that, I think you have to read the context of the player, the age.’

The severity of the challenge is also an issue for Arteta. ‘It could have been really bad, yeah,’ he said. ‘And we are lucky today that he hasn't had a broken foot. That's clear.’

Sports.title: Lewis Hamilton remains wedded to the only life he has really felt at ease in - but Ferrari should not keep him on as a favour to extend his career, writes JONATHAN McEVOY
Sports.content:
Ha, to think Lewis Hamilton once declared that he would be gone from Formula One by now, not hanging about as a grandad of the sport. It was easy to say back then when he was young, and 41 seemed as old as Methuselah. But he cannot give it up, as his comments in Mexico City indicated, remarks that were Muhammad Ali-esque in their sense of self-destiny. 'Firstly, you've never had anyone like me in the 70 years (of F1),' he argued, speaking in all modesty. 'I feel like I am built differently. 'Of course, there are challenges ahead which come with age that I can't foresee. But along this journey there have been so many preconceived ideas, like that your reaction time drops off. 'Did you see my reaction time in the last race (in Austin)? It was faster than some of the youngest people here. Lewis Hamilton has made his intent to stay racing in Formula One for the foreseeable future abundantly clear 'As long as you are willing to sacrifice everything, which I am right now (you can go on). I can't say in four years whether I will want to continue doing what I'm doing, but I am still all in. I will be for the foreseeable future.' For all the Met Gala and the rap songs and the fashion labels he has courted, it seems to me that Hamilton remains wedded to the only life he has really felt at ease in – motor racing, and, like so many sportsmen, he cannot embrace an existence without his essential ingredient. What would he do if he stopped? Who would he be? Where would he make his money? He doesn't need money, but that is not the point. But for his need to race, why would he keep hopping on and off planes, opening suitcases, staying in hotel rooms? Yes, he has factotums to help escort him, but that slog across 20 years must be strenuous. His latest landmark ambition is to race in Africa after Formula One signed a ten-year deal in Rwanda, taking the sport back to the continent for the first time since apartheid ended. But that will not be until the early 2030s, which would make Hamilton minimally 45, probably older because the race is more likely to be staged no sooner than 2031, possibly a year later, once they have built the track outside the capital Kigali (it all sounds very vague: will it even be on, a cynic might wonder?). Fernando Alonso is cited as a precedent for longevity. The Spaniard is 45 and has signed a new deal with Aston Martin this year. To pick from an earlier generation, Juan Manuel Fangio was 46 when he clinched the last of his five world titles in 1957. Is Lewis quite the driver he was? Well, on his day in the right equipment, he is still fantastically good. How could he not be given the talents with which he was blessed? But, surely, he is not quite up to the best of his roaring youth, if only neutered by two, three, four or five per cent. How, otherwise, could he have lost to George Russell in two out of their three seasons together? Was Lewis not meant to be the GOAT, whatever he thought of the ground-effect cars? How did Charles Leclerc pound him so roundly last year in the same red machine? For all the Met Gala and the rap songs and the fashion labels he has courted, he remains wedded to the only life he has really felt at ease in Hamilton, for the record, lies third in the current championship fight, one point behind Russell, five ahead of Red Bull's Max Verstappen and in front of Leclerc. This season has been a vast advance on 2025, without doubt, his victory in Barcelona the clear highlight. Ferrari, however, should not keep him on as a favour to extend his career as if operating an old folks' home. And this Alonso parallel only stands up to so much scrutiny. What evidence is there that he is fully the operator he once was? Still, like Lewis, brilliant, because he is brilliant, but he hasn't won a race for 13 years. I repeat, 13 years. Antonelli, who will secure the title in Mexico's thin air barring disaster this weekend, was six at the time. Alonso can't move on. Hamilton is the same, whatever he once believed. 'Bruiser' Russell vows to fight to the end George Russell has vowed to fight back to claim a world title at some point in his career after this year's disappointment of missing out, admitting he is 'bruised' but insisting 'bruisers' fight back. The British driver would need to win all the next five races to stand any chance of pipping his Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli to the title, a forlorn hope, a fate to which he is resigned. Speaking before Sunday's Mexican Grand Prix, Russell is 123 points off Antonelli with 125 up for grabs if the final two races go ahead in the war-conflicted Middle East. He said: 'I am naturally bruised but bruisers recover. That is the thing with bruisers. This setback will not define me, though I am not satisfied with the year. 'In my career to date I have had more good performances than bad ones in a season. It wasn't even close to 50-50 this year. I believe 2023 was my best in F1 to date. And last year I came away from 75 per cent of races thinking there was a lot I laid out on the table and that I had performed well against my team-mate (Antonelli, whom he beat convincingly) and I felt good. 'This year there have been a lot more bad days than good days.' Russell has won three times, having made a blistering start in Melbourne at the start of a campaign he thought he had a good chance of dominating. He also triumphed in Austria and Azerbaijan, but Antonelli has stood on the top step nine times – a remarkable performance by the 20-year-old Italian. George Russell (left), one the eve of the crowning of Kimi Antonelli (right), is confident he will one day win a world title Russell suffered some ill-luck along the way but admits he has not produced enough championship-winning performances and only deserves to be second best. He is one point ahead of Ferrari's Hamilton in the fight for runners-up spot in the final standings. Giving an insight into his state of mind, Russell said: 'The only silver lining is that my good days have been very good days. I've never had average performances. Why has it been either a good race or a bad race? I don't know. 'In a 20-year career, I have never had a season when I have been perfect every time. But this is my first bad year, my first proper bad year. 'I don't have an answer for it. It's not pressure. I started off perfectly well. I have not felt any more pressure this year than any other. 'I have had pressure every year in different ways. It started off very well, so it is hard to nail down. 'For me this is not negativity. It is reality. I am not here to be told nice things or hear nice things. I need a win. That is why I am not crying and dying about bad performances. I am thinking, 'Why isn't it working?' 'These are questions I am having with myself and with the team.' Casting aside any notion that he might seek a future outside Mercedes, he added: 'The team still have 100 per cent faith in me and that means a lot to me. Because they have followed me since 2016, they know what I am capable of. 'You don't lose that overnight and I haven't lost that this season. If you are a baseball player you are either hitting a home run or you are missing the ball, and that is how it feels right now. 'I am the same driver as I was when I put it on pole in Baku by eight tenths as when I qualified in Austin last weekend in P6. We need to work together to understand why there was so much of a change. 'The team have been brilliant, to be fair. They understand that we need to work on this together. It's not as if you are left in the weeds to sort this out. We are very much in this as a collective.'
