World.title: ICE officer is indicted after striking, injuring immigrant with his vehicle in Houston
World.content:
A Texas grand jury indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, alleging he drove his vehicle into Miguel Parra Hernandez, who was on foot, earlier this month.

The indictment of Morales, 33, was handed up by a Harris County grand jury Friday morning, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said.

The indictment is the first of an immigration agent in Texas. ICE enforcement officer Christian Castro was charged in the January shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis in Minnesota.

Teare said the charge is a second-degree felony punishable by two to 20 years.

“The evidence that we have in this case is as clear as any that I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated,” Teare said in a news conference Friday.

Teare played newly released body camera video that he said belonged to Morales. It was edited to play alongside security camera video from a local business that had been made public soon after the collision. The body camera video showed the officer yanking his steering wheel to the left and seconds later, a wail can be heard.

The video then shows Parra on the ground with his face on the pavement and the officer turns him over. “You ran over me,” Parra cries in Spanish.

The video shows the officer standing over Parra who continues crying in pain. The officer tells him, “You got hit with the car, bro.” The officer tries to pick Parra up from his shoulders, but Parra cries out louder.

The officer is then heard saying, “I was coming in and I hit him with the car.” He suggests trying to put Parra in the car.

Teare said, after the video was shown, “an ICE badge does not give you free rein to injure, kill, or violate the constitutional rights of anyone.”

The Oct. 10 collision left Parra with hip, leg and ankle injuries, including a broken leg, according to his family and representatives. Parra is at a rehab facility under ICE custody, Teare said.

In a statement issued after the collision, ICE said Parra “ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.” The agent was driving an SUV.

But after Teare’s office reviewed video from local businesses and bystanders that was collected by investigators, the DA accused the agent of deliberately running over Parra, allegations ICE said were “reckless” and “false.”

Miguel Parra Hernández. Courtesy FIEL

In an emailed statement shortly after the indictment was announced, an ICE spokesperson said the indictment “is nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians.”

The spokesperson stated that only federal agencies can investigate “federal officers acting in the course of their duties,” and that local governments don’t have the authority to run such an investigation.

Teare, a Democrat, said at the press conference that it’s “false” that they can’t investigate.

ICE repeated its statement that the allegations that Morales struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are “reckless” and “false.”

A senior DHS official told NBC News earlier this month that the department had placed an officer on administrative leave after the collision.

David A. Lindenmuth, Morales’ attorney, said he had not seen the indictment when reached by NBC News, but he said Morales is being charged with “a crime created out of thin air.”

He said Morales was reacting to an oncoming vehicle and had to either strike the other car head-on or “deviate.” Lindenmuth confirmed the oncoming vehicle he referred to was a truck stopped alongside a blue Dumpster.

“This wasn’t something that Mr. Morales was looking for. He wasn’t trying to harm anybody ... He didn’t knowingly strike this person. He did not intentionally strike this person. He did not recklessly strike this person. He was caught between the proverbial rock and a hard place,” Lindenmuth said.

The scene where Miguel Parra Hernández was hit by a vehicle driven by ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales in Houston, earlier this month. KPRC

Two people arrested in a separate operation were in the ICE vehicle when it struck Parra. Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez said they were handcuffed and shackled, which he said no law enforcement agency would deem acceptable.

Teare’s office was able to interview one of the men, Jose Presa Cañada, when he was being detained near the U.S.-Mexico border. Luis Delfín Martínez, also in the vehicle, was immediately detained.

“We’re keeping very very constant tabs on where they are and as they’re sadly being shipped out without any interviews and investigation,” Teare said.

Teare said Morales was hired by ICE in August 2025. He said based on his experience reviewing thousands of job applications and resumes for law enforcement officers around the state, “I’m not familiar with a single agency that would have hired this person.”

Lindenmuth called the comment “atrocious.” He said Morales spent two years in the military and was a military police officer and a paratrooper. He said he also worked alongside immigration officers transporting immigrants arrested by ICE. He said he is an ordained Christian pastor.

“He is a man of faith. To our knowledge he has never been in any kind of trouble before with the law or any kind of excessive force, so he seems like the perfect person to be hired for a law enforcement job,” the attorney said.

Parra has lived in the U.S. for 34 years, having arrived at age 14, and he has no criminal record, his attorney told NBC News. He had been doing stucco work when he was struck, according to an advocate. DHS said he was in the country without legal permission.

ICE had said it was conducting a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Jose Mendoza-Cervantes and was not targeting Parra or another man who was also in a truck with Mendoza-Cervantes before they fled on foot.

But Mendoza-Cervantes’ daughter told Houston immigrant rights group FIEL of Houston and Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno that her father had been dead since 2017.

Teare’s office also is investigating the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July by an ICE officer in a vehicle stop.

Teare said the investigation in the Parra case was accelerated by the fact that Morales and other officers were wearing body cameras and the sheriff’s office and the district attorney’s civil rights divsion chief were able to get onto the scene immediately.

“Nothing about today changes our laser focus on continuing and concluding the investigation into Mr. Salgado’s death as quickly and as thoroughly as we can,” he said.

World.title: Many on ACA plans face a new crisis in 2027: Insurers fleeing the market
World.content:
Courtney Mroch was already paying a high price for health insurance when she learned her insurer, Cigna, was pulling out of Tennessee’s Affordable Care Act marketplace.

The 56-year-old Nashville resident has diabetes and asthma and is a cancer survivor. She pays $1,250 a month for a silver plan this year, up from $850 a month in 2025 — more than her family’s mortgage. To keep costs down, her husband is enrolled in a separate, non-ACA plan that’s less expensive.

“Who knows who will cover me in 2027 or how much more it’ll cost,” Mroch said.

Many Americans are heading into ACA open enrollment with the likelihood of higher premiums and fewer insurance companies to choose from. In most states, the enrollment period begins Sunday, giving people who buy their own coverage about two months to compare plans for next year.

Insurers that offer ACA plans are proposing a premium increase of about 15%, on average, for 2027 — the second straight year of double-digit increases, according to an analysis from KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group, that looked at public filings from insurers across all 50 states and Washington, D.C.

At the same time, 11 insurers have announced plans to leave the ACA marketplaces in 2027 in at least some states where they currently offer coverage, according to KFF. Among them is Cigna, which will exit all 11 states where it offers ACA plans and has more than 350,000 ACA enrollees. Six insurers have announced plans to enter new marketplaces.

“The main takeaway is that more insurance companies are leaving the marketplace than coming in,” said Cynthia Cox, director of the program on the ACA at KFF.

For people shopping for coverage, that could mean fewer insurers to choose from and more people having to switch plans.

“This is going to create a lot of discontinuities in care and coverage for people,” said Miranda Yaver, an assistant professor of health policy and management at the University of Pittsburgh. “If you have a doctor who doesn’t accept the fewer number of options that are available to you, that can be very disruptive, especially if you’re someone who has a chronic illness.”

“And if the fewer available price points don’t work for you, are you going to remain covered?” she added.

Why are insurers leaving?

The departures come after the enhanced tax credits expired at the end of 2025, leading ACA enrollment to fall by roughly 3 million.

Some healthier people moved to cheaper but worse coverage or dropped insurance altogether. Those who remained on their plans tended to have greater health needs and higher medical costs.

Overall, that can make the marketplace less profitable for insurers as healthcare costs rise, said Jennifer Chumbley Hogue, an insurance broker in Texas.

From the consumer perspective, that means “constant upheaval, whether it’s the plan pulling out or the subsidies have changed or the doctor network has changed,” Hogue said.

In an email, a Cigna spokesperson pointed to April comments from CEO Brian Evanko, who said that leaving the ACA marketplace aligns with goals to position the company’s “core healthcare businesses for sustainable growth.”

For some families, rising premiums alone had already forced difficult financial decisions.

Denise O’Connor and her husband saw their monthly premiums in Colorado more than double this year, from just over $900 to about $2,300, forcing them to dip into their retirement savings.

The O’Connors are also covered by Cigna. She plans to work with a broker to find another plan, but her husband is also considering going uninsured for about six weeks until he qualifies for Medicare.

“It’s a worry,” she said. “He’s healthy, but anything can happen at any time.”

Mark Lathrop, who lives in Idaho and owns a winery just across the state line in Washington, said he and his wife are also looking for new coverage after their insurer, PacificSource, decided to leave the ACA marketplace.

The couple is already facing higher costs. They don’t qualify for the standard ACA subsidies, and Lathrop said a comparable plan for 2027 would cost about $17,600, up from about $16,000 last year. He needs an annual MRI to monitor a spinal cord injury, which costs $2,400, making a plan with a lower deductible important. “We don’t know what we are going to do yet,” he said.

In a statement, a PacificSource spokesperson said that the decision to exit the ACA marketplace was not “made lightly” and that it was made to ensure it can “continue fulfilling our mission and serving members for the long term amid growing pressures across the healthcare industry.”

Yaver said the changes could undermine public support for the ACA. As fewer people enroll and those who remain face higher costs and fewer options, the marketplace could become less attractive to consumers — weakening the law without the Trump administration and Republicans ever having to repeal it.

A recent KFF poll found overall public favorability toward the ACA dropped to 58% from 64%. “We don’t see the repeal and replace of 2017, but we’re making it much harder for patients to remain on these plans,” Yaver said.

Hogue urged enrollees to review their options when open enrollment begins, rather than rely solely on the notices they receive in the mail. The premium and subsidies available to them, she said, may be different from the amounts listed in those letters.

“It’s worth the five minutes to take a look,” she said.

World.title: Daniel J. Sullivan left his Alaska hometown before Senate election
World.content:
Petersburg, Alaska — Daniel J. Sullivan, the independent candidate running for Senate in Alaska whose name is almost identical to the Republican senator running for reelection, left his hometown of Petersburg earlier this week, multiple sources confirmed to CBS News.

One resident and former student of Sullivan's said she saw Sullivan on a flight to Anchorage on Monday — two days before The New York Times first reported that he was recruited by operatives linked to Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign. The source added she did not know where Sullivan was headed, but another friend said he and his wife are known among friends as "world travelers."

Dozens of Petersburg residents also told CBS News they never saw or received any campaign materials like mailers, flyers, brochures or signs since the former elementary school teacher announced his candidacy last spring.

"I don't think it's a serious candidacy," said Andrew Worhatch, a Petersburg fisherman. "I haven't seen a platform."

Just days before the midterm elections, a CBS News crew on the ground in Petersburg likewise found no indication of any active campaigning by the candidate, including outside his own home, which sits adjacent to the main coastal highway.

A photo of Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher in Petersburg, Alaska, from a yearbook for the elementary school where he worked.

Still, Sullivan has his supporters — and voters — including Keely Hankins, who said she thinks "Petersburg Dan" is the only candidate capable of representing Southeast Alaska.

"I've known Dan for a long time. I know his family. I know he's raised good children, and he's always been a really great role model for his students," Hankins maintained. "If you intend to vote and intentionally vote, you know who you're going to vote for, and it says 'Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr.,' then it says 'Dan Sullivan, incumbent.' Just read the paper. It's not that hard."

But the new spotlight on the town is not welcomed by some. Darla Kowalski said, "iIt's just embarrassing to think that we, a small fishing village, have such a hoaxer."

Daniel J. Sullivan taught music and fourth and fifth grade before retiring five years ago.

The local school district in Petersburg — a town of around 3,000 accessible only by air or sea — said Sullivan taught music and fourth and fifth grade for nearly 20 years before retiring in 2021.

Republicans have argued for months that Sullivan was seeking to confuse voters in one of the country's closest midterm Senate races, with Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan calling him a "sham candidate." State election officials initially deemed him ineligible for the ballot, but state courts reversed that decision.

The Peltola campaign and national Democrats have denied any connection to Daniel J. Sullivan, with Peltola telling supporters she is "not interested in tricking voters" and "knew nothing about" the second Sullivan. In interviews over the summer, the Petersburg native insisted he is genuinely interested in serving as senator.

After the Times' reporting on alleged efforts to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation, and the Justice Department ramped up a criminal probe. Nobody has been charged with a crime. The Justice Department is also suing in civil court to block the election from being certified if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses due to "voter confusion."

World.title: Appeals court rejects DOJ bid to set aside disputed California ballots
World.content:
Washington — The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit on Friday rejected the Justice Department's request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election.

The panel's 2-1 ruling is the latest setback for the Trump administration's efforts to assert control over state-run elections. Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez said in an unsigned decision that the Justice Department failed to meet its burden in showing that an injunction pending appeal is warranted.

"Major concerns remain that granting the United States's requested relief might result in immense hardship to Defendants and harm the public interest by risking the disenfranchisement of eligible voters and putting the entire tabulation process in jeopardy," they wrote.

Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented.

The administration has alleged California sent ballots to some 20,000 people who may not be U.S. citizens. It wants the state to set those ballots aside and not count them until citizenship can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.

A district court judge already forcefully denied that request and warned that the Justice Department's demands could disenfranchise citizens.

"As the district court found — and we discern no clear error — there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system," the appeals court wrote, adding that the relief requested by the Trump administration is "simple only in the abstract."

The ruling is the latest in an expansive legal battle between the federal government and the state before Election Day in the midterms Tuesday. Millions of people in California have already voted.

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.

Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. Elections officials have said that processed votes are completely anonymized and can't be matched back to the voters who submitted them.

The ruling comes during broader federal scrutiny of local elections, with the Trump administration issuing a raft of subpoenas in Alaska in a spoiler-candidate controversy. The Justice Department has also provided a list of alleged noncitizen voters to officials in Washington state.

Earlier on Friday, a federal judge in Washington ordered the Trump administration to share the disputed list of names with lawyers for the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights and the UCLA Voting Rights Project. They want the list so they can examine who is on the list and assess its impact on eligible voters.

It will be the first time that a nongovernment organization will have the opportunity to evaluate the merits of the list of some 20,000 names.

Prosecutors with the Trump administration have argued that there is just as much to lose from noncitizens illegally voting, arguing that to tally those votes would dilute the voice of citizens.

Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra is an adviser to the UCLA Voting Rights Project.

The two groups sued the Department of Homeland Security in early October to prevent it from using federal immigration data to challenge state voter rolls. The lawsuit cited examples in other states where the federal government's data has been proven to mistakenly include thousands of citizens. It argued that the data-matching methods risk disenfranchising or deterring citizens from voting. On top of that, plaintiffs argued, the lists could disproportionately target naturalized citizens who are legally entitled to vote.

A coalition of unions on Friday also joined the growing list of groups challenging the federal government's efforts.

The unions, including the A.F.L.-C.I.O. and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, are asking a federal judge to temporarily block the Justice Department from demanding that local officials stop counting ballots and to drop threats to criminally prosecute officials who do not comply with their demands.

The top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, Bill Essayli, has warned that "any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy."

On Thursday the Associated Press obtained subpoenas issued to election officials in Los Angeles County. The subpoenas request any documents and communications related to letters sent in July and October by federal officials to state election officials outlining the allegations about noncitizen voters. They also seek any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted. At least three L.A. County election officials have been asked to appear before a grand jury on Nov. 4, the day after the election.

The lawsuit accuses the Justice Department of issuing threats against election officials that could interfere with their ability to process votes.

It is unclear whether the Justice Department intends to bring criminal charges against anyone. The department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.

World.title: Meta settles social media addiction lawsuit, averting trial
World.content:
Meta has settled a social media addiction lawsuit, resolving claims against the technology giant before the case was set to go to trial next month, according to a lawyer for one of the plaintiffs.

The suit was brought by an 18-year-old woman identified in court documents as K.D.B. who alleged that Meta and Snapchat parent company Snap, which remains a defendant in the case, designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior. Another plaintiff in the lawsuit, dubbed S.J., settled with Meta last week.

Terms of Meta's settlement were not disclosed.

S.J. and K.D.B. also originally sued TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube platform, which each separately settled before trial.

The plaintiffs claim that the social media platforms contributed to their mental health struggles.

A spokesperson for the Lanier Law Firm, which is representing the plaintiffs, said they will proceed with their complaint against Snap.

"Each plaintiff alleges that Snap designed Snapchat to maximize the time young users spend on the app, using features such as Snapstreaks, Snapscores, push notifications, and filters, and that their compulsive use of Snapchat caused and contributed to severe mental and physical health injuries, including depression, anxiety, an eating disorder, and self-harm," the spokesperson said.

Snap disputes the allegations and has defended the company's practices.

Jury selection began this week in Los Angeles, with opening statements expected to begin in early November. Lawyers for the plaintiffs have said they expect the trial to last into mid-December.

"We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client," Emily Jeffcott, the trial counsel for K.D.B., said in a statement.

A spokesperson for Meta, which still faces similar litigation alleging that its social platforms harm users' mental health, said the company will continue to defend itself in court.

"Trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellwether process, and this litigation is no exception," she said in a statement. "We will continue to defend ourselves in court, and we stand by our record. We've spent more than a decade building protections for teens, and our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general goes even further with strict time limits, no access at night, and no notifications during school hours."

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion to dozens of states that alleged the company used its social platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, to hook young internet users while concealing the risks.

World.title: Tech stocks crushed as Nasdaq tumbles nearly 1,000 points
World.content:
The Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled more than 970 points, or 3.7%, in afternoon trading, while other U.S. financial markets also swooned as investors pulled back amid growing concerns about the health of the critical technology sector.

Intel's stock plunged more than 30%, while shares of Google's parent, Alphabet, continued to wobble after the company's Class A stock slid more than 12% on Thursday, its worst day since the company went public as Google in 2004. The drop erased roughly $500 billion in Alphabet's market value.

Shares of Nvidia, the maker of advanced chips used to power AI models and a bellwether for the sector, also dropped 5%.

"This has been one of the worst tech earnings seasons in memory, with underwhelming results from a slew of very prominent companies," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a research note.

"The slump in tech stocks (and the attendant deterioration in tech sentiment) isn't simply a financial phenomenon and could undermine industry fundamentals by making it more difficult for companies to raise incremental debt and equity," he added in a separate report.

The negative sentiment around tech spread to other major stock indices on Friday. The S&P 500 shed 183 points, or 2.4%, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 746 points, or 1.4%.

Debt reckoning?

The weaker-than-expected tech earnings reports are heightening concerns that massive investments in AI will not generate the payoff Wall Street expects. Investors are also worried about the debt companies are taking on to finance data center capital expenditures and whether that debt is sustainable.

"Mega-cap stocks have faced increased selling pressure over the past two weeks as elevated AI-related spending and rising financing costs raise concerns over the path to profitability," Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for brokerage firm LPL Financial, said in an email. "Recent earnings reports have added to these concerns, revealing slowing growth in select hyperscalers' core businesses."

Another factor weighing on tech stocks is investor expectations that the Federal Reserve will have to keep raising interest rates to curb economic growth and subdue inflation, which remains elevated.

The central bank left its benchmark rate unchanged this week, but many economists think it will hike rates as early as December and into 2027. That would make it more expensive for companies to borrow money to build the data centers required to power AI services, cutting into corporate profits.

Investors have been banking on the explosive growth of AI, which has propelled the stock market to record highs, to continue to dominate. However, that sentiment is now under threat. In a report earlier this week, Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and global head of equities for UBS' Chief Investment Office, advised clients to "diversify beyond AI."

"While we maintain a constructive outlook on the structural growth of the AI theme, high expectations and potentially wide differences in company outcomes underscore the risks of single-stock concentration," she said. "We think investors should ensure their equity portfolios are broadly diversified."

Still, U.S. stocks remain only 3.4% below their all-time high, boosting the value of workers' 401(k) accounts.

Cryptocurrency prices also slumped after hackers believed to be linked to North Korea stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000, from more than $86,000 earlier this month.

World.title: ICE officer indicted in Texas after allegedly hitting man with vehicle
World.content:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer was indicted on a felony for allegedly hitting a man with a vehicle in Houston earlier this month, a Texas district attorney announced Friday.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said ICE Officer Mario Alberto Morales was indicted by a grand jury on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

Teare said if convicted, the punishment would be a prison sentence lasting between two and 20 years.

Teare accused Morales of hitting Miguel Parra-Hernandez, a 48-year-old Mexican national who the district attorney said has been living in Texas for more than 30 years without documentation. Parra-Hernandez doesn't have a criminal record and didn't have a deportation order against him, Teare said.

Morales engaged in a pursuit of a vehicle being driven by Parra-Hernandez on Oct. 10. During the pursuit, Parra-Hernandez and another person fled the vehicle on foot. At a news conference Friday, a video was played showing the moments when Teare said Morales hit Parra-Hernandez with his vehicle.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, left, and Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez attend a news conference Oct. 30, 2026, in Houston, announcing the indictment of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Mario Alberto Morales. Melissa Phillip/Houston Chronicle via AP

Footage from what Teare said was Morales' body camera showed Parra-Hernandez groaning in pain on the ground after he was hit by the vehicle, which the district attorney said was a 2025 Jeep Grand Cherokee. Parra-Hernandez suffered a broken leg in the incident.

"Like, I was coming in, and I hit him with the car," the officer wearing the body camera said in the footage to someone else.

In the immediate aftermath of the incident, an ICE spokesperson had said in a statement to CBS News that Parra-Hernandez ran in front of the ICE vehicle.

"Morales aggressively steered his vehicle into Parra-Hernandez," Teare said Friday. He also said that Morales ran over both of Parra-Hernandez's legs and that he was still hospitalized.

Parra-Hernandez is heard screaming in the background of Morales' 911 call for an ambulance in a recording played during the news conference. He told a dispatcher that Parra-Hernandez hit his vehicle.

"We're following this guy, trying to pull him over, he jumped out of the vehicle, I tried to get around him, and he hit my car," Morales said in the recording.

911 call after ICE incident in Houston A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer calls 911 after an incident involving a Mexican national in Houston, Oct. 10, 2026. Your browser does not support the audio element.

ICE told The Associated Press that the indictment against Morales was "a political stunt" and that local officials lack the authority to investigate federal officers for performing their duties.

"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE," the agency said in a statement to the AP.

Teare noted that ICE had said agents were pursuing a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who the agency said was a Mexican national and undocumented immigrant. Teare said Friday that Mendoza-Cervantes has apparently been dead for nine years.

World.title: ICE activity is surging ahead of midterms. So is voter turnout.
World.content:
ICE activity is surging ahead of midterms. So is voter turnout.

toggle caption i Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images

Very early on Wednesday morning, Dover, N.J., Councilwoman Sandra Wittner started getting messages about immigration agents. A dozen or more were gathering outside a Walgreens, according to the messages she was getting. Throughout the day, neighbors in north New Jersey saw a spike in Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity.

And New Jersey is not alone. In the weeks ahead of the midterms, various cities and states across the country are reporting a notable rise in ICE activity, according to reports gathered by NPR and its member stations.

"The tactics that the administration has been deploying in communities really appear to be designed to try to intimidate voters," says Wendy Weiser of the Brennan Center for Justice at NYU Law School. Despite that, early turnout is surging .

Sponsor Message

"There was definitely a lot of apprehension and fear," Wittner recalls. "We just really weren't sure if something huge was about to happen. People were not feeling very comfortable or safe."

Wittner is not sure who was detained or where, which is unsurprising: these days it's difficult to report on ICE crackdowns as they happen, because the Department of Homeland Security no longer publicly shares timely information on its operations.

NPR wrote to the agency to ask if there has been a recent surge. It responded: "ICE agents uphold our nation's immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day."

And yet NPR and its member stations have received tips from rural Illinois, Oregon , Detroit and California about surges in ICE enforcement, throughout October.

An official within New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office who was not authorized to speak publicly confirmed that they have noted a surge in ICE activity in the city.

"We're certainly witnessing an uptick in activity, and have been since the summer," says a member of a volunteer group of neighbors in New York. She asked that NPR not use her name, as she is worried about retaliation. Her group goes to the scene where an ICE operation is happening, documents it, reminds those being detained of their rights, and alerts neighbors.

Sponsor Message

"In the past few weeks we've seen numerous large operations, or what we call cluster raids, multiple agents going to one spot and then the next," she said.

On the other side of the country, Oregon Public Broadcasting reporter Troy Brynelson has reported on a similar trend. "What we were seeing in early October and what we've seen continue, at least anecdotally throughout this month, is that ICE activity has really picked up in Portland." Brynelson says it seems to be concentrated in commercial areas. "I'd say it's a noticeable uptick compared to what we've seen over the summer."

Juan Proaño of the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), a civil rights organization says he's concerned because this is happening so close to the midterm elections. "It's not about ICE at the actual polling station, it's ICE at the perimeter of the polling station," he says.

"Mass enforcement actions could be away from the polls, but with social media and the news, it could be enough to dissuade somebody from actually going out to vote."

Weiser of the Brennan Center says there's no indication the raids are affecting turnout. On the contrary, she says there has been a surge in early voting in minority communities across the country. "The good news is: it isn't working. Americans are tuning this out and we are not seeing a significant impact on participation. And we are actually seeing huge surges in participation in communities of color, and in Latino communities, and in all the communities that have been targeted by ICE and DHS."

Even so, she says that intimidation at the polls is illegal, and should be reported.

World.title: NPR special: 5 takeaways from a year of listening to swing voters
World.content:
NPR special: 5 takeaways from a year of listening to swing voters

toggle caption i Ryan Murphy/AFP via Getty Images

Every election, there is a crucial sliver of voters who help determine which candidates win.

These are voters who bounce from one side to the other — the rare swing voters.

And all throughout 2026, NPR has had a front-row seat to how these folks think, listening in as voters in different swing states reflect on President Trump, the political issues that matter to them, and who they might vote for going forward.

In this case, these voters supported Joe Biden in 2020 and then swung to backing Trump in 2024.

They all participated in the Swing Voter Project, which hosts online focus groups every month. They are run by messaging firm Engagious and market research recruiting firm Nelson Recruiting. NPR is a partner on the project.

Sponsor Message

So just ahead of Election Day, what have we learned from swing voters this year? Here are five takeaways:



These Biden-to-Trump voters quickly soured on the president Voters are able to draw a direct line from Trump's decisions to their feelings about the economy It's not like Democrats are popular either! There appears to be a convergence among voters on the left and right in support of economic populism There's broad concern about artificial intelligence and the proliferation of data centers

Click the audio player above to listen to a special, hour-long discussion about these takeaways and the voters.

This special — "Swing voters and the issues that matter" — was edited by Ben Swasey and produced by Lexie Schapitl.

World.title: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
World.content:
Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance

toggle caption i Matt Slocum/AP

A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm says a North Korean unit was likely behind the hack that impacted more than $6 billion on Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. It said Friday that it was beginning to recover assets for users.

The cryptocurrency exchange said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. It said it will cover all losses.

The company said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach."

Sponsor Message

TRM, in a post on its website Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said.

"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.

In February last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.

Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was "likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor," its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. DPRK stands for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea's official name.

Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

Sponsor Message

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.

Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform, and stepped down as the company's CEO. U.S. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.

Zhao posted Thursday on X that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.

Binance said on X it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

World.title: Why is the Cheesecake Factory at the center of the latest culture war?
World.content:
Why is the Cheesecake Factory at the center of the latest culture war?

toggle caption i Kayla Bartkowski/Getty

They say there's no such thing as bad publicity. If that's true it's been a golden week for the Cheesecake Factory restaurant chain.

The furore began when former President Obama, stumping for Democrats in Ohio this week ahead of the midterms, joked about President Trump's White House refurbishments, saying they looked "like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere."

The late Iraqi dictator was known for building lavish palaces, with gold walls, cabinets of gold-plated rifles, a golden throne and of course plenty of depictions of the man himself.

Trump is also well-known for his love of anything gilded and Obama joked he'd been "supergluing gold medallions to the mantel in the Oval Office," while also paving over the Rose Garden and "building a ballroom that's bigger than the White House."

toggle caption i Sue Ogrocki/AP

And the Cheesecake Factory? The beloved U.S. restaurant chain was started in 1978 by David Overton, whose mother reportedly made a fine cheesecake, and now has 218 locations across the country and an annual revenue of $1.03 billion.

Sponsor Message

But it's as well known for its kitschy decor as its food, with The Atlantic writer Elaine Godfrey describing it in an article this week "as if ancient Egypt and Tuscany had a baby in Las Vegas."

Obama first made the "home renovations" remarks at the political rally on Saturday, where he also portrayed the Trump administration as out of touch with ordinary Americans suffering from a cost of living crisis and the economic consequences of the president's war in Iran.

Obama said the Trump administration had resulted in "two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption" and that those at the helm were not "serious people."

toggle caption i Hadi Mizban/AP

The administration was quick to respond, with President Trump defending his taste, saying: "I've taken care of the White House, I've fixed it with the finest artisans in the world."

"The White House was in terrible shape. The White House is now in the best shape it's been since 1792," he told reporters when asked about Obama's quip, adding that Obama was "not a smart guy."

The official White House X account posted a photo of the Cheesecake Factory's famously large menu, saying "Since we're talking about The Cheesecake Factory... The only thing bigger than the menu is the list of President Trump's accomplishments."

Sponsor Message

Allegations of elitism

Vice President Vance reacted by accusing Obama of being out of touch with ordinary Americans. "Obama, without even trying to be, just can't help himself for being super elitist," he wrote on X.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also sought to capitalize on the backlash, having lunch at a Cheesecake Factory near the White House on Monday. He ate a French Dip Cheeseburger and told journalists afterwards: "I had a great meal, always have a great meal, and I would just tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try," in an apparent reference to the Obamas who are known to holiday on the exclusive island.

toggle caption i Mark Schiefelbein/AP

On the topic of taste in decor, Bessent, who used to manage a hedge fund, also made an apparent jibe about the new Obama Presidential Center in Chicago.

"This is the man who built the museum [that] looks like Darth Vader's tomb," he added.

Obama was undeterred, taking up the theme again at a rally in Georgia on Wednesday, and saying that he was surprised that instead of hitting back on his criticisms about policy and corruption, the White House was more upset about the Cheesecake Factory remark.

"The president wasn't even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison! That part didn't bother him," said Obama.

"They mobilized a whole of government response to that joke. Not to inflation, but to that joke. The White House even called the Secretary of the Treasury. This is the man who is in charge of the economy. The person who's supposed to be figuring out how to make your life more affordable," he added.

"The guy who's supposed to be figuring out how to lower inflation. And reduce interest rates. They told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory."

Sponsor Message

Obama also stressed he had been a proud patron of the restaurant for many years.

"I am the father of two daughters. Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory?"

toggle caption i Mariam Zuhaib/AP

Later in the week, restaurants and affordability came up again. Trump told supporters at a political rally in Texas that they could spend the $5,000 he's promised every adult citizen if the Republicans keep Congress on dining out at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida.

"The problem is that for $5,000, the most you'll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert," Trump joked.

"I'm not even sure you could buy that," he said, before rescinding the advice: "No, don't go there. That's not a good place if you're price-conscious."

World.title: Binance flags 'potential security issue,' says approximately $6.3 billion impacted
World.content:
Binance flags 'potential security issue,' says approximately $6.3 billion impacted

toggle caption i Matt Slocum/AP

LOS ANGELES — Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said Thursday it's investigating reports of a potential security issue as its founder said the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." The company said late Thursday the estimated total impact was at more than $6 billion, which could be one of the most significant of such security incidents on record.

It wasn't immediately clear the extent of the damage hackers might have been able to cause, and Binance had not explicitly confirmed that funds had been pilfered. The company said its teams are "working around the clock" to resolve the issue.

"Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement.

"Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information," the statement continued.

Sponsor Message

The company wrote on its X account that the estimated total impact sat at around $6.3 billion. It said it has worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with roughly $3 billion frozen on-chain so far.

"Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," the company wrote.

"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," it added.

Binance said it will share more technical details once the investigation is complete and when the facts are "fully verified."

"Our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," the company wrote in a separate post earlier Thursday.

Binance also said all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while it conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement.

Stablecoin providers Tether and Circle each said they froze funds Thursday in response to the incident.

Jeremy Allaire, co-founder and CEO of Circle, wrote on X that the company had frozen the equivalent of more than $800 million in currency associated with the incident "in coordination with law enforcement." Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X that the company froze the equivalent of more than $1.5 billion in currency related to "a potential Binance exchange hack."

Sponsor Message

The price of bitcoin dropped 3.2% Thursday evening to under $79,000.

Binance was founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who in 2023 pleaded guilty to a felony related to his failure to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as CEO. President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.

Zhao posted on X on Thursday that "User funds are safe!" but added that the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

Zhao was released from prison last year after being sentenced for violating the Bank Secrecy Act. He was the first person ever sentenced to prison time for violations of that law, which requires U.S. financial institutions to know who their customers are, to monitor transactions and to file reports of suspicious activity. Prosecutors said no one had ever violated the regulations to the extent Zhao did. Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of some of the Trump family's crypto enterprises.

Before it was shut down, the Veterans Affairs Servicing Purchase (VASP) program, created under the Biden administration, helped tens of thousands of veterans who had fallen behind on their payments by rolling missed payments into a new, low-interest mortgage. The mortgage industry and housing groups warned the administration not to kill the program without first creating a viable replacement. Without one, vets had to modify loans at higher interest rates. An NPR investigation found that more than 15,000 veterans experienced monthly payment increases of at least $150 after their loans were modified due to financial hardship. More than 700 veterans saw their payments rise by $1,000 or more.

Sponsor Message

Behind the story

by Rob Stein , NPR's science desk correspondent and senior editor

Mary Long/Getty Images

I've been doing stories about the organ transplantation system for decades. One of the most fundamental guiding ethical principles in organ donation has long been the "dead donor rule." That rule, stated simply, says: Organs should only be retrieved for transplants from a person who is dead, and death should never be accelerated to try to boost the chances their organs will be usable. To make sure that's the case, there's long been a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital, and the organ retrieval teams standing by to try to procure their organs.

But over the years, I've heard many stories from family members who nevertheless felt pressured to donate their loved one's organs. So when I got a tip that the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network, which runs the nation's organ system, was planning to relax that firewall, I instantly knew that was a big story.

I rushed to confirm the documentation that the network's board of directors had indeed endorsed the change, which would go into effect Nov. 18. I then reached out to bioethicists and others for their reaction to this major change. The revision was part of a set of new policies designed to boost donations and improve patient safety. Those changes were spurred by disturbing revelations about mistakes, including patients literally being wheeled into the operating room to remove their organs when they were still alive. Some of the changes were praised as improving safety. But many bioethicists and even some transplant surgeons and patient and organ donation advocates say relaxing the firewall between care and organ retrieval teams is dangerous. The fear is it could lead to families and caregivers discontinuing treatment too soon, and deepening distrust in the organ donation system.

World.title: The two most interesting risks to Anthropic
World.content:
The two most interesting risks to Anthropic

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

A TILE GAME is giving a boost to Chinese factories. Our very own Jennifer Pak reported that Chinese manufacturers have not had the easiest few years with U.S. tariffs and the war in Iran pushing up costs. Well, the aged game of Mahjong is giving them a surprising boost. That's because it's having a moment in the U.S. and some entrepreneurial citizens in China are enjoying the benefits. Mahjong sets can sell for like $300-$400 in the States … and want to know how much they cost to make? ~$30. One businessman said he used to make the game primarily for Chinese consumers. Now, every set is exported to the U.S.

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America

Coming up:



The risks to Anthropic's (and AI's) business

Why we're saying 'buyout' and not 'layoff'

How young people are doing with AI summaries

New's We're Watching

The two most interesting risks to Anthropic - U.S. Securities & Exchange Commission

What to Know: Anthropic gave the world 94 pages of risks to its business (slash the entire AI economy) in its IPO prospectus aka the S-1. It wouldn't be Anthropic if they didn't discuss the "existential risks" to humanity and society several times. And isn't that an important risk to disclose? Another that stood out: the AI boom has a glaring point of failure. The majority of advanced semiconductor manufacturing is concentrated in one place, Taiwan, and if anything were to happen there, it could disrupt the entire AI economy. Think earthquake, Chinese military action, blockades. But I want to focus on a different risk, because it is FASCINATING!

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images North America

Committing to the past at a premium: Anthropic is worried about aging out of the tech that's powering its AI, while paying the same prices. What does that mean?! AI companies have to lock into pricey contracts for all sorts of softwares, hardware, data center, and squadrons of GPUs. But technology is advancing quickly right now. New GPUs, for example, could come along that can do the same amount of work for way less money. Then Anthropic is stuck like CHUMPS in a contract paying a premium for old hardware, while some competitors may be doing more for less.

Why buyouts and not layoffs? - The Wall Street Journal

What To Know: Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its staff this week. And doesn't that sound better than "Microsoft laid off 60,000 employees this week"?? Skydance ALSO offered a buyout to employees on Monday, though it's not clear how many would be eligible. And here at NPR, we've been a fan of the term buyout too. So what's the real difference in offering a buyout versus just laying off staffers?

The difference: Morale? Morale. There's something about a "mega-layoff" that doesn't inspire worker confidence. A "buyout" not so much. Really? Ok, I guess. The WSJ reported the focus in C-suite land is on the ratio of employees to AI agents inside companies. Companies have to find ways to pay for the ever-increasing costs of AI … and you know … actual human workers expect to be paid.

Andy Challenger, Chief Revenue Officer of Challenger, Gray & Christmas, a consulting firm, told the Journal that it can help staffers emotionally by making it a little easier to let go. It also tends to motivate older staffers to retire a little bit early, which may be the company's goal.

Today's Indicator

There are more bots than humans online. Here's what that means

If you HAVEN'T listened: I never thought I'd yearn for the days when the internet felt wholesome. Where you could go to blogs and random sites and make friends across the world. Well, more than half of internet traffic now comes from non-humans, aka bots. They're pouring into the digital veins of the World Wide Web, ignoring a lot of ads, generating all kinds of comments, nonsense and what have you. One interesting takeaway: this shift from human-to-bot traffic changes the business model of the internet. If humans let bots do their shopping for them, then ads suddenly become less useful. And if ads don't pay out for websites, then who pays for them?

Comment: After listening to today's episode of The Indicator, I had to write y'all. I'm a substitute teacher for middle school students in a public school district. This district serves mostly upper middle class students. I recently had a class of 8th graders given a research assignment. Seems pretty easy (enter the topic in Google, read some websites) so I was surprised when students began complaining that "everything is blocked". Pretty disheartening and hard not to blame Google for forcing AI on all users/introducing the summaries in the first place!
