World.title: Democrats seek to weaken the Republican lead in state legislatures
World.content:
Democrats seek to weaken the Republican lead in state legislatures

toggle caption i Aimee Dilger/AP

While races for Congress or governors' mansions may dominate the airwaves, some of the most competitive and significant contests are farther down the ballot.

More than 6,100 seats are up for election in state legislatures, which make most of the laws on education, taxes, reproductive rights, crime and social media access, among other things.

"The fact of the matter is the day in, day out basis, state governments, state lawmakers, state governors have a greater impact on our everyday lives than what takes place in Washington, D.C.," said John Kennedy, a political science professor at West Chester University in Pennsylvania.

Sponsor Message

Republicans control the legislature in 28 states, while Democrats have control of 18 legislatures. The remaining four are divided or run under power-sharing deals.

Both parties are sizing up their prospects

Committees for both national parties are picking their races to promote, with Democrats trying to seize on the anti-incumbent mood and low popularity of President Trump.

"By taking advantage of this once-in-a-generation opportunity and environment to build power, we can capture new majorities," said the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee in listing its target districts around the country.

The Republican State Leadership Committee acknowledged in an April strategy memo that 2026 poses, "a political environment that is likely to be one of the most challenging for state Republicans in recent years." It said it's taking a "defensive-first posture" to hold onto seats already held by the GOP.

Democrats are pouring millions of dollars into trying to flip Republican-held chambers in several states, especially Wisconsin, Michigan, Arizona, New Hampshire, Minnesota and Pennsylvania.

That would give some Democratic governors greater power to pass their policy priorities or let Democrats block GOP initiatives.

The elections for Pennsylvania's divided legislature highlight the stakes

For example, in Arizona Republicans hold a four-seat majority in the state Senate and a six-seat advantage in the House of Representatives, giving Democrats a chance to take one or both chambers. If they take both, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs, if she wins reelection, would have an easier time implementing blocked efforts, such as rolling back school vouchers and appointing agency leaders.

Sponsor Message

In other states, Democrats are simply looking to reduce Republican power or break the supermajorities that prevent Democratic governors from vetoing their bills, like in North Carolina and Kansas (if Democrats hold the governor's office there).

The potential for a party shift may be the most pronounced in Pennsylvania, where Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, is in a constant policy battle with a split legislature where Democrats hold a slim majority in the state House but Republicans hold a four-seat majority in the Senate.

Democrats have not won a trifecta — full control of the state's executive and legislative branches — in more than 30 years. It could come down to the results of a few close state Senate races in the Philadelphia suburbs.

The incumbent Shapiro, running for reelection, is already making a list of what he hopes to accomplish "in the first 30 days" if that happens.

"We're going to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour," he said at a campaign rally. "I'll tell you what else we're going to do — we will codify abortion rights into law in the commonwealth of Pennsylvania. I'll tell you what else we're going to do — we're going to build more affordable housing and take on those utility companies that keep jacking up our rates here in Pennsylvania."

While abortion is legal in Pennsylvania, Democrats want to reduce restrictions and add language that would make it clearer and less subject to judicial interpretation. Republican lawmakers have blocked those moves.

Republican candidate says Shapiro should work more across the aisle

Kennedy said Shapiro would try to do a lot with a Democratic legislature.

"Part of his whole image … has been he's someone who gets things done," he said. "And so I suspect if they have the opportunity, there's going to be nothing short of a very ambitious agenda."

Shapiro's Republican challenger, state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, has accused the governor of using the divided legislature as an "excuse" for not getting things done.

Sponsor Message

"The governor has consistently said … he can't do anything because he has a divided legislature," she said during their only public debate. "Well, that's not what real leadership is. Real leadership — they call the leaders to the table, and you negotiate."

The winners could use redistricting to reinforce their gains

In other states, Democrats are looking to create a bulwark against the ability of Republican governors to push through legislation. In New Hampshire, they hope to win a majority in the 400-member state House of Representatives, thereby providing a check on Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who's running for reelection.

If Democrats gain ground, it will counter a successful years-long strategy by the GOP. Kennedy explained that the shift toward Republican-held chambers stems from the 2010 midterm cycle, when they made sweeping gains in state legislatures. That gave Republicans the power to solidify their hold through redistricting.

And after the rush of mid-decade congressional redistricting before the 2026 elections, some legislatures might turn toward redistricting their own chambers in the next election cycle.

Carmen Russell-Sluchansky covers politics for WHYY.

World.title: Trump tried to hurt Canada with tariffs. In Michigan's Senate race, they may hurt him more
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Michigan’s Senate race is among the most hotly contested in the U.S. midterm elections, and the turning point may centre on a campaign ad in which the Republican candidate holds a Canadian beer.

"Drinking a Labatt and cheering on the Red Wings — it doesn’t get more Michigan than that," proclaims Mike Rogers, acknowledging the symbolic ties between the cross-border neighbours.

Then the ad quickly turns to the issue that has come to dominate the state’s tight political race.

"Here in Michigan, we know Canada is not our enemy," Rogers says, before stressing "we need to end this tariff war now."

WATCH | Mike Rogers' tariff war ad:

By doing so, Rogers did what few Republicans have: directly repudiated Donald Trump’s trade war. It's an act that would have been unthinkable just months ago.

Tariffs are felt across Michigan’s economy, particularly its signature industry. Many auto parts and vehicles made north of the border face a 25 per cent levy when they enter the United States. In the new year, that number will jump to 50 per cent, unless the two countries can strike a new trade deal.

Michigan's auto manufacturers have been hammered, causing Detroit’s biggest firms to hemorrhage money — and increase the price of a new car. By one estimate, Trump’s tariffs have added $5,700 US to cars built in the highly integrated cross-border sector.

Even for those not in the market for a new car, the National Taxpayers Union finds tariffs have cost the average American family $6,000 each year.

At the start, President Trump claimed other countries would pay those extra costs. But Americans increasingly don’t believe that. Polling conducted by the libertarian CATO Institute finds 75 per cent of respondents say tariffs will be important to how they vote in the midterms.

"We want more manufacturing," said Glenn Stevens of the automotive industry lobby group MichAuto. "But we do not want that at the expense of our partnership and our trade relationship with Canada."

While his organization seeks to be non-partisan, he knows the Senate race in Michigan is so close that "it is going to swing probably on 10,000 votes." And politicians are "trying to get to that undecided voter."

Michigan trades heavily with Ontario

Poll after poll shows the top issue for Michigan voters is the cost of living.

"A lot of people still don't understand tariffs," said longtime Michigan pollster Ed Saropolus. But now they’ll say, "'I know they're not good for my bottom line.'"

Trump’s problem has become the problem of every Republican candidate — especially those in states that are highly reliant on trade with Canada.

Republican strategist Jason Roe said 'there is no question the president has hurt himself' politically in Michigan with the tariffs on Canadian goods. (Perlita Stroh/CBC)

Michigan does more business with Ontario than it does with virtually every other U.S. state.

"We probably feel the effects of the trade fight with Canada more than any other state," Republican strategist Jason Roe told CBC News on a visit to the state this month. "There is no question the president has hurt himself" politically in Michigan.

"Control of Congress and control of the Senate could very well be decided right here in Michigan. We have three competitive congressional seats. Democrats only need four [nationally]."

It's a tight race between Rogers and Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, with both parties and associated political action groups spending hundreds of millions of dollars in the campaign in Michigan alone.

Supporters of Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers go door-knocking in Lansing, Mich. (Turgut Yeter/CBC)

With the president’s national approval rating at a dismal 36 per cent, Republican candidates like Rogers are looking to create distance from Trump’s less-popular policies and actions.

That works its way into the message Rogers' supporters deliver when door-knocking across the state.

"Mike Rogers is working to look at the Canadian tariffs and see which ones are costing Michiganders and reduce those," Aiden Haas of the Michigan College Republicans told his team in mid-October as they set out to rally support while going door to door in Lansing.

El-Sayed: Trump tariffs are 'dumb'

Despite the tariff-related tension, the Trump-friendly network Fox News has been focusing on the Democratic candidate's religion.

There are near-daily segments pushing fears about El-Sayed, a charismatic physician who could become the first Muslim U.S. senator, should he win the state.

Republicans accuse him of being a socialist and radical Islamist. He rejects both claims regularly.

In television ads, El-Sayed has called Trump’s tariffs "dumb." He has said he supports targeted tariffs to restore Michigan manufacturing, but calls the action against Canada "a vanity trade war that Donald Trump has decided to inflict upon all of us for no clear, observable reason."

Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is putting U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada on the ballot in Michigan in the midterms. (Sylvia Thomson/CBC)

Amid this trade tension, the personal attacks on El-Sayed have kept the race competitive, with polling suggesting a near-even split in support between the two candidates.

Michigan has only elected Democratic senators in the last 26 years. But it did vote for Trump by a 1.5 per cent margin in 2024. Where goes Michigan, often so goes the United States, in its politics.

Strategist Roe, no fan of the president, says he’s tried to stay optimistic about the chances for Republican congressional candidates in Michigan.

But he says "it's hard when one of the focal points of our messaging in 2024 was we were going to lower the cost of living, to now be in a situation in which the cost of living is obviously very difficult for most Michiganders to navigate."

World.title: Carney says, unequivocally, Canada seeking to become the EU's 1st associate member
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is working to become the European Union's first associate member, his most definitive statement on the issue to date after hosting the bloc's leaders in Montreal this week.

It still remains unclear what that would look like and cost.

This year's Canada-EU summit saw Canada and European officials finalize a number of negotiations and launch a long list of new commitments as part of a deeper alliance, but the issue of what to call the allies' deeper partnership has somewhat overshadowed the work between Ottawa and the 27-member bloc given some members are against the proposal.

"We are working toward the deepest possible partnership, short of accession because of our geography, with Canada becoming the European Union's first associate member," said Carney in his closing remarks.

"Over the coming months, we will determine the substance, scale and scope of this form of membership."

WATCH | Canada and EU launching 'alliance for the future,' Carney says: Canada and EU launching 'alliance for the future,' Carney says | Duration closed caption 1:22 Standing with the presidents of the European Commission and European Council in Montreal, Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada and the EU are 'working towards the deepest possible partnership, short of accession… with Canada becoming the European Union’s first associate member.'

Carney previously stayed away from using the "associate member" title, instead arguing the nomenclature doesn't matter.

By Friday, though, he he added a timeline to the debate, saying the plan is to conclude negotiations in June, when he'll join European Council meetings.

He also said he, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa will convene the College of the European Commissioners and Canada's federal cabinet in March.

Von der Leyen first raised the prospect of making Canada an associate member — a status that doesn't currently exist in the bloc — in a speech last month and has continued to spearhead the initiative despite objections from some members, notably Germany.

No talk of cost

Speaking on background after the news conference, a Canadian official couldn't answer what what legislation would be needed in Canada and across the EU member states.

"It's a concept," the official said, noting there's no existing formal process to becoming an associate member.

Asked what the cost of joining as an associate member could be, Carney said "we don't view this as paying for something, we view this as coming together."

While von der Leyen, Costa and Carney are all now championing the title, it's far from a done deal. EU members would have to vote, and Carney has said a new partnership with the European Union will be put up for debate and a vote in Canada's Parliament.

"Canada is by far the most European of the non-European countries," Costa said on Friday morning.

Canada-EU sign agreements

Division over what to call the partnership was apparent in the crafting of the joint statement released at the end of the summit.

Sources with knowledge of what happened said the "associate member" term was removed from the draft version, given some members' disapproval. One source said Germany called it a red line. Instead, the final document calls for "an ever-closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself."

Outside of the title, the document makes clear Ottawa and Brussels have lots to agree on as they move ahead on what's being dubbed the "alliance for the future"

On Friday the two sides announced they finished negotiations between Canada and the European Investment Bank to support investment in critical Canadian resources, notably critical raw materials and another on countermeasures to fight anti-competitive activity.

They also wrapped negotiations on a digital trade agreement between the EU and Canada meant to improve legal certainty and facilitate cross-border data flows, as well as finalized an agreement giving Canadian researchers and businesses access to European supercomputers.

Canada will also join a EU program for aid to Ukraine, called Ukraine Support Loan.

When it comes to next steps, the two sides have agreed to expand opportunities for Canadians and Europeans to study, work and conduct research. There's also a promise to launch talks to secure international connectivity between Canada, Europe and Asia through new subsea cable infrastructure.

The document includes commitment on a long list of other areas, including the Arctic, foreign information manipulation and interference and advancing co-operation on artificial intelligence (AI) security and safety.

It also calls for reforming the World Trade Organization instead of replacing it, and doing more on border security and fighting climate change.

"It means, at its base, sovereignty," said Carney. "Greater resilience [and the] ability to withstand shocks together."

But it is unclear how much all the new programs will cost either.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne dodged questions on Thursday, saying Canadians should see only “opportunities.”

WATCH | EU chief revisits 'associate membership' for Canada: EU chief floats 'association without accession' for Canada | Duration closed caption 0:58 After Canada's 'associate membership' of the EU was reportedly removed from a proposed joint statement on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen mentioned the idea again on Thursday, suggesting a partnership 'that comes closer to membership than anything we've done before.'

Canada's Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre called the summit a "grand theatrical meeting to sign a bunch of meaningless declarations filled with big words."

"No one's mortgage or grocery bill will come down," he posted on social media earlier this week.

Carney points to EU's strong belief in democracy

The summit was billed as a way to deepen ties with like-minded leaders in the wake of an unpredictable and volatile White House under U.S. President Donald Trump.

While the three leaders in Montreal were in step around their common goals, shifting political winds on the continent could test that alliance, notably in France and Germany — both heavyweights within the bloc.

In France, presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally is leading in polls ahead of the spring 2027 election. Le Pen, an advocate for strict immigration limits, has criticized the EU-Canada trade pact.

In Germany, the far-right and isolationist Alternative for Germany (AfD) continues to gain ground in regional parliaments and national polls.

Asked Thursday if he has concerns about dealing with a potentially different political makeup, Carney praised the EU's adherence to democratic values.

"One of Europe's strengths is democracy, freedom and a core belief in the rule of law. There will always be different governments, governments of different stripes in Europe," he told reporters.

"Over the course of decades, the European Union has continued to develop, and strengthen, throughout, and be enriched by the national democratic processes of those countries."

Carney also downplayed the notion he was looking to secure commitments with the EU before the French election. "We're not tying it to any political cycle, but to the fundamentals of what they deliver … for Canadians," he said.

Asked earlier this week about the summit potentially attracting retaliation from Trump or right-wing leaders in Europe, a senior Canadian government official told reporters the gathering isn't directed against anyone, but reflected deep interests between Canada and the EU.

World.title: 'You can't just get out': How 2 boys were recruited into the drug trade at the age of 12
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Kai was 12 years old when he began to warn his mother he might not make it home.

"[If] I don't make it home by four o'clock, just know that I got snatched and somebody put me in their car and kidnapped me," he would tell her.

His mother, whom CBC's the fifth estate is calling Aria for her protection, moved her family to another city when Kai was a boy to disconnect from his father, who had a criminal past and street associations.

She enrolled Kai, whose name has also been changed for his protection, in community centres and drop-in spaces in Winnipeg to keep him busy and away from trouble

But Aria believes those spaces exposed her son to people who would exploit him.�

Watch the full documentary, "Missing Boys: Lured into Danger," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m .

She believes some staff abused their positions, allowing gang members to manipulate her son and coerce him into the drug trade — sending him thousands of kilometres away from home.

Fifth estate host Mark Kelley, left, sits down with a boy who was recruited by a gang when he was 12. He says he has been sent out of town to sell drugs more times than he can count. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Kai said men in their 20s and 30s presented themselves as people he could trust.

"People call it grooming, people call it using. There's many words for it, but it's just being taken advantage of because you're innocent," Kai said.

For the last two years, the fifth estate has investigated the disappearances of young Black boys from the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) who are groomed and lured into drug trafficking networks in Ontario cities as far away as Sarnia and Thunder Bay, and sent further north into Indigenous communities like Ginoogaming, a First Nation.

Now, the fifth estate has heard directly from boys who live this dangerous life and say they were sent across the country to sell drugs, revealing a network that reaches even farther.

We now know of this activity taking boys as young as 12 as far west as British Columbia, as far north as Yellowknife and as far east as Halifax — places where drugs are sold at exponentially higher prices — up to 10 times the price in some cases.

The business of going OT

In an interview with CBC's the fifth estate, Kai recounts his first trip out of town, also known as “going OT,” when he was 12.

"You don't know what's in those bags. You don't know what you're delivering for people … you just think, 'I'm helping the older guy, because I want to be cool like him,'" he said.

Kai said the older men picked him up, told him where he would stay and expected him to sell drugs. He was left in a remote community eight hours north of his home in Winnipeg.

LISTEN: The Missing Boys: When It All Went Wrong

Kai said he did not fully understand what he was getting into. He had to figure it out in a place where he did not know anyone and his family was out of reach.

"You're not telling family members," he said. "Because not only do they not know where you are, you don't know where you are."

The first trip taught him more about what he calls the rules of "the game," where the three outcomes are freedom, jail or death.

And he says he was forced to gamble for the gangs.

"You can't just get out ... whoever sent you there is expecting you to come back with a prize," Kai said. "And if you don't come back with anything … God forbid something happens to you."

Now 14, Kai has made more trips out of town than he can count.

WATCH | Sent north by gangs: On the front line of the drug trade | Duration closed caption 0:49 Kai, not his real name, 14, says he has been sent by gangs to remote northern communities where drugs can sell for 10 times the price.

Jamal, another teenager whose name has been changed for his safety, started going OT at 12. He had been away from home for more than a week and his mom reported him missing.

The now-18-year-old who lives in the Toronto area said he has been sent to communities in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario.

Jamal's farthest trip took him to Yellowknife. He was even convinced to pay his own way.

Like Kai, Jamal said it was in Grade 7 when he was first approached to work for a gang. His family had spent a year bouncing between houses and he grew close to older people in his neighbourhood who were often around his cousins.

"I always just had the respect and looked at them like an older role model," he said.

Jamal said those role models could offer him an escape from the instability at home.

"If things were stable at home, I wouldn't really have a reason to go outside," he said.

Jamal said the adults he worked for were selling drugs bought internationally — and worked with cartels.

Then Jamal tells the fifth estate how the boys cross the country — a key piece of information — as many families are baffled as to how their boys are boarding planes and driving to remote locations when they are too young to have a driver's licence and don't have identification.

Jamal said fake names and identification are provided for them.

"It doesn't even matter who you are, how young you are. You can go anywhere in Canada," he said. "It's actually quite easy."

The adults behind the operation

The fifth estate previously found adult traffickers use the boys as disposable mules and legal shields that often take the fall when police make drug busts.

A 2026 federal Justice Department report found that the proportion of Black youth in correctional supervision in Nova Scotia, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia remained at around 12 to 13 per cent from 2019 to 2024. That's almost two times more than their combined share of the population for that age group, across all four provinces.

Black boys often face well-known socio-economic challenges including high unemployment , and bias within justice and educational systems that can make them more vulnerable to the pull of organized crime.

"Many of these [youths] are exploited … they're seen as disposable to the people who are running these networks," said Winnipeg police Insp. Josh Ewatski.

Winnipeg police Insp. Josh Ewatski tells the fifth estate the drugs supplied by gangs have been linked to international cartels. Young boys are often used for street-level dealing so gang members don't have to expose themselves to violence or being arrested. (Oliver Walters/CBC)

In May, Ewatski led a team involved in what police called Manitoba's largest drug bust. Investigators seized 525 kilograms of cocaine, methamphetamine and fentanyl in Winnipeg.

Those arrested included people associated with Canada's highest ranks of organized crime including the Hells Angels, Wolfpack Alliance and a Mexican cartel.

"Most of the drugs of cocaine and methamphetamine will come from Mexico up to the U.S. and into Canada," Ewatski said.

He described a sophisticated network where multiple drug trafficking organizations are working together to move drugs into remote communities.

He says it's associates of these international criminal networks who are recruiting and using boys.

For more on the story, listen to "The Missing Boys," a four-episode series on the new CBC podcast When it All Went Wrong.

Ewatski said boys are used for street-level dealing and to work in stash houses. He said they often don't know who they are working for.

"These kids are used so [those running the networks] don't have to expose themselves to being arrested or being shot."

Leaving a gang can be just as dangerous. Ewatski said some boys become trapped by debts they are told they owe their recruiters.

“If they're out, they're going to be out in a violent way," he said. "Possibly even dead."

Denny Heathen, a reformed gang member, now counsels youth and leads prayer circles in his community of Prince Albert, Sask. (Shelley Ayres/CBC)

Denny Heathen spent much of his 20s working for a gang in Prince Albert, Sask. He said some recruiters targeted boys between 15 to 18 and told us that the boys who were targeted had a look of desperation.

"They wanted purpose," Heathen said.

Recruiters offered attention, money and the promise of protection, presenting themselves as brothers or older mentors.

"These are puppets," he said. "You just got to make them feel like they're appreciated, like they are going to be taken care of."

WATCH | A price for getting out: What it takes to get out of a gang | Duration closed caption 0:24 A former gang member tells boys in the drug trade that getting out will come with a price.

Kai remembers the grooming process well.

“You're a little kid in a community centre trying to play basketball and then you see these guys … walking around with the large prize in their hand."

The prize was money — an amount that felt impossible to a boy too young to get his first job.

During his interview with the fifth estate, Kai pulled out a thick stack of $100 bills to demonstrate how quickly money could influence a boy to sell drugs.

"All it takes is this and you're influenced."

He said the amounts involved can be enormous in First Nations communities where an oxycodone pill can sell for $200.

"That substance that is being put in these boys' pockets and these boys' hands to go deal over the province … people will do anything for."

The boy who never came home

On March 27, 2025, Jay'siiah Webb-Long walked out of his family's home in Brampton, Ont., carrying a single duffel bag that appeared nearly empty.

Doorbell camera footage provided by the family to the fifth estate shows the 15-year-old placing a single box in the recycling bin on his front porch, scanning the street before disappearing out of frame.

His story made national headlines.

Jay'siiah Webb-Long, 15, was last seen outside his home in Brampton, Ont. on March 27, 2025. (Saskatchewan RCMP)

"Somebody had sent me photos after his disappearance," said Shenice Long, his mother.

"She had sent photos of him holding stacks of money. So, at that point, I said, 'OK, somebody has sent him far out … to make money.'"

Long said she remained in contact with her son for weeks after he left home. But he would not tell her where he was.

Jay'siiah's family told the fifth estate they are frustrated with action from Peel Regional Police and the RCMP in Saskatchewan, citing for example that it took Peel police eight weeks to alert the public that Jay'siiah was missing.

Long said police used a phone number she never had for her son to trace his location to Pelican Narrows, Sask., a northern community about 3,000 kilometres from his home in Brampton. This number only surfaced when the public alert came out and a young woman came forward.

"I heard of Saskatchewan, but … I don't have family there. I don't know anyone there," Long said.

In July 2025, Saskatchewan RCMP took over the file as a homicide investigation. They didn't alert the public of this shift until September 2025.

Police told the family a search was delayed by winter weather. In the spring, investigators told the family they planned to search near Pelican Narrows — led with cadaver dogs.

Pelican Narrows, Sask., a community of about 4,000 and located about 500 kilometres north of Saskatoon, is part of the Peter Ballantyne Cree Nation. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

On May 13, human remains were found near a sewage lagoon just outside the community. An autopsy confirmed two days later that the remains belonged to Webb-Long.

RCMP believe his death was a homicide. The investigation is ongoing and no charges have been laid in connection with his death.

Missing — and not always reported

In 2024, 322 male youth were reported missing to Toronto police. Statistics Canada data shows Black boys account for almost half of those missing, despite representing less than 10 per cent of the city's population of that age group.

The fifth estate has found not every family reports their youth missing. In the case of Jay'siiah Webb-Long, his mother didn't file a formal report until three weeks after he had left home. She told the fifth estate she had called Peel Regional Police after 48 hours but they dissuaded her because she was still in contact with him.

"One youth missing is too [many]," said Christene Lewis, who is a violence intervention specialist and works with families in Toronto and surrounding areas. She supports many families who have youth that go missing and go "OT." It's a life she knows because she lived it.

"I come from the gang culture," Lewis said. "I come from feeling isolated, I've come from feeling like the streets were more loyal to me than my own family was."

Christene Lewis, a violence intervention specialist, works with families in Toronto and surrounding areas who have youth who go missing. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Lewis said some parents hesitate reporting their child missing because they fear their kids will be treated as runaways rather than young people at risk. Others feel shame and embarrassment.

Lewis said there is also a breakdown of trust between marginalized communities and police.

"They don't feel like the police even care."

Lewis's advice to parents: Always report a missing kid and keep following up.

"If they didn't hear you the first day, call the next day," she said. "Don't give up."

WATCH | Parents urged to be vigilant: A message for parents of missing kids | Duration closed caption 0:30 A woman who works with the families of missing kids says they should stay vigilant and always report to police.

Aria remembers when it first became clear her son had gone to a First Nations community to sell drugs.

"He was telling stories like he came back from camp," she said.

He would leave home sporadically, returning home with designer clothing and money.

Aria said she has also had the windows of her home shot at three times.

Now, when Kai goes missing, she reports him and collects evidence that might help police locate him.

"This is not something you make peace with," she said. "This is something that's wrong."

'Nobody's just going to let you go'

Jamal said the people who recruited him continue to contact him and tell him he owes them money.

''They're going to keep texting you, telling you that they got this opportunity … nobody's just going to let you just go."

Kai has also tried to leave. He spent the summer away at camp and returned determined to get out of gang life.

"Now that I realize what kind of hell on earth is like … I never want to go back there," he told the fifth estate in August.

But Aria said the messages continued.

She found text messages about Kai from a sibling that read: "I will not be returning your little bro" and "he's my slave.”

She believes the messages are proof her son is being trafficked.

Aria, a Winnipeg mother whose name has been changed for protection, worries gangs will never loosen their grip on her son. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Kai left home again the night before he was set to start Grade 10. He returned home and left again several times.

Aria fears that even if Kai manages to break free from the gangs, they will continue to chase and manipulate him, tempting him with money and a sense of belonging.

Kai is facing drug trafficking charges.

"This monster exists and it's going to exist on his path as a young man, as an adult," Aria said. "I don't think that this monster ever goes away."

World.title: Dune 3 popcorn buckets are even more unhinged than the original
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Remember when Dune: Part Two gave the world that suggestive popcorn bucket that stopped you in your tracks and made you wonder: is this even allowed? Well, it's back. And this time it brought a friend.

Yes, you read that right. The movie merchandise widely deemed to be NSFW is making a comeback ahead of Dune: Part Three. And movie theatre chains didn't dial it back. They've doubled down.

Clearly, simply putting popcorn in a bag just doesn't cut it anymore.

Riding the viral success of the last movie's merchandise, two new suggestive designs are being sold — and they've already got people talking.

First up is a "shareable" popcorn tub featuring not one, but two sandworms. According to American theatre chain AMC, the design makes it "easier to share."

Cineplex is also rolling out an updated version of the original single-worm bucket, complete with a functional vibrating 'sandworm thumper'. (Cineplex)

And if two sandworms weren't enough to get the internet talking, Cineplex is also rolling out an updated version of the original single-worm bucket, complete with a functional "sandworm thumper."

For anyone who hasn't seen the film, a thumper is the device used to pound the desert and attract giant sandworms. The best (or worst) part of the sandworm thumper bucket? It has a working design: this one vibrates. Yes, you read that correctly.

The memes are so back

The original popcorn bucket kicked off countless memes when it dropped in 2024. Director Denis Villeneuve, in an interview with the New York Times, said his reaction to the bucket was: "Hoooooly smokes. What the [expletive]!?"

It even inspired a sketch on Saturday Night Live, which featured a teenager with a rather unconventional use for the popcorn bucket — proving everyone on the internet was thinking the exact same thing.

Naturally, fans took zero time reacting to the latest designs, flooding social feeds with unhinged memes and 18+ reactions.

For this story's purposes, we're keeping it PG. You can dive into that wormhole at your own risk.

"What if we both reached for more popcorn and accidentally touched hands inside the DUNE: PART 3 popcorn bucket 👉🏻👈🏻 >.<🩵✨" one user wrote on X . "Holding my wife's hand in the Dune 3 popcorn bucket, you sick freaks should take notes," another joked.

Over on Instagram, the comment sections were just as suggestive as you might've guessed.

"Double the worms double the fun," one user commented on Cineplex's post.

"Ya'll play too much 😂." said another. "Me ordering 12 of them 🧐🧐🧐," a third added.

Movie theatres have been selling novelty popcorn tins and containers for years. But the success of the previous Dune bucket seemingly inspired theatre chains to get more creative — and increasingly outrageous — with the designs.

Other notable mentions include: an entirely transparent bucket for You Can See Everything; a giant dinosaur footprint bucket for Jurassic Park Rebirth; a Trojan horse bucket for The Odyssey; and a red purse for The Devil Wears Prada 2.

Hitting theatres December 18, Dune: Part Three continues the sci-fi saga based on Frank Herbert's novels.

World.title: Feds tap Delta, B.C., port expansion as 'project of national interest'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government has listed Roberts Bank Terminal 2 in Delta, B.C., as a "project of national interest" to expand and diversify Canada's trade capacity.

In a news release, the government said the listing will give the project the "immediate regulatory certainty" it needs to be built at the Port of Vancouver, while keeping environmental safeguards and holding consultation with Indigenous communities.

The project, which is a proposed three-berth container terminal at Roberts Bank, will be led by the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority.

A final investment decision is expected by mid-2027, according to the release.

The national interest designation, the release says, "accelerates the project's commercial operations by up to four years, from 2039 to 2035."

The Roberts Bank Terminal 2 project is expected to add 2.4 million containers of annual capacity at the port, increasing container capacity at the Port of Vancouver by about 50 per cent.

The government said the project will support about 17,000 jobs across Canada's supply chains and contribute about $3 billion annually to the national GDP.

The port authority has selected TerraMarine as its preferred construction partner after a competitive procurement process.

More to come.

World.title: 'The woman from the hole': Winnipegger's comical quandary becomes Halloween costume
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Christine Keilback might just have the greatest sense of humour ever.

She laughed off her misfortune after plunging shoulder-deep into a hole in the boulevard near her Winnipeg home in April — a predicament that brought out emergency crews and led to media coverage.

Now she's getting a howl out of a Halloween costume inspired by it all.

"It's so lighthearted and it's such a good spoof on what happened. I mean, how could I not be happy to see that? It's been fun," Keilback said.

On Thursday she met Vanessa Desorcy, who was dressed as a Keilback lookalike — from the jacket, hair and eyeglasses right down to a leaf-covered ring at her armpits filling the role as hole.

Keilback maintained her sense of humour even after the earth opened up beneath her. (Submitted by Lynda Regan)

"I'm absolutely thrilled to meet Vanessa. I'm so glad to have this opportunity, because it made my day," Keilback said outside her house after embracing Desorcy .

"It was so funny. I laughed and laughed, and it was, it was the best. [Her] attention to detail on the costume, I mean … were we separated at birth? Maybe."

Keilback, 58, was out with friends in the evening of April 25. When they dropped her off, she dropped out of sight.

Keilback had stepped into a small hole that suddenly widened and collapsed farther as she fell. She tried to boost herself out, but every foothold crumbled away.

One of her friends ran for a broom and shovel to span the gap and give her a brace to hook her arms around.

"In the beginning I was afraid … because the perimeter of the hole was falling away. So that scared me," Keilback said, reflecting back.

But once she realized she was safe and unhurt, and fire rescue folks were on the way, the absurdity of it all hit.

The Winnipeg Fire Paramedic Service's technical rescue task force uses a frame and winch to rescue Keilback. (Submitted by Lynda Regan)

Keilback posed for pics with her friends before the rescue task force used a frame and winch and straps to lift her out.

In all, she was in the hole for about 40 minutes.

Keilback's sense of humour about it all radiated across interviews, from local media to international coverage by People.com and the BBC.

The story popped back into Desorcy's head a few days ago while brainstorming for a Halloween costume for her work party.

"I remember reading the story when it happened, and it just brought me so much joy — of course, as soon as I knew that she was fine. It was amazing, and she had such a good outlook on it," Desorcy said as Keilback stood by with a beaming smile.

"And so in the last couple of days, it all just came together [as a costume]."

Desorcy, left, shares a laugh with her costume influencer, Keilback. (Randall McKenzie/CBC)

One of her co-workers knew immediately who she was, but a couple others were confused initially, Desorcy said.

"So I crouched down and did the smile and then they got it right away: 'You're the woman from the hole,'" she said.

"I love stories like that. They just make hard days feel lighter and they make everything more fun."

That's also why Keilback's story was featured as #TheMoment on CBC's The National with Adrienne Arsenault shortly after it happened.

"I could not have been happier to have that happen, to have Adrienne Arsenault say your name out loud — and it was for falling in a hole. Like, not for any sort of contribution I made to the community or anything," Keilback laughed. "I fell in a hole and I was a good sport about it.

"But still, I'll take it."

Keilback chats with emergency workers from a hole in front of her property on Lipton Street in Winnipeg in April. (Submitted by Lynda Regan)

Desorcy wasn't the only one who found inspiration in Keilback's amusing misfortune.

Keilback's next-door neighbour created a Halloween display on the front lawn. It's a skull and hands coming out of the ground, with broom handles and a sign reading "Help me."

"You gotta love neighbors. This is the best neighborhood to live in," Keilback said.

That was the first tribute she saw, and she figured it would be the only one.

"But Vanessa surprised me," she said.

After some more laughs and another hug, the women offered some advice for those traversing city boulevards and neighbourhoods this weekend.

Neighbours created this Halloween display in tribute to Christine Keilback. (Randall McKenzie/CBC)

"Have a good Halloween and watch out for holes," Desorcy said.

"Yeah, be safe. Stick to the sidewalk," Keilback added.

A spokesperson for the City of Winnipeg said the hole was due to a previously removed catch basin and lead.

A catch basin is a drainage structure that collects stormwater runoff and traps debris. The lead is the connecting pipe that transports water from the basin to a main line.

Crews found a similar situation on the opposite side of the road, where a second catch basin would have been located, the spokesperson said at the time.

World.title: A spacewalk to remember: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says seeing Earth 'changed' him
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk said he was overwhelmed with emotion looking at the Earth during a seven-hour spacewalk on Thursday.

"Your mind doesn't know what to do with that image," he said. "It's exciting."

Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon successfully installed seven of eight new solar panels on the International Space Station during the spacewalk. Kutryk became the fifth Canadian to perform such a feat.

Speaking to media as he floated inside the space station on Friday morning, Kutryk said the experience changed him. He said seeing the blue planet from the outside made him feel "very small" and "almost insignificant."

"[I feel] like I want to make every decision I make in my life going forward, and just try to be a better person, the best person I can," said Kutryk.

He described seeing the Earth while hovering in the vacuum of space as "very confusing" and "a sensory overload."

'A changed perspective'

He added that he was stunned by the beauty and fragility of the planet.

Kutryk, who was born in Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., said he could see his home province from space. He posted several photos of Canada as seen from the space station on social media.

"I do think that we come back to Earth with a changed perspective," he said.

He and Menon had to work in both the darkness of space and through blinding sunlight, on top of the distracting view of the Earth. He said his years of training paid off and the work went off without a hitch.

WATCH | A view inside the International Space Station: Joshua Kutryk's 1st spacewalk just part of Canada's huge day in space | Duration closed caption 1:59 A huge day for Canada's space program as Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk installed solar panels on the International Space Station in his first spacewalk, while fellow Canadian astronaut Jenni Gibbons worked on capsule communications.

This is Kutryk's first space mission. Before him, the last Canadian to perform a spacewalk was David Saint-Jacques in 2019.

Saint-Jacques led the news conference at the space agency's headquarters in Longueuil, Que., with Eleanor Olszewski, the minister responsible for Prairies Economic Development Canada.

Saint-Jacques said Kutryk is "a real role model for Canadian youth."

As an Albertan, Olszewski added that she felt "tremendous pride" seeing Kutryk make history.

Kutryk and his crew's mission is crucial, Saint-Jacques said, as the station is nearly 30 years old and its original solar panels have lost efficiency. According to agency, the new panels, paired with previously installed arrays, will help increase power generation capacity on the station by up to 30 per cent.

'Incredibly proud'

Mathieu Caron, director of the agency's astronauts, life sciences, and space medicine directorate, said the job couldn't have been done without Canada's decades-long contribution to space exploration.

Menon rode the Canadarm 2 robotic arm to perform the maintenance work. The spacewalkers also received support from the robotics team in Longueuil, where Canadian astronaut Jenni Gibbons gave the duo step-by-step instructions.

"We're all incredibly proud," said Caron.

While he tried to focus on the task at hand, Kutryk says he will make sure to take in the view during his second spacewalk next week, when he and Menon are scheduled to install the eighth solar panel.

World.title: 5 unforgettable Patrick Stewart performances as Jean-Luc Picard
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Patrick Stewart, who died Wednesday at the age of 86, had dozens of credits to his name on screen and stage over a more than 60-year career, but for many people he will always be Capt. Jean-Luc Picard, of the U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701-D.



Many Reddit threads and YouTube comments marking Stewart's death are mourning Picard as much as the real man.



"RIP Captain," one Reddit user posted. "You helped change my life for the better."

"Picard was an incredibly well-written and well-acted character that Stewart made real," replied another.



Though Picard had his moments in four movies and on the recent sequel show Star Trek: Picard, the very best moments of the character are all within the 176 episodes of Star Trek: The Next Generation, which ran from 1987 to 1994.

WATCH | Tributes pour in for Stewart: Tributes pour in for X-Men, Star Trek actor Patrick Stewart | Duration closed caption 2:22 Tributes are pouring in for actor Patrick Stewart, known to millions as Charles Xavier of X-Men, and Captain Jean-Luc Picard of Star Trek. Stewart died at age 86 after being diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia.



Here are five of Stewart's best Picard performances to seek out. (Warning: Spoilers in the descriptions.)

'Make now always the most precious time'

'The Inner Light,' Season 5, Episode 25

Often argued for as the best Star Trek episode of the almost 1,000 made so far, "The Inner Light" is a Stewart tour de force.



When an alien probe knocks the captain unconscious, he wakes up as a villager on a dying planet. In what passes for 25 minutes on the Enterprise, the childless Picard lives for four decades as a man named Kamin, aging before our eyes and raising two children to adulthood.

The entire episode is a masterpiece, but Stewart imbues simple moments of family with a ferocity and humanist integrity that has made many Trek fans weep.



"Seize the time, Meribor. Live now," he tells his adult daughter as they contemplate the imminent end of their planet. "Make now always the most precious time. Now will never come again."

'There are four lights!'

'Chain of Command,' Part II, Season 6, Episode 11

Stewart prepared for this episode, where Picard is brutally tortured, by reviewing tapes provided by Amnesty International, a group Stewart supported and spoke for.



Much of the episode is him alone in a room with another esteemed British actor, the late David Warner. Their scenes crackle with intensity as Cardassian officer (read: space Nazi) Gul Madred attempts to brainwash the captain into thinking there are five lights shining in the room, when there are in fact only four.



The episode offers a brutal depiction of suffering that Stewart throws his full body into. It also contains maybe the biggest "Hell yeah!" moment in the series when Picard refuses to break, yelling, "There are four lights!"



But even better is Stewart's haunted face in the final scene, when he admits the torture had worked, that he would have told his captor anything, and that "more than that, I believed that I could see five lights."

WATCH | Stewart dead at 86: Star Trek, X-Men actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86 | Duration closed caption 4:10 Patrick Stewart, the British stage actor who famously played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men, has died. The 86-year-old died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after 'a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,' according to a statement on his social media page.

'Shaka, when the walls fell'

'Darmok,' Season 5, Episode 2



Picard is captured on a planet by an alien race that cannot communicate clearly with humans.



Over the course of the episode, Picard and his crew come to realize that the Children of Tama speak entirely in metaphor, using phrases like "Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra" to mean "co-operation" and "Shaka, when the walls fell" to mean "failure."



Stewart shines twice: first, in a campfire scene, where he tells his alien counterpart the story of the Epic of Gilgamesh; second, when he saves the day by communicating with the Children of Tama's ship, speaking an invented language in a way that is nevertheless commanding and affecting.

Stewart signs a Star Trek: Deep Space Nine banner in Las Vegas on Aug. 14, 2005. Stewart played Picard in that spinoff's pilot. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)

'There is nothing left but dry bones ... dead friends'

'Sarek,' Season 3, Episode 23

This episode features Mark Lenard as the Vulcan Sarek, the father of Mr. Spock from the original 1966 Star Trek series.



Sarek is dying of the sci-fi equivalent of Alzheimer's disease and Picard joins minds with him so that the Vulcan can carry out one last mission. The mind-meld makes Sarek more stable, but floods Picard with a lifetime of repressed emotion.



In an almost four-minute scene, Stewart screams, rants, smiles, cries, fights, longs, regrets, embodies Sarek as portrayed by Lenard — and finally, crumples. It's impossible to look away.

Stewart in 1998's Star Trek: Insurrection. (Paramount Pictures/Getty Images)

'I would rather die as the man I was...'

'Tapestry,' Season 6, Episode 15

In Star Trek's take on It's a Wonderful Life, a dead Picard is visited in the afterlife by recurring guest antagonist Q, who offers him the chance to do his life over.



Stewart gets to play Picard as his usual self, as a brash, young ensign, and as an uncertain, middle-management version of himself that happens in Q's alternate reality.



Stewart caps it off by getting stabbed through the heart (as needs to happen in the "right" reality), looking at the blade and laughing. A scene that could have been hokey is not just believable, but exhilarating.

Episodes of Star Trek: The Next Generation are available to stream on Paramount+ in Canada.
