“We learned only in 1981 that a forced-labor camp had operated inside the museum during the final months of the occupation,” says Valentyna Avramenko, head of the Tarasova Svitlytsia section.

She recalls a visitor from Moscow who wandered through the galleries as if he knew every corner of the building. It turned out that he was a native of the area who, as a teenager, had been caught in a roundup.

Young people were deported to the Reich for forced labor, while children as young as 13 or 14 were made to dig trenches and build fortifications. Several hundred schoolchildren were held inside the building, half-starved, sleeping on damp, rotting straw alongside horses. A toilet had been hacked directly into the parquet floor. Armed guards marched the children to the banks of the Dnipro with shovels and forced them to work under gunpoint. If one escaped, the others were beaten almost to death.

Staff at the reserve began tracking down the former child prisoners and recording their testimonies. Those who had survived long enough were later helped to submit applications for compensation from Germany. Why had no one spoken about the camp sooner?

The author found the answer herself in an archival leaflet issued by the Taras Shevchenko partisan unit, which operated in the forests of the Cherkasy region:

“We will find and kill everyone who helps the Germans build defensive lines along the Dnipro!”

Makohon’s bust: From Kaniv to Volodarka

In Davidzon’s second photograph, Shevchenko’s bust has a bullet hole in its forehead. The resemblance to the monument in Borodianka, shot up by Russian forces in 2022, is chilling.

The author was told that Ivan Makohon, a prominent Soviet Ukrainian sculptor, had created the plaster bust in 1937 specifically for the opening of the museum in Kaniv. But the work’s fate after World War II remains unknown. It is held neither in the museum’s exhibition nor in the collection of Ukraine’s National Art Museum.

The sculptor’s son, Ihor Makohon, himself a painter, sculptor and graphic artist, is now 90 and lives in Italy. He was surprised to hear the story of the wounded, missing Kobzar.

“There must be some misunderstanding! I visited Kaniv in the mid-1950s and took photographs. The bust was on the second-floor balcony, completely undamaged.

“In 1961, my father decided to modify the composition slightly, adding shoulders. The new version was more monumental. Two plaster casts were made in the workshop at the Kyiv Art Institute, where Professor Makohon taught, and the mold was preserved.”

More than 60 years passed. In 2024, Ihor Makohon received a request from Volodarka, a district center in the Kyiv region. Local residents wanted to install a “historic” Shevchenko monument by Makohon and asked for his permission.

Ihor Ivanovych not only found the original mold but also arranged for the bust to be produced.

“We cast the bust in concrete with the lads and took it to Volodarka. There was enormous interest, and a lot of people gathered,” he recalls.

The unveiling took place on the Feast of the Intercession of the Holy Mother of God, which Ukraine also celebrates as the Day of Defenders and Defendresses. The project fulfilled an idea conceived by Oleksandr Ushynskyi, a local resident, environmentalist, researcher of the Holodomor, Maidan protester and war veteran.

In 2014, Ushynskyi volunteered for the front, defended Donetsk airport and later established a community museum dedicated to the Russian-Ukrainian war in his hometown. The monument in Volodarka became the 1,385th monument to Shevchenko in Ukraine and around the world.

The nazis, the communists and Russian propaganda

“Both the Nazis during World War II and the Soviets used Shevchenko to manipulate Ukrainians’ minds for propaganda purposes,” says Ihor Solovey, head of the Center for Strategic Communications and Information Security under Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture.

“The Nazis tried to exploit our national sentiments under the guise of ‘friendship.’

“They took passages from Kobzar and amplified them to turn people against Soviet rule. The message was supposedly about resistance to Russian oppression, mixed with all sorts of vile nonsense about ‘Jewish Bolshevism.’ They even put Taras’s words on posters – the familiar line: ‘Muscovites are strangers; they bring you harm.’

“To present themselves as benefactors, the Nazis deliberately published his poetry and prose during the occupation and ran articles about Shevchenko that served their purposes. They wanted people to believe that Ukrainian culture was free and flourishing under the Reich.”

“The Communists did exactly the same thing. They just dressed it up differently to persuade Ukrainians to fight the Germans. Think of the famous rallying cry: ‘Drench freedom in the enemy’s blood!’” Solovey continues.

Eighty years have passed. In June 2026, Ukraine’s Security Service announced that a 57-year-old woman from Kaniv had been formally notified of suspicion over the dissemination of “materials justifying and denying the Russian Federation’s armed aggression against Ukraine.”

The woman reportedly referred to the invasion as a “special military operation,” urged support for the Russian army and openly promoted pro-Kremlin narratives among acquaintances and colleagues. According to investigators, she was one of the deputy heads of the Shevchenko National Reserve.

Modern Russian propaganda reproduces methods first used under the Russian Empire and later adopted by the Soviet Union. One is to present Shevchenko primarily as part of Russian culture, pointing to the fact that he wrote his diaries and prose in Russian.

Another is to portray him as a “pan-Russian poet,” downplaying the importance of his work in shaping Ukrainian national identity.

But those carrying out Russia’s full-scale war on Ukrainian soil increasingly see Shevchenko, his monuments and his museums not as shared cultural heritage, but as an adversary and a source of resistance.

World.title: Mayor and entrepreneur: Transparency International calls for dismissal of Georgian officials over business ties
World.content:
TI identifies 24 officials heading private companies

Transparency International Georgia (TI) has identified 24 serving public officials who simultaneously hold directorships at 30 private companies, in violation of anti-corruption legislation.

The officials include mayors, deputy mayors, heads of municipal councils and representatives of state agencies.

Georgian law prohibits public officials from simultaneously engaging in business activities. TI says officials whose violations are confirmed must be dismissed.

Under the law, newly appointed officials have 10 days to relinquish their positions as directors of commercial organisations. Failure to comply requires them to leave public service.

What the law says

Article 13 of Georgia’s Law on Combating Corruption restricts public officials from engaging in business activities and managing private companies. The aim is to separate public and private economic interests and reduce the risk of conflicts of interest.

At the same time, the law allows public officials to own shares in commercial enterprises, which gives them a different legal status from that of a company director.

Transparency International Georgia argues that simultaneously holding public office and managing a private company creates corruption risks. The organisation calls on the government to take action in accordance with the law.

World.title: Council of Europe chief: Ban on opposition parties in Georgia could be challenged in Strasbourg court
World.content:
Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset has said that legal issues surrounding the initiative to ban opposition parties in Georgia could come before the European Court of Human Rights.

On 21 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court began hearing a case brought by the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition groups: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. The lawsuit alleges that these parties violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits parties whose aim is to overthrow or forcibly change the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments is that the parties refuse to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. All five parties deny the allegations. Hearings are scheduled to continue until 30 October. The court must deliver its final ruling by 24 June 2027. A simple majority is required to uphold the claim, meaning four of the seven judges must vote in favour.

Berset made the statement at a meeting of the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe in Strasbourg on 27 October.

He described the deterioration of democratic processes in Georgia as alarming and urged the authorities to protect political pluralism.

Berset commented on Georgia’s political situation after Nadine Pittfield, a British politician and head of Derby City Council, asked about developments in the country and the Constitutional Court case seeking to ban five pro-Western opposition parties.

Berset said the deterioration of democratic processes in Georgia, new laws restricting civic space and pressure on the opposition were causes for serious concern.

“All of this undermines political pluralism and the country’s commitments as a member of the Council of Europe,” Berset said.

He noted that Council of Europe member states must respect the European Convention on Human Rights and the case law of the European Court of Human Rights.

Berset stressed that any decision to ban a political party must have a strong legal basis and strictly comply with the principles of necessity and proportionality.

He said he would refrain from predicting the outcome of the ongoing constitutional dispute in Georgia, but did not rule out the possibility that important legal aspects of the case could eventually come before the Strasbourg court.

He urged Georgia’s ruling majority to protect political pluralism and stressed that his statement was not intended to influence the Constitutional Court’s decision.

The Secretary General noted that he had always sought to take an active role in the work of the Council of Europe delegation in Georgia and maintain close contact with the authorities.

“In September, during a meeting with Prime Minister Kobakhidze in New York, I discussed the decline of democratic processes in Georgia and stressed the importance of honouring the country’s commitments. I would also like to mention the Venice Commission’s recent recommendations on restrictive legislation in Georgia.

“The situation is quite difficult at the moment. Membership of the Council of Europe means more than joining a club of countries. It entails accepting high-level commitments based on the European Convention on Human Rights, as well as an obligation to comply with court rulings,” Alain Berset said.

He noted that he regularly meets representatives of the Georgian government because Georgia is one of the Council of Europe’s 46 member states.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 31, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 35th day of the second Karabakh war:

- President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to the German ARD TV channel on October 28.

- The territory of Tartar, Aghdam, and Agjabadi districts came under artillery fire.

- The Defense Ministry has announced the latest situation on the frontline as of October 31. The list of destroyed military equipment of Armenian troops has been announced. In response to the artillery fire at Gubadli district, a return fire was opened at Armenian troops.

- Qiyameddinli village of Agjabadi districts was fired upon. Armenian Armed Forces tried to lay the groundwork for future provocations by bringing phosphorus-laden cargo in the direction of Khojavend.

- A video of the destruction of equipment and manpower of Armenian troops has been released.

- Fighting continued in the direction of Aghdara, Khojavend, Gubadli.

- The reconnaissance and sabotage group of the Armenian Armed Forces was destroyed, and a video of the destruction of two military vehicles was released.

World.title: Provocation by alleged Iranian agents staged outside Azerbaijani Embassy in London (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
Photo: The Embassy of Azerbaijan in the United Kingdom

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 30. A provocative rally has been held outside the Embassy of Azerbaijan in the United Kingdom in London.

The Azerbaijani Embassy in London reported that a group of 10–15 people taking part in the rally carried Iranian flags and portraits of Ruhollah Khomeini, the first Supreme Leader of the Islamic Republic of Iran.

The protesters, most of whom were women, used loudspeakers to chant various slogans and alleged that women in Azerbaijan were facing pressure over wearing hijabs.

Notably, the protesters sought to use religious slogans and political symbols to manipulate issues related to Azerbaijan’s domestic policy.

The rally can be viewed as another provocative attempt by alleged agents of influence linked to Iranian intelligence services to target Azerbaijan’s independent policy and sovereign decisions.

Particular attention is drawn to the attempt to portray Azerbaijan’s decision to introduce a unified school uniform as a move against religious freedoms.

This suggests that Azerbaijan’s independent decision-making, policies based on its national interests and right to determine its domestic affairs are a source of serious concern for certain circles. As a result, attempts are being made to stir up an international outcry against the country under various pretexts and to use religious issues as a political tool.

However, the organizers and participants of these small-scale rallies should remember that provocative campaigns aimed at interfering in Azerbaijan’s internal affairs and targeting its independent policies will not achieve their objectives.

World.title: Azerbaijani judoka crowned European champion
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 30. Azerbaijani judoka Islam Rahimov achieved a remarkable feat by winning a gold medal at the U23 European Judo Championships in Naples, Italy.

He secured the medal after defeating the Netherlands' Jochem van Harten by ippon in the 66kg final.

Rahimov secured his second consecutive U-23 European title, having also won gold in the same weight category in 2025, when he defeated van Harten in the final.

The championships featured 275 judokas from 36 countries.

World.title: TEMPO-Kazakhstan seeks to expand steel pipe exports to Turkmenistan (Exclusive)
World.content:
ASHGABAT, Turkmenistan, October 30. "TEMPO-Kazakhstan," a Kazakhstani manufacturer of electric-welded steel pipes, is interested in expanding its exports to Turkmenistan and invites local companies to collaborate, the head of the export department at company, Boris Ryabukha told Trend on the sidelines of the 31st International Conference and Exhibition "Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan" (OGT 2026) in Ashgabat.

Ryabukha noted that the company’s production capacity is approximately 400,000 metric tons of pipes per year, with export potential reaching 200,000 metric tons.

"This is our first time attending the exhibition in Turkmenistan. We decided to set up a booth to make our presence known in the market and to study the Turkmenistan market," Ryabukha said.

According to him, the company manufactures electric-welded steel pipes with diameters ranging from 57 to 630 millimeters. The products are used in various industries, from housing and utilities to the transportation of oil and gas via main pipelines.

"We are open to cooperation, we wish to expand our exports to the republic, and we invite local companies to collaborate with us," noted the company representative.

In particular, the company is interested in partnering with metal trading companies, traders, and organizations involved in the construction of utility networks and the laying of pipelines.

Ryabukha reported that construction is currently underway on the plant’s second phase, which will enable the production of large-diameter pipes—up to 1,420 millimeters. This will expand the company’s production capacity.

He also noted that "TEMPO BAKU" is actively operating in the Azerbaijani market, offers a wide range of products, and collaborates with various clients. According to him, the company is open to partnering with new partners in the region.

"TEMPO-Kazakhstan" is part of the "TEMPO" group of companies, a Russian industrial holding that brings together enterprises from various industries. The manufacturing facility is located in the city of Saran in the Karaganda Region of Kazakhstan and specializes in the production of electric-welded steel pipes with diameters ranging from 57 to 630 mm for the oil and gas sector, construction, and housing and utilities. The plant’s stated production capacity is up to 400,000 metric tons of pipes per year.

The Group's sales division is responsible for selling products in domestic and international markets. Among the entities affiliated with the Group are "TEM-Kazakhstan Trading House" LLP in Astana and "TEMPO BAKU" in Azerbaijan.

World.title: 'Changing of the guard' as fashion retailers return to physical stores
World.content:
Australian retail is experiencing a strange phenomenon: brands with strong online footprints are moving back into bricks and mortar.

The wave of legacy Australian fashion brands falling into insolvency has not deterred Princess Polly, which has been opening stores on the Gold Coast and in Brisbane.

"I think there is going to be that bit of a changing of the guards for the brands and retailers that are maybe downsizing or reducing their footprint," chief merchandise officer Courtney Dres said.

"Then the younger, newer brands are coming in and starting to make a little bit of a splash."

Courtney Dres says customers are telling the company they want physical stores. (Supplied: Princess Polly)

In the past few years, Mosaic Brands, the owner of Katies, Millers and Noni B, has collapsed.

On its tail was Cue Clothing Co, Veronika Maine, Betts and Jeanswest, which have entered administration. Country Road Group has downsized its physical presence.

Even 188-year-old department store David Jones is reportedly on life support and weighing cutting store numbers amid the exit of numerous brands.

The outlook for retail is not rosy. Data from CreditorWatch shows the retail insolvency rate has been increasing since June 2022.

Chief executive Patrick Coghlan expects that to increase in the fashion sector due to its reliance on discretionary spending.

"Conditions are likely to get still tougher in the fashion retail space before they improve," he said.

Mr Coghlan said moving from online to in-store trade needed "to be carefully managed".

Experiencing the brand

Beauty brands Oz Hair and Beauty, Adore Beauty, activewear brand Kikiva and furniture company Mocka have opened physical stores in the last few years.

When Princess Polly opened in Pacific Fair on the Gold Coast in July hundreds of customers queued up in the early hours, drawn in by prizes and the chance to be seen at the launch.

Princess Polly's Gold Coast launch was well-attended. (Supplied: Princess Polly)

"[The customers] are just so excited to be there and so excited to experience the brand in person," Ms Dres said.

"I think that really tells us all we need to know about continuing the rollout of our retail stores."

Princess Polly, which is owned by US-listed A.K.A Brands, opened more than a dozen shops in the US before expanding into Sydney last November, the Gold Coast and, as of this weekend, Brisbane.

Physical space can add value

Queensland University of Technology retail expert Gary Mortimer said moving into omnichannel trade could add value, provided the transition was handled properly.

"You wouldn't expect an online pure-play retailer to suddenly open 64 stores, because it wouldn't be sustainable," he said.

"But they may open three stores, or they may open a bunch of stores, but only temporarily … and that will then create a level of experience and excitement and entertainment which draws people to the online site."

Gary Mortimer says speed of delivery is a key value for customers. (Supplied: Gary Mortimer)

Dr Mortimer said value was not just about price.

"Speed is now becoming the currency of retailers," he said.

"It's not about shopping online because that's convenient — it's consumers' desire for immediate gratification."

Ms Dres said that was part of the Princess Polly strategy.

"Basically, as soon as you buy it online, it almost immediately is packed and shipped out," she said.

"But of course, retail is a way to be able to be instant."

VRG GRL's store locations have been informed by customer feedback and data. (Supplied: VRG GRL)

Shifting expectations

VRG GRL co-founder Daniella Dionyssiou says returning to in-store trading feels like a return to the brand's roots.

The business started trading as Verge Girl in 2008 with one Brisbane store and opened a second store in 2014 before moving fully online in 2019.

Daniella Dionyssiou and Natalia Suesskow launched their business when they were 17 and 19. (Supplied: VRG GRL)

Ms Dionyssiou says customer expectations have shifted since then.

"It's no longer just about the product, but the experience and value a brand brings beyond the transaction," she said.

"The brands seeing the greatest success are those that understand their customers and have a clear sense of what makes them unique."

An abundance of sales data is available to e-commerce businesses, but social media can also help to inform strategy and create a "brand halo", or the in-store experience leading to online purchases.

"You look at a brand like Mecca … they've done an excellent job in really blending both the social media side of their business, their online business and the physical business together," retail analyst James Stewart said.

Customers shop differently

Ms Dionyssiou, whose business has opened stores in Sydney and plans to open more in Queensland, says the process has its challenges.

How Cue fell out of fashion Cue had a reputation for reinvention, with the proof hanging in the wardrobes of generations of women. But what inspired the start of the brand in 1968 has led to its demise.

"Physical retail brings a different set of considerations, from managing stock across locations to understanding what customers are drawn to when they can see and try on our collections in person," she said.

Ms Dres said every store opening had been a learning experience.

"We can't ignore the fact that obviously retail is a very competitive environment, and customers, of course, will vote with their wallets," she said.

James Stewart says the biggest risk businesses face is losing the interest of their customers. (Supplied)

Mr Stewart does not believe insolvencies in the sector necessarily mean retailers opening physical stores are putting themselves at risk.

He said the number one reason retail brands failed was because they lost relevance.

"Retailers have been opening and closing for generations," Mr Stearrt said.

"I don't think that just because you're in a physical environment that's necessarily a sign that you might fail, or alternatively, a bad investment. It could be an excellent investment."

World.title: Quick hits: Mix-up ends schoolmates' mammoth stand, Breetzke brings the fight
World.content:
Ryan Rickelton was left fuming after a mix-up ended a mammoth partnership with schoolmate Wiaan Mulder, as Matthew Breetzke didn't back down on a day of toil for the Aussies.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Breetzke's tongue takes the fight to Australia

After a simmering, tempestuous end to day three, the chat continued as the Proteas looked to fight back on day four.

Matthew Breetzke and Mitchell Starc drew the battlelines early, with the pair sharing a few tense words and Starc providing a mixture of death stares and wry smiles.

And Breetzke, who had provided Marnus Labuschagne with a remarkable leaping send-off on day one, was never likely to back down.

With him and Starc a couple overs into their stoush, the quick had the South African ducking underneath a bouncer.

Rising from his haunches, Breetzke cocked his head and poked out his tongue in Starc's direction, before grabbing his box and holding the pose.

It was quite the statement from Matthew Breetzke. (Fox Cricket)

Things were heating up — but the chat began to dissipate when Breetzke fell, before almost completely disappearing as Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder got stuck into their work.

2. Cummins's breakthrough wicket

At the start of South Africa's second innings, Pat Cummins had gone 314 balls without a Test dismissal, with his last wicket coming in the second innings in Durban.

For a man who averages a scalp just about every 22 balls in Test cricket, that's a fair drought.

The Australian captain ran in hard late on day three, and came close to breaking through with a line-ball LBW call, but started day four at Newlands still in search of a pole.

It took over an hour of play, but finally, he broke through.

Bowling back of a length and to a leg-side field, Cummins had the well-set Breetzke (43) out hooking to Mitchell Starc at backward square leg in.

Pat Cummins gave Australia the breakthrough in the opening session, with the wicket his first since the first Test of the series. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

After 372 wicketless deliveries, Cummins had broken the longest dismissal drought of his Test career, and the Proteas were five down with just an 81-run lead.

3. Schoolmates Rickelton and Mulder break Australia

Rickelton was enormous on day four.

The wicketkeeper-batter played with supreme confidence and hardly presented an opportunity to the Aussie attack, managing the ebbs and flows of his innings to perfection.

Up the other end, Mulder was just as impressive, grinding the Australians into the dirt as he and Rickelton batted for the majority of the day in a mammoth 134-run, 319-ball partnership.

The pair looked completely at home together in the middle, and so they should — Rickelton and Mulder attended secondary school together at Johannesburg's St Stithians College.

Ryan Rickelton's gritty century on day four helped bat South Africa into a potential position of victory. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher)

After 218 balls and a whopping 12 overs in the 90s, Rickelton pushed the leg-side single that brought up his second Test ton, which he celebrated by embracing his old buddy on a red-letter day for St Stithians.

4. Rickelton fumes after being barbecued

With Cummins seemingly long out of ideas, Rickelton having just brought up his century, and Labuschagne into his fourth over of the day, Australia was not even threatening to take a wicket.

But there was trouble brewing for the old friends in the middle.

Mulder had nailed his reverse sweep to backward point, where Josh Inglis made a fantastic stop and followed it with a quick release.

From the non-striker's end, Rickelton had raced out of the blocks and found himself all the way up the other end of the pitch.

Unfortunately for the centurion, Mulder was ball watching and completely unmoved, with Rickelton unable to get home as Labuschagne broke the stumps.

Centurion Ryan Rickelton was burnt by partner Wiaan Mulder. (Fox Cricket)

Speaking to ABC Sport at stumps, Rickelton was far from impressed — if not overly surprised — by his old schoolmate.

"Wiaan, he grates me sometimes because he drifts away in exactly that moment," Mulder said.

"He hit the shot and he just kind of ball-watched and it was an easy one, but sometimes he isn't really present and he can drift away.

"So it does frustrate me and I'm really irritated about that because we could have got a lot more tonight."

We hadn't seen a run-out all series before day four, but only a matter of minutes after the first, we were treated to a second.

Again, it was Labuschagne at the heart of it, brilliantly throwing down the stumps to have Gerald Coetzee on his way.

5. Mulder puts on a show late

With South Africa having lost 4-16 and No.11 Kagiso Rabada joining Mulder at the crease, the start of the Australian run chase loomed large.

But Mulder had other ideas.

Test cricket live South Africa sets Australia a target of 288 to win the third Test and the series after an thrilling comeback on day four in Cape Town.

The all-rounder farmed the strike smartly, and after batting within himself for the majority of the day, began to take the game to the Australians.

After becoming the day's second St Stithians alumnus to cross three figures, he battered the Aussies, taking Cummins and then Nathan Lyon for massive leg-side sixes in consecutive overs.

With Temba Bavuma opting against a late declaration, Mulder and Rabada extended South Africa's lead by a further 36 runs before the centurion holed out on the final ball of the day.

Australia will begin its fourth innings at the start of the series' deciding day, requiring 288 runs for victory.

World.title: Pelvic pain clinic teaches school students not to suffer in silence
World.content:
It took Amy Harper about 20 years to be surgically diagnosed with endometriosis.

The 37-year-old teacher said she did not know what symptoms to look for and was told by countless doctors she did not match the diagnostic criteria.

In 2024, after finally being diagnosed, Ms Harper looked to the Milton Pelvic Pain Clinic on the NSW south coast for fertility support.

She was surprised to discover the specialist care clinic offered a school outreach program.

"I was the year 12 girls' adviser at the time and I thought it was really important before they left school that they understood some of these female health concerns," Ms Harper said.

" It would have saved a lot of millennials like me the heartache of so much pain … and I could've got help sooner. "

One of 33 federally funded pelvic pain clinics across the country, the Milton facility is especially focused on school-aged education and outreach in an effort to speed up diagnosis of chronic conditions such as endometriosis.

Peak body Endometriosis Australia estimates about one in seven Australians assigned female at birth are affected by the disease, with diagnosis taking, on average, six and a half years.

"It makes me really happy that as a teacher hosting this program I've been able to help a lot of people," Ms Harper said.

After years of infertility, endometriosis sufferer Amy Harper gave birth to her daughter Matilda in early 2026. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

'Symptoms listened to and believed'

About twice a month, clinic nurse Susan Wilford travels to classrooms across south-east NSW to give lessons on reproductive health to pre-teen and high school-aged girls.

"I do a chat describing the menstrual cycle, endometriosis, PMOS, and some other common causes of pelvic pain, dysfunction or menstrual irregularity," she said.

An anonymous question box is also available to make students feel comfortable asking whatever is on their mind.

Ms Wilford said when she developed the program in 2024, she was trying to dispel misinformation and help students understand whether they might have a chronic condition.

Susan Wilford says the average time to diagnosis chronic conditions such as endometriosis is concerning. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

"I thought it was a key way to get information out there at a prime time in someone's life when they're trying to ascertain whether their symptoms are typical or atypical," she said.

"It's really important for teenagers to realise that … [periods are] going to be uncomfortable to some point versus an unexpected level of pain that really is disrupting your life."

Susan Wilford visited Moruya High School in October and had students ask questions via anonymous handwritten notes. (ABC South East NSW: Jacinta Counihan)

Awareness, pain management

Both staff and students have made self-referrals to Milton Pelvic Pain Clinic after accessing its school outreach program.

Mckenzie Wright attended the program when it was at Vincentia High School.

She had been surgically diagnosed with endometriosis before she attended the outreach lesson but was still struggling to manage her symptoms.

"The clinic gave me a TENS machine," Ms Wright, now 21, said.

"It helped me go to school. It helped me go to work, because I was able to have something that I could wear and have on me as kind of a backup for pain."

Mckenzie Wright says she was diagnosed faster than average because she knew what symptoms to look out for and sought specialist care early. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Ms Wright said the program also helped her peers better understand her condition.

"I think normal health classes don't really go into depth about women's health," she said.

Ms Wilford said many self-referred patients had received a diagnosis sooner than if they had not accessed care.

"The most heartwarming part of the clinic is to watch people have their symptoms listened to and believed," she said.

Milton Pelvic Pain Clinic, south of Sydney, is one of 33 federally funded centres in Australia. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Assistant Health Minister Rebecca White said Milton's model of care was unique among federally funded pelvic pain clinics.

"So long as they're delivering on those baseline access-to-care priorities, we're comfortable for the [clinic] to negotiate with the Primary Health Network for any additional inclusions they might think are important for their local community, just like Milton has done," she said.

World.title: New tennis number one as Zverev finally reaches the top
World.content:
Alexander Zverev, who spent years waiting for his moment to reach the summit of ​his sport only for a new golden generation to surge past him, has finally climbed to the top of tennis' world rankings.

Zverev had long been one of the brightest talents to emerge in the 2010s, but his path, like that of his peers, was largely blocked by the enduring dominance of Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal, Novak Djokovic and Andy Murray.

Despite ​winning two ATP Finals titles on either side of ‌an Olympic gold medal in 2021, Zverev struggled to make a similar impact at the grand slams as Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz formed a new roadblock when the greats began to decline.

All that changed this year, however, as Zverev, 29, capitalised on injuries to his major rivals and found another level to claim the French Open and US Open ‌titles.

"It's incredibly special," said Zverev, who will take over from Sinner on Monday and become the 30th man to top the world rankings since they were introduced ⁠in 1973.

"It's something I've worked towards for years and you have to show great tennis the whole ‌year to be in this position."

Zverev will become only the second world ​number one, after Daniil Medvedev, from the crop ‌of players now largely in their late 20s and early 30s who emerged during the "Big Four" era but never displaced them.

The summit had been within Zverev's reach before, but a serious ankle injury at the 2022 French Open derailed his push, and Grand Slam success continued to elude him on his return as Sinner and Alcaraz accumulated 12 majors between them.

Zverev wins US Open final Alexander Zverev wins his second grand slam title of the year with a dominant victory over American Ben Shelton in the men's US Open final.

With Alcaraz's season stalled by a wrist injury and Sinner suffering a knee injury, Zverev's consistency and ​durability ‌were decisive this year as he triumphed at Roland Garros and Flushing Meadows and reached the Wimbledon final.

"I've had a lot of difficult moments in my career: the lost grand slam finals, the injury in 2022," Zverev said.

"But I always somehow kept believing, kept going. This year I also took the ⁠step of changing my game a little and rebuilding it, at 29. The way ‌this season has gone is a dream."

Zverev's path to ‌the top has also included turbulence away from the court, with allegations of domestic abuse, which he has repeatedly denied.

A German court closed a case involving his former partner ‌Brenda Patea after a 2024 settlement without a finding of guilt, and the ATP ended a separate investigation into allegations by Olga Sharypova in 2023, citing insufficient evidence.

Zverev's 3-8 record against top-10 opponents this season may leave room for debate over whether the top ‌ranking makes him ​the best player, but noted coach Patrick ⁠Mouratoglou said staying fit and sustaining excellence were skills in themselves.

For Zverev, who has managed type 1 diabetes since childhood, durability has been a constant issue.

"A player is not only performing on court, it's also being healthy, managing your body," Mouratoglou said.

"If someone is never injured and others are often injured, the one that's not injured will probably end up having a higher ranking … staying healthy when you're a professional athlete ⁠is a real skill."

Zverev said reaching number one late in his career had left him better prepared for the responsibility that accompanies the ranking, both as the face of the sport and the player everyone ‌wants to beat.

"The number one position ‌brings a lot with it," said Zverev, Germany's second men's world number one after Boris Becker in 1991.

"You have to ​be a good role model, do a lot of things right and on court that means more than returning and serving well. I still have Carlos and Jannik. Hopefully, I can keep competing with them over the next few years."

Reuters

World.title: Before captain, a king: The dramatic life of Patrick Stewart
World.content:
Long before he trekked aboard the USS Enterprise, Sir Patrick Stewart trod the boards on stages across the globe.

"The stage would prove to be a safe space, a refuge from real life in which I could inhabit another person, living in another place and time," Stewart wrote in his memoir.

The Royal Shakespeare Company wrote a tribute to Stewart, who died yesterday aged 86, calling him one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation.

"Despite being one of the most recognisable Shakespearean performers in the world, Sir Patrick remained deeply connected to Stratford-upon-Avon and the RSC throughout his career," the company said.

The Royal Shakespeare Company said his contribution was "beyond measure", with his knighthood for services to drama and his star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame as markers of a career that spanned 70 years.

But before he was a household name, a young Stewart cut his teeth as an ensemble member touring Australia.

Patrick Stewart as Launce, with his dog Crab, during rehearsals for Two Gentlemen of Verona in 1970. (Getty Images: Evening Standard/Hulton Archive)

Stewart joined an amateur drama group at 12 and memorised Shakespeare for fun as a teenager.

He would go on to win a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching his career as a character actor.

Theatre programs archived at the National Library of Australia show that a 21-year-old Stewart toured with the Old Vic company across 1961 and 1962.

Stewart had ensemble roles in Twelfth Night and The Lady of the Camellias, both directed by Robert Helpmann and starring Vivien Leigh.

ABC archives show that reporters made sure to capture the moment Leigh and Helpmann landed on the tarmac in Australia to be greeted by adoring fans, but likely didn't know that just out of frame was a star-to-be in young Stewart.

Loading...

From the Young Vic, Stewart went on to join the Royal Shakespeare Company and stayed for 14 years, playing roles including Mark Antony, Henry IV, Shylock and Oberon.

In 1975, he would return to Australia to play Ejlert Løvborg in Hedda Gabler with the company.

From royal crowns to the captain's chair

Although often revered as a classical actor, Stewart denied this title, saying: "I was not a trained classical actor, I just had a training".

"What I did happen to do was spend a huge number of years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, but doing just as much modern drama as I was doing blank verse," he told the ABC in 1995.

Ian McKellen and Patrick Stewart dance during a curtain call in 2013. (Getty Images: J. Countess)

After joining Star Trek, he found himself frustrated at the implication from reporters that doing a syndicated television show must have meant he was "slumming it".

Stewart had a very different point of view.

"All of those years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, all of those years sitting in the throne of England, all of those years wearing those crowns and speaking that blank verse was nothing but a preparation for sitting in the captain's chair of the Enterprise," he said.

It was Stewart's understanding of profession that made him so versatile, that every prior piece of work in an artist's portfolio contributes to the next, regardless of the piece being set in futuristic space or written in Elizabethan England.

Always returned to theatre

Star Trek may have been Stewart's launch into the broader global audience, particularly in America, but he continued to return to the stage, often rehearsing shows while filming.

In 1988, Stewart premiered his one-man adaptation of A Christmas Carol.

The performance started as a three-hour rendition, performed in a church in Yorkshire.

Several years later, it would make its Broadway debut.

The revised version would be staged time and time again, nabbing a Laurence Olivier Award for Best Entertainment in 1994.

In 2007, Stewart played the role he'd waited 50 years for — Macbeth.

Patrick Stewart in Macbeth at the Gielgud Theatre in 2007 in London. (Getty Images: Chris Jackson)

The Times of London said his performance was "an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humour".

"I learned it when I was 14. I memorised all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great," Stewart told The Associated Press.

"And they stuck, so I didn't have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job.

" Nearly 50 years I've waited. "

In 2009, Stewart starred with his dear friend Sir Ian McKellen in Waiting for Godot.

McKellen wrote of his friend on social media, retelling the moment Stewart told him about taking a role on Star Trek.

"'But Patrick, think of your stage career in the UK. Do you really want to risk getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?'" McKellen said he asked at the time.

" Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did. "

Audiences will feel lucky to have seen Patrick Stewart deliver time and time again.

But in his own words, he felt just as lucky to see them too.

"I enjoy what I do so much that I do actually feel sucked into it, particularly the live theatre, the performing side of it," he told the ABC in 1995.

"I'm one of those really fortunate individuals, I do feel blessed in this, who ended up doing as a profession what I would've done for nothing."

World.title: Fears blue whale decline signals changes in Bonney Upwelling ocean current
World.content:
Every summer, the coast near the Victorian and South Australian border becomes a rich feeding ground for marine wildlife.

A strong ocean current, the Bonney Upwelling, drags cold water and deep-sea nutrients to the ocean's surface, attracting marine mammals, migratory birds and fish to the region from November to May.

Scientists are unsure if pygmy blue whales have declined in population or shifted migration habits. (Supplied: Pete Gill)

Over the past few years, marine scientists have noticed shifts in the ecosystem, prompting fears the upwelling could be producing less food for wildlife.

The ocean current helps drive two key industries in the region, fishing and tourism, and is so important for locals that they celebrate it with the annual Bonney Upwelling Festival, which takes place this weekend in Portland.

Changes to the upwelling have some people wondering what impact it might have, not only on the region's environment, but also on its economy.

Whales in decline

Pete Gill, who has monitored pygmy blue whales along the coast near Portland for 28 years, said whale sightings had halved in that time.

The endangered pygmy blue whale migrates to the waters from Cape Otway, in Victoria, to Robe, in South Australia, to feed every summer.

"Back in the early 2000s, we'd be seeing 12 to 18 whales each survey on average, but now we're seeing five or six," Dr Gill said.

Pete Gill has conducted more than 300 aerial surveys of the ocean near Portland in the past three decades. (Supplied: Pete Gill)

When he compared the results of aerial surveys he conducted in 2000-2004 and 2020-2024, he found that blue whale sightings had dropped by 51 per cent.

Dr Gill said it was not yet clear whether the population had dropped or if the whales had shifted their migration habits, but it seemed the region no longer offered the rich food source it once did.

"We have to assume that there's something going on with climate change," Dr Gill said.

"Where there's food, whales will come.

"If there's a big supply of krill, we think that they use their deep voices to call other whales in.

"It's like saying, 'OK, there's a lot of food here, come and join in'.

"But if there's only scattered patches, they will probably stay silent."

Food source disappearing

The upwelling sweeps large swarms of krill closer to the coastline, where they thrive in the nutrient-rich cold water, and become a feast to fish, seabirds and marine mammals.

In the past, whales and other filter feeders would have been able to find krill easily near the surface of the ocean.

But Dr Gill said he did not see many swarms of krill near the surface anymore, forcing wildlife to venture further and use more energy just to catch a meal.

The upwelling current drags phytoplankton and zooplankton to the ocean surface. (Supplied: Alex Shute)

"If it's at the surface, the whale doesn't have to go to all the effort of diving down 200 metres or deeper looking for krill," he said.

He has observed a 65 per cent decrease in surface krill swarms since the early 2000s.

"If there's no krill for blue whales, then there's no krill for food for other species as well," Dr Gill said.

A colony of Australian fur seals that feed on fish in the Bonney Upwelling system has also been found to be suffering from malnourishment and population decline.

A festival of the sea

Portland's annual Bonney Upwelling Festival kicks off this weekend, marking the start of the seven-month-long current, bringing anglers, whale watchers, and other tourists to the region.

The Upwelling Festival features a parade, market stalls, live music and talks on marine science. (Supplied: Nicole Cleary)

Glenelg Shire Mayor Karen Stephens said the upwelling was the main driver of tourism in Portland.

"The Upwelling Festival is all about our whales and encouraging people to come and experience that," Cr Stephens said.

" It brings people from outside of our area into it and it gives them an opportunity to explore. "

Karen Stephens says caring for the environment is vital for Portland's economy and tourism. (ABC South East SA: Grace Whiteside)

The upwelling also makes Portland a prime location for tuna fishing, which Cr Stephens said was essential to the local economy and another drawcard for visitors.

"It's really important to us that we do protect the environment," she said.

Impact of climate change

Marine ecologist and Deakin University PhD candidate Alex Shute has been studying the past 30 years of trends in the Bonney Upwelling.

He said that in the past five years, there had been greater variability in the strength of the Bonney Upwelling current, and believed climate change could be the cause.

Pete Gill says he first noticed there were fewer pygmy blue whales in 2012. (Supplied: Pete Gill)

"We have found there are some years where it's fairly weak and then years where it is really quite extreme," Mr Shute said.

" With climate change, it is generally expected you would have a stronger upwelling. "

In 2024, the Bonney Upwelling was the strongest on record, but Mr Shute said a stronger current did not lead to more nutrients and krill.

"It's all about balance," he said.

"If you're having a very extreme year, that may go beyond a temperature threshold of a certain zooplankton, and then that will generally affect the entire food chain."

World.title: Brand used fame to 'facilitate' sex but consent was key, he tells jury
World.content:
In Russell Brand's iPhone 5 was a contact by the name of T [redacted] AP **.

She was a 21-year-old who had been "picked out" to meet the then-33-year-old comedian after his 2009 stand-up gig Scandalous at London's Apollo Theatre.

The woman's name has been suppressed by the courts, but the acronyms and symbols around it represent Mr Brand's labelling system for women back then.

Warning: This article contains details some readers may find distressing.

The T stood for "Tart", the 51-year-old explained to London's Southwark Crown Court, where he is now on trial for raping her.

Tart was a word he used to identify women available for "casual hook-ups", he said.

Russell Brand in 2009, the year he is accused of raping a 21-year-old he met after a stand-up comedy show in London. (Supplied: Met Police)

AP stood for "anal play": the sexual act the young woman had performed "upon first meeting me" in the theatre's dressing room, he told the jury.

The two asterisks by her name, he said, were a symbol to "never ever forget this individual".

That individual alleges a week later Mr Brand "painfully" raped her at his house before telling her "to clean up the mess you have made".

Russell Brand denies that he raped her, telling the court she had consented.

Outlining his method for storing women's phone numbers formed part of Mr Brand's defence argument this week as he recounted the night they met.

He spent more than four hours on the stand responding to the allegations himself, telling the court he had struggled to convince any other friend or acquaintance to give evidence on his behalf.

Mr Brand 'comfortable' using fame to attract women

A press pack has greeted Russell Brand and his wife Laura at court every day. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

Five other women, who met the actor and comedian in various work, social or political settings, have also accused Mr Brand of either rape, sexual assault or attempted indecent assault between 1999 and 2009, allegations Mr Brand also denies.

Mr Brand said while he used to be promiscuous, obsessed with sex and misused his fame "very, very selfishly" to "facilitate sexual access", he never did anything non-consensual.

At the time, by his own admission in court, Mr Brand was on the cusp of fame and "increasingly focused" on his "promiscuity" and "womanising".

He had not yet married — and later divorced — US singer Katy Perry, which he said catapulted him into "staggering fame" in 2010, but was starting to be recognised in some circles.

"I have been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and have dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering and idiocy," he told the court.

"I was in a position of fame.

"As I became more successful and famous, I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access, which I agree was wrong."

Consent the key issue in trial

Russell Brand denies all the charges. (Reuters: Toby Shepheard)

But the issue at the heart of this case is consent.

Mr Brand has acknowledged having sexual relations with some of his accusers, at times recounting them in graphic detail from the witness box. But he insists every encounter was consensual.

It was a point the judge, Justice Joel Bennathan, made unmistakably clear during cross-examination.

"You knew consent was the million-dollar question," he told Mr Brand.

Consent was "fundamental" to Mr Brand, the comedian told the jury, and "in many ways more important than sex itself".

But the prosecution alleges Mr Brand believed in "birthright orgasm" and was so consumed by sex and women, he "didn't care if a woman protested", he "could not leave without a conquest".

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC cross-examining Russell Brand during his trial this week. (Elizabeth Cook via AP)

"All you were concerned about was getting yourself off, wasn't it, Mr Brand?" prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC asked him.

"I had a variety of complex concerns like any human being," he responded.

When the Crown prosecutor asked Mr Brand if his only two hobbies at the time were sex and comedy, he responded: "West Ham, animals, veganism."

The court heard that Mr Brand told a friend in 1999 that his "main ambition was that one day he would have slept with well over 5,000 girls".

Under cross-examination, Mr Brand said he did not recall that conversation but agreed he may have said it.

Mr Brand recalls bathroom 'encounter' he previously could not remember

One woman, who has accused Mr Brand of sexually assaulting and raping her at a London bar in 2004, told the court Mr Brand pulled her into the toilets, locked the door and would not let her go as he raped her.

Woman tells court alleged rape by Russell Brand 'happened so fast' Russell Brand, 51, denies the allegations as he is tried for three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

Mr Brand initially could not remember the incident, the court heard, but a recent visit to the bar and that cubicle had helped him recall "the encounter".

He told the jury having sex in public toilets was not uncommon for him at the time.

"In media, in the early 2000s, people going in and out of bathrooms didn't attract a huge amount of attention," he told the jury.

Mr Brand told the jury he now remembered the woman was "wide-eyed", greeted him with "enthusiastic flirting" and was "happy" to go into the bathroom "to fool around".

The court heard Mr Brand blamed the allegations on a 2023 UK documentary, Russell Brand: In Plain Sight: Dispatches.

When that documentary aired sexual assault allegations against Mr Brand into lounge rooms across the UK, he was performing on stage to a sold-out crowd.

The prosecution will rely on the fact six women who do not know each other came forward with allegations, arguing that is beyond coincidence.

Six women, who the prosecution said had not "sought the limelight, "had nothing to gain" and were not after financial compensation.

But the defence says there is another link: the 2023 program that led to the comedian's arrest, suggesting it encouraged some of the women to rewrite their history with Mr Brand and corrupted their memories of what took place.

Loading...

Mr Brand and his wife only defence witnesses to take the stand

The actor said his life had been all but "consumed" by the allegations since, at the expense of his marriage and relationship with his children.

Mr Brand agreed with his lawyer that friends and colleagues would now not touch him with a "barge pole" since the allegations came to light.

His wife of nine years, Laura, was the only person other than Mr Brand himself to physically take the stand in support of him.

Ms Brand, who hosts a weekly podcast with her husband, has walked hand in hand with the Hollywood star every day, listening intently to the evidence and diligently taking notes.

Speaking clearly and confidently, she told the jury she knew Mr Brand had slept with a lot of women but he had never made her do anything sexually she had not wanted to.

Russell Brand has arrived at court every day with his wife Laura. (Reuters: Chris J Ratcliffe)

Mr Brand was the most animated he has been throughout the trial during his wife's 20 minutes of evidence, nodding along and mouthing words in her direction, particularly when she spoke about his recent baptism in London's River Thames.

Two other ex-partners of his — the only other witnesses in his defence — provided written statements saying while he was "unfaithful" and "promiscuous", he never engaged in an intimate act with them without their consent.

Speaking to the jury, the prosecutor said while Mr Brand "may now treat women with kindness and respect" and "may now have a different view of consent", they needed to consider what the now 51-year-old was like up to 25 years ago when the alleged offending occurred.

All the evidence in the trial has now concluded, and next week the jury is expected to retire to decide whether or not Mr Brand raped, sexually assaulted and attempted to indecently assault six women over the course of a decade.

World.title: Two Dan Sullivans are running in Alaska. Trump thinks one is a decoy
World.content:
Something fishy is going on in Alaska ahead of the midterms, but it has nothing to do with the state's famous seafood and everything to do with two men with the same name.

Two Dan Sullivans are running for the US Senate on November 3.

One is Dan S Sullivan, Alaska's Republican incumbent who is seeking a third six-year term. The other is Dan J Sullivan Jr, a retired elementary-school teacher who entered the race in May.

When the two appear together on the ballot in print, Daniel J Sullivan is listed first, with no party designation, followed by Dan S Sullivan, registered Republican incumbent.

A sample election ballot shows the two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. (AP: Haven Daley)

US President Donald Trump isn't too happy about it.

"They [the Democrats] found a guy named Dan Sullivan. They put him up to get [voters] a little confused," he said at a rally for the Alaskan incumbent in mid-October.

This week, he directed the Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race if Republicans do not win Alaska, believing Daniel J Sullivan is a "decoy" aimed at siphoning votes away from the Republican candidate.

Republicans argue voters intending to vote for Dan S Sullivan may confuse him with Dan J Sullivan and accidentally select his name on the ballot. Some Alaskans have dismissed the notion, arguing they are smarter than the Grand Old Party (GOP) gives them credit for.

The bizarre issue, which has been playing out for months, deepened on Wednesday, local time, when The New York Times reported the campaign of rival Democrat candidate in Alaska, Mary Peltola, had recruited Dan J Sullivan in an effort to dilute the GOP vote.

Moment in Maine sums up Trump's troubles A political debate in Maine offered multiple reminders of times when Donald Trump has dismissed Americans' concerns as either conspiracy theories or stupidity.

Both Ms Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) have denied participating in such efforts.

Dan J Sullivan has insisted he is running in good faith, saying his namesake is "making decisions that I don't think are necessarily moving our state forward". He has, however, acknowledged that having the same name as the incumbent has been a boon for his campaign.

"I knew that my name recognition would get me immediate publicity," he told The New Yorker in August.

"It's succeeded beyond my wildest hopes."

The Alaskan campaign has now kicked up a debate about ballot stacking tactics, widely-watched US Senate races and Republican allegations of election interference just days before the midterms.

A tale of two Dans

Back in May, the battle of the Dans came to a head when a top state elections official ruled Dan J Sullivan ineligible for the primary ballot.

The official concluded Dan J Sullivan's declaration of candidacy was filed "with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality".

But the Alaska Supreme Court later overturned the decision, ruling he was qualified to run after finding the decision to strike him from the ballot was unlawful.

US Senator Dan Sullivan is running against another Dan Sullivan in next week's midterms. (Reuters: Jacquelyn Martin/Pool)

"It's all because of my name, and you know, there's nothing I can do about my name," Dan J Sullivan told a local news outlet after the decision.

"I was frustrated. I felt it's time for a change, and so I wanted to jump into the race and make my feelings and my thoughts known …They tried to make it more than that, and you know, that's their prerogative."

It isn't the first time a candidate has run against a namesake in the United States, nor is it the first time Dan S Sullivan has run against another of the same name.

When the Republican first ran for Senate in 2014, he appeared on the same ballot as Dan A Sullivan, the mayor of Anchorage, who had run for lieutenant governor.

But Republicans think the presence of Daniel J Sullivan, whom they refer to as "Decoy Dan" or "Fake Dan", on this year's ballot is a Democratic dirty trick.

That is despite Alaska's ranked-choice voting system making the situation "better for the Republican incumbent," according to David Smith, associate professor of American politics and foreign policy at the University of Sydney's US Studies Centre.

"If [someone] wanted to vote for Dan Sullivan but didn't know which one to vote for … as long as they put both of them above the Democrat [candidate], then Dan Sullivan is going to end up with the vote," he added.

"So it's really hard to see how this could unfairly change the election result at all."

Democrats accused of ballot stacking

Alaska is considered a high-stakes midterms race, and Ms Peltola, a Yup'ik Alaska Native and former congresswoman, hopes it will form part of next week's blue wave predicted by some pollsters.

Mary Peltola is running as the Democratic candidate for Alaska's US Senate seat. (AP: Mark Thiessen)

If successful, she would become the first Democrat in nearly two decades to represent the state in the Senate.

"We've seen increasingly … that Democratic candidates seem to be competitive in states that went heavily for Trump in 2024. And Alaska is one of those states," Dr Smith said.

But Ms Peltola's campaign was rocked by The New York Times report suggesting that since the summer of 2025, her team had tried to recruit a Dan Sullivan to run for Senate.

Elisa Rios, Ms Peltola's former campaign manager and longtime aide, who was fired amid a staff shake-up in August, told the newspaper the DSCC had introduced the Peltola campaign to a political operative and Ohio native named Jerid Kurtz.

At a later meeting, this aide said he had recruited a Dan Sullivan who he described as "amenable to running if it would help Ms Peltola", the Times reported.

Dan J Sullivan and Ms Peltola did not respond to the ABC's requests for comment.

The tactic of selecting rival candidates with the same name to run, referred to as ballot-stacking, has, according to Dr Smith, been used by both parties in the past, and is generally considered legal.

Political parties may also seek candidates who appeal to a similar group of voters as the main rival, or stoke confusion to potentially influence the outcome of a close race.

Young men turn on Trump Many young American men swung behind Donald Trump in 2024, but polls show they are largely abandoning Republicans.

Dr Smith said the tactic was used by Republicans during the 2024 campaign in Alaska when the GOP fought to keep another Democrat on the ballot who was actually in prison in New York at the time.

Steve Jarding, a former communications director for the DSCC, told top political website The Hill that ballot stacking was normal when he was at the Senate committee in Washington.

During a campaign stop in Soldotna on Friday, Ms Peltola labelled the Times report a "distraction".

"Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight," her campaign said.

But that hasn't stopped Republicans from seizing on the issue.

Loading

Trump jumps on election interference allegations

With the case of the Alaskan Dans making national headlines days out from the midterms, Mr Trump and his attorney-general, Todd Blanche, have begun to ramp up allegations of election interference.

Mr Trump has called for Ms Peltola to be criminally prosecuted and removed from the ballot in the Senate race.

"I think they should be prosecuted. To me, that's voter fraud at the highest level," he told reporters.

Donald Trump has directed the DOJ to sue to block certification of the Senate race if the Republicans do not win Alaska. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

The DOJ's lawsuit, filed on Thursday, said Alaska should be prevented from certifying the result if senator Dan Sullivan loses by fewer votes than his namesake receives, pending an investigation.

The probe would determine if voters mistakenly supported the wrong Sullivan, though it does not explain how this process would work. Votes are supposed to be confidential.

"I think name recognition [of] Senator Dan in Alaska is at 100 per cent," said Alaskan veteran political reporter James Brooks.

"As is name recognition for his leading Democratic challenger. People in Alaska have been inundated with ads, mailers, phone calls, and at this point it's difficult to find anyone who doesn't know what's happening."

Dr Smith doubted the DOJ lawsuit would proceed given states mostly run their own elections according to their own laws.

"Federal Congress can make laws regarding federal elections, but they haven't made any laws about this situation," he said.

"The fact that the federal government has said that this lawsuit will only apply if Dan Sullivan loses is another thing that makes it completely invalid. The federal government is not supposed to be a partisan entity; it's not supposed to be filing lawsuits on behalf of one candidate."

He believed Republicans were using this issue to sow seeds of doubt about the broader midterm elections.

"I think that they're definitely going to try to de-legitimise the election results," he said.

"The big question is going to be, will there actually be anything they can do about it?"

As for those seeking the Senate seat in Alaska, with so much resting on the outcome, winning this race will be nothing like shooting fish out of a barrel.
