World.title: Concerns for welfare of two Australians after Spanish train crash
World.content:
WorldEuropeAustralians abroad Concerns for welfare of two Australians after Spanish train crash David Crowe and Jack Gramenz Updated October 31, 2026 — 6:06am ,first published 8:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australian authorities are working to confirm the welfare of two Australians linked to this week’s deadly train crash in Spain, amid fears for at least 14 foreign nationals who are listed as missing. A high-speed train on Wednesday smashed into the rear of another on the line running south from Madrid, killing at least 69 people and injuring almost 200. Loading Australian diplomats are supporting the family of two Australians in connection with the collision, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said on Friday. The department expressed its “heartfelt condolences” for all affected by the train crash, but made no comment on the fate of the Australians involved in the tragedy.



“Owing to our privacy obligations, we are unable to provide further comment,” a spokesperson said in a statement. The Spanish foreign ministry initially said that 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, but it outlined new details on Friday afternoon in Madrid – about 2am on Saturday, AEDT – about the countries involved. A crane operates at the site of wrecked train carriages in Spain on Friday. AP Photo/Bernat Armangue The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said there were 51 individuals of 23 different nationalities caught up in the crash, including two confirmed fatalities, but authorities are still working to find missing passengers and identify the dead. Some foreign nationals emerged from the two trains unharmed, Spanish media outlet Heraldo reported on Friday. It cited government sources to report that there were nine injured foreign nationals, two fatalities and 22 whose status was yet to be determined.



The foreign nationals yet to be accounted for come from countries including Argentina, Australia, Canada, Czechia, France, Japan, Mexico, South Korea, Tunisia, the United States and Venezuela, according to multiple reports in Spanish media. Healthcare workers and officials are facing major challenges in establishing the facts and treating the injured. The president of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, Emiliano García-Page, confirmed the death toll of 69 on Friday, but he cautioned that this depended on further work. “We cannot rule out the possibility of more deaths,” he said. The foreign nationals reported dead include one passenger from Portugal and one from Argentina, according to Spanish media.



In a sign of the horrific nature of the crash, emergency workers have been recovering partial remains in the wreckage from the carriages. Officials from the Castilla-La Mancha government said it would take time to identify the dead. “Testing ​is proceeding slowly, although families will be contacted throughout the day so that they can come ⁠and collect their results,” said Esther Padilla, a government spokesperson, on state television network TVE. Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente blamed the disaster on human error, with a control centre in Madrid failing to tell the driver of a high-speed Renfe AVE service that another train, run by private operator Iryo, was stationary on the tracks ahead. But the minister’s comments provoked a furore, with rail unions accusing him of “scapegoating” the rail control workers and demanding his resignation, while the train operators offered different accounts of what drivers had been told.



Related Article Analysis

Tragedy Leaked recordings reveal final moments before the Spanish train disaster The Renfe AVE train had 397 passengers, while the Iryo train was carrying 147. The accident comes with memories still fresh of another crash between high-speed trains in southern Spain in January involving trains from the same two companies. The Spanish accident authority issued a preliminary report estimating the Renfe train ​was travelling at ⁠a speed of between 160km/h and 200km/h when the collision occurred. The public debate about the crash has focused on whether the controller at the Atocha railway station in Madrid told the Renfe driver to “resume normal operations” rather than telling the driver to keep to 40km/h because there was a stationary train ahead.



Related Article Tragedy ‘Inexplicable’: How the catastrophic train crash in Spain unfolded “The sequence of malfunctions, instructions, and actions eventually led to the collision, in the absence of the necessary mitigating barriers,” said the report from the Independent ​Authority for the Technical Investigation of Accidents and Incidents. The rail centre operator who authorised the Renfe AVE train to resume its journey with normal operation, and therefore reach speeds of 160km/h or more, was questioned by authorities on Thursday. Spanish newspaper El País said he invoked his right to remain silent before the Civil Guard. With Reuters Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Inside the crumbling marriage of a ‘love rat’ pilot accused of murder
World.content:
RAAF pilot Robert Crawford is on trial in Brisbane, accused of murdering his wife Frances.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In the cold night air outside his home, Robert Crawford looks up from the bottom of a retaining wall, the glow of a police officer’s torch illuminating his face. His wife, Frances, lies lifeless in her floral pyjamas on the grass. Her hand rests on her chest, and her right ugg boot is close to her leg. Blood runs from her nose across her face. An orange ride-on mower is next to her, overturned on its left side, its wheel turned hard to the right and stuck in reverse. Footage from responding officers, filmed in the early hours of July 30, 2024 and played to a Supreme Court jury this week, shows the former Royal Australian Air Force pilot explaining the lead-up to his wife’s death. He has pleaded not guilty to murder. His defence team says Frances died in a tragic accident. The Crawford property in the Upper Lockyer Valley. Prosecutors say the 49-year-old staged the scene to look like she was killed when the mower she was riding rolled over the wall.



The RAAF pilot was a “love rat”, the prosecution says, whose wife discovered his double life. In admissions to the court, Crawford had a string of extramarital affairs with at least 10 women over a decade, including three air force colleagues. He killed Frances, either through strangulation or with blunt force, so he would not lose millions of dollars in a divorce, the prosecution says. Taking into account settlement finances and Frances’ life insurance policy, her untimely death would become very profitable for Crawford, at about $5.4 million, the jury heard. “Robert Crawford loves money,” Crown prosecutor Chris Cook told the court earlier in the week, “… loved it so much that he killed for it.” Robert Crawford (centre) is on trial, accused of murdering his wife. AAPIMAGE The footage shows Crawford climbing back up the retaining wall in his pyjama shorts and a jumper, on what paramedics would later tell his trial was an “incredibly cold night” in the Upper Lockyer, on the family’s sprawling 40-hectare property, estimated to be worth up to $2.6 million. Crawford told a Triple Zero operator in a 3.37am call that he believed his wife was moving the mower because she was worried about sprinklers coming on.



By 4.27am, Crawford is at the kitchen table, a grey blanket draped over his shoulders. He starts to cry. Sergeant Glen Thomas asks him: “What happened here tonight?” Crawford is softly spoken, often inaudible in the footage, as he talks about how he discovered his wife. A paramedic prepares him a cup of tea as he rocks forward, his forehead almost touching the table. Frances Crawford was found dead at her rural property in the Lockyer Valley. Nine News He tells the officer he went to bed about 11.30pm after studying. He says he believed Frances was watching a Korean show on Netflix. When he woke up and discovered his wife wasn’t in bed, he checked the house, calling “where are you”, he says. “I checked the rooms, the guest rooms and stuff, couldn’t see anything there, couldn’t see anything out the front, couldn’t see anything,” he says.



He talks about taking the mower out to fix the battery, and Frances asking him to move it because their sprinklers were due to come on overnight. Text messages on the pair’s phones discussing the mower have been tendered to the court. Crawford explains he went outside, aided by the torch on his phone, and saw the mower had fallen over the retaining wall. “All I could see was her legs,” he sobs, gesturing with his hands. He says he managed to pull his wife out from under it. In the Triple Zero call, Crawford tells the operator “she is so cold”. A pump, pump, pump noise can be heard in the background as he attempts to resuscitate her. A marriage marred by affairs Just a year before her alleged murder, Frances Crawford stood in her kitchen, a tissue in her hand, surrounded by concerned police.



Her husband lingered outside, dressed in a grey bath robe, his RAAF flight suit peeking out from underneath. Frances was measured and articulate as she told officers what had happened early on July 20, 2023. Frances Crawford’s death came after years of her husband’s extramarital affairs, the court has heard. Though still married, the Crawfords had separated, and she had changed the locks. But her husband broke in that morning, pulling louvres off their patio window. Frances became emotional as she told officers how her husband had cheated on her. “I have forgiven and forgiven and forgiven, I cannot keep going,” she says in the body-worn footage shown to the jury. “For me,” her voice breaks. “I can’t live with that any more. I don’t see that his personality is going to change, and I’ve spent 25 years trying to make peace, trying to make it work.”

World.title: Family wants apology over health minister’s handling of media complaint
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Family wants apology over health minister’s handling of media complaint Matt Dennien October 31, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Brisbane family who publicly shared their fraught health system experience now wants an apology from the minister after he made disputed claims about the saga in parliament and defended this by suggesting speaking to media waived patient confidentiality. Nicole Wilson, 36, says she was left with a heart condition after a close call in late September which saw her driven to hospital by her neighbour, collapsing in front of them in her doorway after three Triple-Zero calls failed to deliver an ambulance to her home. Wilson, an asthmatic who was later told she was lucky to have survived after being diagnosed with a bacterial infection and bilateral pneumonia, detailed her experience alongside mother Marysha Smith in Courier-Mail story published last Friday. Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls is facing calls to apologise over his handling of the matter in parliament. Matt Dennien But the pair are now speaking out again, saying Health Minister Tim Nicholls aired elements of Wilson’s medical history beyond those they themselves shared – and which were untrue – in an attempt to undermine her concerns or scare others into silence.



“He’s lucky I don’t sue him,” Wilson told this masthead when approached about Nicholls’ comments. “It’s wrong”. Australian Medical Association Queensland President Erica Gannon has said even when patients chose to raise issues with their care in the media, “they should still have confidence private details will remain private”. Labor has echoed the calls. Nicole Wilson and her mother, Marysha Smith. The development comes amid growing claims the Crisafulli government has been seeking to silence public criticism, and ongoing health system pressures brought into recent sharp focus by the death of 51-year-old Nick Bradford while waiting for an ambulance. After being asked about the matter during question time on Wednesday, Nicholls described seeking a briefing about the story after being made aware of it and that Wilson had “a significant medical history, including a worsening of her condition for two days [prior].”



“In fact, the clinical notes, as I am advised, report that her mother had requested she go to the hospital but the patient had refused to do so at the time of the worsening of her circumstance,” Nicholls said – which both Wilson and Smith say did not happen. At this point, Deputy Opposition Leader Cameron Dick sought to raise a point of order, saying Nicholls was revealing personal details about the condition of someone who had been in the care of Queensland Health, and the state should be struck from the record. “I am very conscious of my obligations. I know that the details have already been provided by the patient themselves in the Courier-Mail story – the timeframe and details are already there,” Nicholls said, laying out the timeline of calls and call-backs. “I think it is appropriate that where the patient themselves discloses the details to the public, as the member would know, confidentiality is lost.”



Nicholls’ office is yet to respond to questions from this masthead, sent on Thursday, seeking clarification about which specific section of health legislation lays out such a scenario. Nor has it responded to the further comments of Wilson, Smith, Gannon and the opposition. While there are strict rules around the disclosure of patient information, MPs speaking in parliament are protected by parliamentary privilege and accountable only to the rules MPs set themselves around this power. Labor opposition health spokesperson Mark Bailey, in a statement, said Nicholls’ should have reached out to Wilson on hearing of the incident to check on her and assure her it was not acceptable, with government action likely only to lead to more such cases. “Instead, he sought to diminish her difficult experience by breaching her privacy in parliament without her permission,” Bailey said. “Queenslanders expect the government to hear their stories and treat patients with respect.”



Smith said she was unsure how Nicholls had received the disputed detail of events. “I’m just more worried about the ambos – they should have come and got her,” she said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Europeans, Australia object to Russia
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Europeans, Australia object to Russia Michael Koziol Updated October 31, 2026 — 5:50am ,first published 4:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Atlanta: The US was forced to cancel the traditional “family photo” of foreign ministers at the G20 in Atlanta after diplomats from around the world refused to appear alongside Russia’s Sergey Lavrov, who is attending at the invitation of the American hosts. The photo had been scheduled for 10am Friday (Atlanta time) but did not take place. There was no statement from the US about the cancellation, but an official said they did not want the issue to become a distraction. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, second from left, at the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta on Friday (US time). Megan Varner/Pool Reuters via AP Foreign Minister Penny Wong made it known she would not participate in a photograph with Lavrov, a source with knowledge of the matter said. Reuters reported Canada also objected. The Europeans publicly made clear they would boycott any family photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because ... there is no normalcy with Russia,” said German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul ahead of Friday’s session.



Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Milliband, had also signalled that he would not pose with Lavrov. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said. During Friday’s opening session, Wong spoke about the brutality of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in front of Lavrov and their counterparts - including the war’s contribution to food insecurity and pressure on global markets. Foreign Minister Penny Wong, next to her Brazilian counterpart Mauro Vieira, at the G20 in Atlanta. Megan Varner/Pool Reuters via AP A spokesman for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the family photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine,” he said. The incident in Atlanta is the latest fallout from the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its president, Vladimir Putin, into the global economy and community despite the ongoing war against Ukraine, which Putin started.



President Donald Trump recently waived new sanctions that were set to apply to Russia and its trading partners as a result of legislation championed by the late Republican senator Lindsey Graham. He announced plans to buy 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel, and millions more at a later date – though it was not clear Moscow could fulfil the order, with production battered by Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The US has attempted to reintegrate Vladimir Putin’s Russia into the global community. AP Photo/Brynn Anderson Trump has also invited Putin to the G20 leaders’ meeting in Miami in December. It is not clear whether the Russian leader will attend. In Atlanta, Wong held a bilateral meeting with Wadephul, after which the German posted a photograph of them embracing, and praised the free trade deal between Australia and the European Union, which Labor is trying to ratify over Coalition objections.



View post on X Wong was also due to meet with Argentinian Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno and the high representative of the EU, Kaja Kallas. On Saturday, she will attend a meeting of the Quad with India, Japan and the US. She is due to hold a bilateral with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and participate in a trilateral meeting with the UK and Canada. Related Article Opinion

Trump diplomacy Donald Trump is not only coddling Vladimir Putin. He is becoming Vladimir Putin Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Rubio opened the summit by saying the world was in a “moment of choosing”, confronted by threats to energy and food markets, global supply chains and freedom of navigation.



“We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises, many of which pose severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order,” he said at the beginning of the first plenary session, before reporters were evicted. “The G20 must work together to confront these threats.” With Reuters, AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Theatre is Michael Paynter’s ‘idea of hell’ but he’s making an exception for John Farnham
World.content:
The acclaimed performer has a lot in common with the legendary Australian singer he plays in Whispering Jack. And it’s not just that they’ve both been Jesus.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One voice was better than the rest at this year’s AFL grand final, and it wasn’t Kylie Minogue’s. No shade on Kylie but the man who sang the national anthem a cappella had the best pipes on field. That’s not a controversial statement: there’s a rocking power to Michael Paynter’s voice and those who’ve heard it tend to become fans. Anyone, for instance, who saw him in the 2024/25 stage production of Jesus Christ Superstar, for which he received rave reviews and industry awards in the titular role of Jesus. Those, too, who know him as a much-loved part of the Australian music scene, including as a member of the Jimmy Barnes and Icehouse touring bands. And those who went to his The Great Australian Songbook concerts, which began in February as seven gigs and ended up as 30 concerts running right through to September, the venue sizes doubling as they went along. Barring the few songs for which a special guest joins him each night, it’s Paynter solo on stage, with a guitar and a piano, singing household hits such as Flame Trees, You’re the Voice, Even When I’m Sleeping and We Are Australian. So popular has it been that a return Songbook tour was recently announced for 2027, to include more than a dozen regional centres as well as every capital city. Singer, guitarist, pianist – Paynter does the lot, along with being an accomplished songwriter and music producer. But for most at the Melbourne Cricket Ground that last Saturday in September, or watching it on TV, his was not a familiar name. Not like Kylie or even G Flip, her support act. That’s changing fast, however, and will likely shift again when Paynter takes on the role of The Voice himself, John Farnham, in Whispering Jack: The John Farnham Musical. The Sydney Theatre Company will premiere the show on November 15 ahead of a likely national tour with commercial producer Michael Cassel Group and Gaynor Wheatley, the widow of Farnham’s late manager and best friend, Glenn Wheatley. There’s a certain synchronicity to Paynter playing Farnham. Paynter was born in 1986, the year Whispering Jack came out. They’ve both been Jesus in Superstar (Farnham in 1992) and have both done versions of the great Australian songbook (Farnham released a Songbook album in 2005). It’s more than that, though. They both know what it’s like to be the next big thing – then not. And just as Farnham’s second wave came at the age of 37, so Paynter, at 40, appears to be moving from a career supporting others into one in which it’s finally him owning centre stage.



Michael Paynter (Jesus) and Mahalia Barnes (Mary Magdalene) in Jesus Christ Superstar. Jeff Busby I’m meeting Michael Paynter at his favourite cafe in Oakleigh, in Melbourne’s south-east. He walks in punctually and I’m struck by three things I’d noticed at his Sydney Songbook concert back in April. The first: he’s ripped. Paynter is a gym junkie and it’s there in his physique, which he shows off on stage via tight black T-shirts and fitted pants that finish slightly above a set of clean white sneakers, typically worn with invisible socks. Second, he’s a friendly bloke, with more than a dash of the loveable dagginess Farnham was renowned for. Third, he’s a man of God, with a silver cross hanging on a chain around his neck. He wears it offstage and on. The cross makes sense when Paynter tells me he’s the son of pastors, who left their jobs as an art teacher (mum) and bank manager (dad) to set up a non-denominational church on Victoria’s Mornington Peninsula. That was in 1986; he was christened at their first service. Music was a regular part of life for the family, which included daughter Bethany, who also works for the church. “Dad has a great voice and mum’s a great piano player,” Paynter says. He started piano lessons at the age of five and by 12 had also picked up the guitar, mainly to impress girls. It was a happy upbringing, which he’s felt embarrassed about in the past. Not very rock ‘n’ roll, and he very much wanted to be rock ‘n’ roll. “I created a bunch of demons in my closet when I signed to a record label but they were of my own making, because I had a very normal, non-traumatic upbringing.” Loading Related Article Good Weekend She took over as his manager. Now Gaynor Wheatley is helping bring John Farnham’s story to the stage Paynter orders a cold brew, no milk, which I assume is to do with lactose being bad for the voice, which I’ve heard from singers before. “No,” he says with a laugh. “Where you eat and where you breathe are two different holes, so unless you’re lactose-intolerant and it causes problems … ” Most of the ritualistic things singers do “are up here”, he says, tapping his head. “It’s fine, I have them as well.” It’s simply that he really loves coffee. “It’s like whisky – if you have a good whisky don’t put it with coke or ice, just have a whisky.”



When Paynter finished school he enrolled in a double law/business degree at Victoria University. He’d won a statewide school music competition and was performing on the side, and when Mushroom Records founder Michael Gudinski asked him to play guitar for his teen daughter, who went by the stage name of Kate Alexa, he quit the degree to focus on music. Gudinski wasn’t the only bigwig to notice Paynter’s talent. So too did then Sony boss Denis Handlin, who put him on the kind of development deal labels offered budding singer-songwriters back then. “They don’t exist any more but it was kind of like, here’s $5000, come back in five months with five songs, and if they’re good, we’ll sign you and turn them into something.” He came back; they signed him. Paynter spent a decade with Sony, much of it living in Britain and the US, where he joined the songwriting teams for big names including the Black Eyed Peas and James Blunt, and toured with the likes of Seal and Miley Cyrus. “It didn’t make me arrogant – well actually that’s debatable – but it gave me an inner confidence to believe in what I do.” In 2010 he wrote the single Love the Fall, recording it with The Veronicas, who took it to number 19 on the ARIA charts. “Looking back [its success] was because it featured The Veronicas, I’m very aware of that,” he says. “But it was a great song and it opened a lot of doors for me.” Michael Paynter with a poster of John Farnham, after the Whispering Jack announcement in January. Steven Siewert At a certain point the music industry changed, however, and in 2011 Paynter and Sony parted ways. “To invest in a singer or a band and hang in there for the long haul was gone,” he says. “It was the quick buck, TV every night, 10 million eyeballs. It makes complete sense. So they moved to that model and let a lot of singers and bands go.” In his own version of “if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em”, in 2013 Paynter auditioned for the second Australian season of The Voice, where he got as far as the top four before bombing out. “I sang horribly,” he says of his final performance. “TV can be nerve-wracking at the best of times. There was a lot riding on it for me and I wasn’t my best self.” He was by now living back in Melbourne, in his late 20s, and keen to start a family with his wife, Keinzley, who he’s known since kindergarten. “That was the end of me wanting to be an artist,” he says. “I just didn’t want to do it any more. I lost the drive to be famous.”



Instead, he started a business with his friend Michael De Lorenzis to write, mix and record songs for other artists. MSquared ran for 15 years, snaring two ARIAs and three Golden Guitars, before the pair decided to close it last year. In tandem Paynter continued working as a session player – at weddings and pubs, for bands such as Bachelor Girl and Killing Heidi, and for a while, was tour manager for The Veronicas. In 2011 he started playing with Icehouse, then from 2020, with Jimmy Barnes’ band. You’d be lucky to have people speak about you the way people in this industry speak about John. Michael Paynter He and Keinzley had three young daughters and between family life, producing and gig work, he was fully occupied. The last thing he was thinking about was a musical. Then, in 2024, Mahalia Barnes was cast as Mary in a new production of Jesus Christ Superstar. They couldn’t find their Jesus. She knew Paynter through her dad, Jimmy. She knew he dug Jesus. She suggested him and he got the part. “I got two standing ovations a night, in the middle of the show,” says Paynter with incredulity. As Superstar was coming to an end, word started getting around that a Farnham musical was in the works. There’s always a tension in musicals: do you veer towards an actor who can sing or a singer who can act? With a character like Farnham it was a no-brainer: any musical would be stillborn if the lead didn’t have a knockout voice. People started suggesting Paynter, but he initially wasn’t keen. “There’s a lot about theatre I don’t like,” he says bluntly. “You’re doing the same thing, in the same place, at the same time, with the same people, in the same clothes, the same way, for a year. That’s my idea of hell.” The world he was used to was much more free-flowing. “Every stage is new, you’re on a plane every second day. Writing songs you’re in a new studio, with a new person, every time. There’s a lot of movement and that keeps me interested.” It didn’t help that he’d been working at MSquared while doing Jesus Christ Superstar, which meant 9am-5pm songwriting, recording and managing other artists, then jumping in the shower, scoffing down some food, and getting to the theatre for his evening shift.

World.title: Trump revives final midterm rallies after erupting over idea he was ‘sick’
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS midterms Trump revives final midterm rallies after erupting over idea he was ‘sick’ Michael Koziol October 31, 2026 — 5:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Atlanta: US President Donald Trump revived two midterm election rallies the day after cancelling them in an abrupt change of strategy at the end of a long campaign. Trump will now hold in-person rallies on Sunday (US time) in the midwestern states of Kansas and Iowa, where Republicans are fighting to hold seats in the US Senate. Trump tosses hats to a crowd at one of his rallies in Chillicothe, Ohio. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein “Rallies are BACK ON!” a White House official said on Friday. “President Trump loves his supporters, and in addition to nearly 20 ​tele-rallies, he will hold back-to-back rallies ​in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday.” The reversal came less than 24 hours after the Republican National Committee announced Trump’s scheduled rallies would not take place because the party was in a strong position in both those states, and the president would focus on telephone events.



Trump has held rallies nearly every day since the start of October, criss-crossing the country on his taxpayer-funded plane and appearing mostly in red states, or swing states such as Michigan, where Senate contests are especially close. On Thursday, the president unleashed on a reporter who asked whether the Kansas rally had been cancelled because he was “sick of travel”. He appeared to interpret the question as an indictment of his health. Donald Trump bristled at questions about his cancelled rally and told the reporter: ’You look like hell.” X/@CSPAN “You’re sick to ask that question,” Trump told Reuters reporter Jacob Bogage. “Look at this guy, he’s way out of shape. Look at how badly … You are disgusting, put yourself in shape, you look like hell.” Later, an official White House account, Rapid Response 47, posted screenshots taken from Bogage’s personal Instagram page that showed him tasting snacks in a car. The video had been from an unflattering low angle. “Sloppy!” the White House said.



Trump, 80, denied he had any issues keeping up with the travel schedule: “You’ve been following me for two weeks; I feel perfect.” The decision to resurrect the rallies comes as polls suggested Democrats were ahead in Kansas, though within the margin of error. A CNN/SSRS poll had the Republican incumbent Roger Marshall trailing Democrat Adam Hamilton 45-49, in a state that has not sent a Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years. Donald Trump dances at a campaign rally in South Carolina on Thursday. AP Photo/Scott Kinser Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the Senate, with 35 up for re-election this year. It is widely expected Democrats will gain control of the House of Representatives, where Republicans hold a slim majority. Meanwhile, Leo XIV became the first Pope to vote in a US election. The Vatican confirmed the American Pope cast a mail-in ballot in Chicago, where he was born, adding that he had always exercised his right to vote whenever he was eligible to do so.



Related Article US midterms ‘I feel betrayed’: Is the heartland about to turn on Trump and the Republicans? The final stages of the midterm election campaign have been dominated by discourse around Trump’s rally appearances and a bombshell New York Times story revealing the Democrats recruited a so-called “decoy” candidate in Alaska with the same name as the incumbent Republican senator. The Department of Justice is suing the state of Alaska to block certification of the election results in the event Republican Dan Sullivan loses, arguing voters will be confused by the appearance of “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr” on their ballot paper. The paper clearly distinguishes between Dan Sullivan the incumbent Republican and the unaffiliated challenger. Calling into a Kansas City radio station on Friday, Trump suggested voters in Alaska would not understand what the word “incumbent” meant. A sample election ballot is displayed in Anchorage, Alaska. AP



“You need about 190 IQ to figure out the ballot,” he said. “Most people don’t know in Alaska – in a lot of other states too – what does ‘incumbent’ mean? They don’t know what ‘incumbent’ means.” Alaska judge Sharon Gleason set the federal government a Friday afternoon (US time) deadline to respond to the state’s request to dismiss the legal challenge, with a reply deadline set for Saturday. The election is on Tuesday. In some recent rally appearances, Trump has sounded hoarse. He has also attracted attention for occasional vocal slip-ups and his focus on men’s bodies, especially the Republican senator from Ohio, Jon Husted. Loading But the president is doubling down on the routine. On Thursday, he posted a TikTok video praising Husted’s physique.

World.title: This single word will leave you breathless – literally
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

This column has 530 words. Or some 2600 letters, since counting characters is our focus this week. Take titin, say. Not the Belgian journo who takes Snowy the dog on big adventures but a protein boosting a muscle’s elasticity.

Five letters. Two syllables. Titin may seem one more silhouette on the page, until the word performs its own Tardis trick, elasticising outward to reveal its alter ego of methionyl­threonyl­threonyl­glutaminyl­alanyl­prolyl­threonyl­phenylalanyl­threonyl­glutaminyl­prolyl­etc-etc. That’s 102 letters, and just one slice of titin’s polysyllabic heft of 189,819 letters. Give or take, that’s the Gettysburg Address times 167, a speech in which Abraham Lincoln diverted the course of America’s civil war by the time titin had put on its socks.

Mary Poppins’ 34-letter “supercalifragilisticexpialidocious” is nothing compared the full rendering of “titin”.

E. coli is equally windy. Extended fully, the bacterium brags 1909 letters. Chemists in general have an occupational bug for long words, placing a compound’s every element on show, much like a traveller disgorging their suitcase on the customs counter.

Mary Poppins, of course, provided the longest word most of us know. At 34 letters, supercalifragilisticexpialidocious was coined by Robert and Richard Sherman for the 1964 film. Dictionary sleuths have tried to derive the mouthful, sourcing each syllable to define the adjective as “atoning for being teachable via delicate beauty”. Not that meaning matters as much as the delight’s length.

World.title: Concerns for welfare of two Australians after Spanish train crash
World.content:
WorldEuropeAustralians abroad Concerns for welfare of two Australians after Spanish train crash David Crowe and Jack Gramenz Updated October 31, 2026 — 6:06am ,first published 8:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australian authorities are working to confirm the welfare of two Australians linked to this week’s deadly train crash in Spain, amid fears for at least 14 foreign nationals who are listed as missing. A high-speed train on Wednesday smashed into the rear of another on the line running south from Madrid, killing at least 69 people and injuring almost 200. Loading Australian diplomats are supporting the family of two Australians in connection with the collision, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said on Friday. The department expressed its “heartfelt condolences” for all affected by the train crash, but made no comment on the fate of the Australians involved in the tragedy.



“Owing to our privacy obligations, we are unable to provide further comment,” a spokesperson said in a statement. The Spanish foreign ministry initially said that 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, but it outlined new details on Friday afternoon in Madrid – about 2am on Saturday, AEDT – about the countries involved. A crane operates at the site of wrecked train carriages in Spain on Friday. AP Photo/Bernat Armangue The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said there were 51 individuals of 23 different nationalities caught up in the crash, including two confirmed fatalities, but authorities are still working to find missing passengers and identify the dead. Some foreign nationals emerged from the two trains unharmed, Spanish media outlet Heraldo reported on Friday. It cited government sources to report that there were nine injured foreign nationals, two fatalities and 22 whose status was yet to be determined.



The foreign nationals yet to be accounted for come from countries including Argentina, Australia, Canada, Czechia, France, Japan, Mexico, South Korea, Tunisia, the United States and Venezuela, according to multiple reports in Spanish media. Healthcare workers and officials are facing major challenges in establishing the facts and treating the injured. The president of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, Emiliano García-Page, confirmed the death toll of 69 on Friday, but he cautioned that this depended on further work. “We cannot rule out the possibility of more deaths,” he said. The foreign nationals reported dead include one passenger from Portugal and one from Argentina, according to Spanish media.



In a sign of the horrific nature of the crash, emergency workers have been recovering partial remains in the wreckage from the carriages. Officials from the Castilla-La Mancha government said it would take time to identify the dead. “Testing ​is proceeding slowly, although families will be contacted throughout the day so that they can come ⁠and collect their results,” said Esther Padilla, a government spokesperson, on state television network TVE. Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente blamed the disaster on human error, with a control centre in Madrid failing to tell the driver of a high-speed Renfe AVE service that another train, run by private operator Iryo, was stationary on the tracks ahead. But the minister’s comments provoked a furore, with rail unions accusing him of “scapegoating” the rail control workers and demanding his resignation, while the train operators offered different accounts of what drivers had been told.



Related Article Analysis

Tragedy Leaked recordings reveal final moments before the Spanish train disaster The Renfe AVE train had 397 passengers, while the Iryo train was carrying 147. The accident comes with memories still fresh of another crash between high-speed trains in southern Spain in January involving trains from the same two companies. The Spanish accident authority issued a preliminary report estimating the Renfe train ​was travelling at ⁠a speed of between 160km/h and 200km/h when the collision occurred. The public debate about the crash has focused on whether the controller at the Atocha railway station in Madrid told the Renfe driver to “resume normal operations” rather than telling the driver to keep to 40km/h because there was a stationary train ahead.



Related Article Tragedy ‘Inexplicable’: How the catastrophic train crash in Spain unfolded “The sequence of malfunctions, instructions, and actions eventually led to the collision, in the absence of the necessary mitigating barriers,” said the report from the Independent ​Authority for the Technical Investigation of Accidents and Incidents. The rail centre operator who authorised the Renfe AVE train to resume its journey with normal operation, and therefore reach speeds of 160km/h or more, was questioned by authorities on Thursday. Spanish newspaper El País said he invoked his right to remain silent before the Civil Guard. With Reuters Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Inside the crumbling marriage of a ‘love rat’ pilot accused of murder
World.content:
RAAF pilot Robert Crawford is on trial in Brisbane, accused of murdering his wife Frances.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In the cold night air outside his home, Robert Crawford looks up from the bottom of a retaining wall, the glow of a police officer’s torch illuminating his face. His wife, Frances, lies lifeless in her floral pyjamas on the grass. Her hand rests on her chest, and her right ugg boot is close to her leg. Blood runs from her nose across her face. An orange ride-on mower is next to her, overturned on its left side, its wheel turned hard to the right and stuck in reverse. Footage from responding officers, filmed in the early hours of July 30, 2024 and played to a Supreme Court jury this week, shows the former Royal Australian Air Force pilot explaining the lead-up to his wife’s death. He has pleaded not guilty to murder. His defence team says Frances died in a tragic accident. The Crawford property in the Upper Lockyer Valley. Prosecutors say the 49-year-old staged the scene to look like she was killed when the mower she was riding rolled over the wall.



The RAAF pilot was a “love rat”, the prosecution says, whose wife discovered his double life. In admissions to the court, Crawford had a string of extramarital affairs with at least 10 women over a decade, including three air force colleagues. He killed Frances, either through strangulation or with blunt force, so he would not lose millions of dollars in a divorce, the prosecution says. Taking into account settlement finances and Frances’ life insurance policy, her untimely death would become very profitable for Crawford, at about $5.4 million, the jury heard. “Robert Crawford loves money,” Crown prosecutor Chris Cook told the court earlier in the week, “… loved it so much that he killed for it.” Robert Crawford (centre) is on trial, accused of murdering his wife. AAPIMAGE The footage shows Crawford climbing back up the retaining wall in his pyjama shorts and a jumper, on what paramedics would later tell his trial was an “incredibly cold night” in the Upper Lockyer, on the family’s sprawling 40-hectare property, estimated to be worth up to $2.6 million. Crawford told a Triple Zero operator in a 3.37am call that he believed his wife was moving the mower because she was worried about sprinklers coming on.



By 4.27am, Crawford is at the kitchen table, a grey blanket draped over his shoulders. He starts to cry. Sergeant Glen Thomas asks him: “What happened here tonight?” Crawford is softly spoken, often inaudible in the footage, as he talks about how he discovered his wife. A paramedic prepares him a cup of tea as he rocks forward, his forehead almost touching the table. Frances Crawford was found dead at her rural property in the Lockyer Valley. Nine News He tells the officer he went to bed about 11.30pm after studying. He says he believed Frances was watching a Korean show on Netflix. When he woke up and discovered his wife wasn’t in bed, he checked the house, calling “where are you”, he says. “I checked the rooms, the guest rooms and stuff, couldn’t see anything there, couldn’t see anything out the front, couldn’t see anything,” he says.



He talks about taking the mower out to fix the battery, and Frances asking him to move it because their sprinklers were due to come on overnight. Text messages on the pair’s phones discussing the mower have been tendered to the court. Crawford explains he went outside, aided by the torch on his phone, and saw the mower had fallen over the retaining wall. “All I could see was her legs,” he sobs, gesturing with his hands. He says he managed to pull his wife out from under it. In the Triple Zero call, Crawford tells the operator “she is so cold”. A pump, pump, pump noise can be heard in the background as he attempts to resuscitate her. A marriage marred by affairs Just a year before her alleged murder, Frances Crawford stood in her kitchen, a tissue in her hand, surrounded by concerned police.



Her husband lingered outside, dressed in a grey bath robe, his RAAF flight suit peeking out from underneath. Frances was measured and articulate as she told officers what had happened early on July 20, 2023. Frances Crawford’s death came after years of her husband’s extramarital affairs, the court has heard. Though still married, the Crawfords had separated, and she had changed the locks. But her husband broke in that morning, pulling louvres off their patio window. Frances became emotional as she told officers how her husband had cheated on her. “I have forgiven and forgiven and forgiven, I cannot keep going,” she says in the body-worn footage shown to the jury. “For me,” her voice breaks. “I can’t live with that any more. I don’t see that his personality is going to change, and I’ve spent 25 years trying to make peace, trying to make it work.”

World.title: Family wants apology over health minister’s handling of media complaint
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Family wants apology over health minister’s handling of media complaint Matt Dennien October 31, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Brisbane family who publicly shared their fraught health system experience now wants an apology from the minister after he made disputed claims about the saga in parliament and defended this by suggesting speaking to media waived patient confidentiality. Nicole Wilson, 36, says she was left with a heart condition after a close call in late September which saw her driven to hospital by her neighbour, collapsing in front of them in her doorway after three Triple-Zero calls failed to deliver an ambulance to her home. Wilson, an asthmatic who was later told she was lucky to have survived after being diagnosed with a bacterial infection and bilateral pneumonia, detailed her experience alongside mother Marysha Smith in Courier-Mail story published last Friday. Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls is facing calls to apologise over his handling of the matter in parliament. Matt Dennien But the pair are now speaking out again, saying Health Minister Tim Nicholls aired elements of Wilson’s medical history beyond those they themselves shared – and which were untrue – in an attempt to undermine her concerns or scare others into silence.



“He’s lucky I don’t sue him,” Wilson told this masthead when approached about Nicholls’ comments. “It’s wrong”. Australian Medical Association Queensland President Erica Gannon has said even when patients chose to raise issues with their care in the media, “they should still have confidence private details will remain private”. Labor has echoed the calls. Nicole Wilson and her mother, Marysha Smith. The development comes amid growing claims the Crisafulli government has been seeking to silence public criticism, and ongoing health system pressures brought into recent sharp focus by the death of 51-year-old Nick Bradford while waiting for an ambulance. After being asked about the matter during question time on Wednesday, Nicholls described seeking a briefing about the story after being made aware of it and that Wilson had “a significant medical history, including a worsening of her condition for two days [prior].”



“In fact, the clinical notes, as I am advised, report that her mother had requested she go to the hospital but the patient had refused to do so at the time of the worsening of her circumstance,” Nicholls said – which both Wilson and Smith say did not happen. At this point, Deputy Opposition Leader Cameron Dick sought to raise a point of order, saying Nicholls was revealing personal details about the condition of someone who had been in the care of Queensland Health, and the state should be struck from the record. “I am very conscious of my obligations. I know that the details have already been provided by the patient themselves in the Courier-Mail story – the timeframe and details are already there,” Nicholls said, laying out the timeline of calls and call-backs. “I think it is appropriate that where the patient themselves discloses the details to the public, as the member would know, confidentiality is lost.”



Nicholls’ office is yet to respond to questions from this masthead, sent on Thursday, seeking clarification about which specific section of health legislation lays out such a scenario. Nor has it responded to the further comments of Wilson, Smith, Gannon and the opposition. While there are strict rules around the disclosure of patient information, MPs speaking in parliament are protected by parliamentary privilege and accountable only to the rules MPs set themselves around this power. Labor opposition health spokesperson Mark Bailey, in a statement, said Nicholls’ should have reached out to Wilson on hearing of the incident to check on her and assure her it was not acceptable, with government action likely only to lead to more such cases. “Instead, he sought to diminish her difficult experience by breaching her privacy in parliament without her permission,” Bailey said. “Queenslanders expect the government to hear their stories and treat patients with respect.”



Smith said she was unsure how Nicholls had received the disputed detail of events. “I’m just more worried about the ambos – they should have come and got her,” she said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Europeans, Australia object to Russia
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Europeans, Australia object to Russia Michael Koziol Updated October 31, 2026 — 5:50am ,first published 4:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Atlanta: The US was forced to cancel the traditional “family photo” of foreign ministers at the G20 in Atlanta after diplomats from around the world refused to appear alongside Russia’s Sergey Lavrov, who is attending at the invitation of the American hosts. The photo had been scheduled for 10am Friday (Atlanta time) but did not take place. There was no statement from the US about the cancellation, but an official said they did not want the issue to become a distraction. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, second from left, at the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta on Friday (US time). Megan Varner/Pool Reuters via AP Foreign Minister Penny Wong made it known she would not participate in a photograph with Lavrov, a source with knowledge of the matter said. Reuters reported Canada also objected. The Europeans publicly made clear they would boycott any family photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because ... there is no normalcy with Russia,” said German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul ahead of Friday’s session.



Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Milliband, had also signalled that he would not pose with Lavrov. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said. During Friday’s opening session, Wong spoke about the brutality of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in front of Lavrov and their counterparts - including the war’s contribution to food insecurity and pressure on global markets. Foreign Minister Penny Wong, next to her Brazilian counterpart Mauro Vieira, at the G20 in Atlanta. Megan Varner/Pool Reuters via AP A spokesman for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the family photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine,” he said. The incident in Atlanta is the latest fallout from the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its president, Vladimir Putin, into the global economy and community despite the ongoing war against Ukraine, which Putin started.



President Donald Trump recently waived new sanctions that were set to apply to Russia and its trading partners as a result of legislation championed by the late Republican senator Lindsey Graham. He announced plans to buy 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel, and millions more at a later date – though it was not clear Moscow could fulfil the order, with production battered by Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The US has attempted to reintegrate Vladimir Putin’s Russia into the global community. AP Photo/Brynn Anderson Trump has also invited Putin to the G20 leaders’ meeting in Miami in December. It is not clear whether the Russian leader will attend. In Atlanta, Wong held a bilateral meeting with Wadephul, after which the German posted a photograph of them embracing, and praised the free trade deal between Australia and the European Union, which Labor is trying to ratify over Coalition objections.



View post on X Wong was also due to meet with Argentinian Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno and the high representative of the EU, Kaja Kallas. On Saturday, she will attend a meeting of the Quad with India, Japan and the US. She is due to hold a bilateral with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and participate in a trilateral meeting with the UK and Canada. Related Article Opinion

Trump diplomacy Donald Trump is not only coddling Vladimir Putin. He is becoming Vladimir Putin Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Rubio opened the summit by saying the world was in a “moment of choosing”, confronted by threats to energy and food markets, global supply chains and freedom of navigation.



“We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises, many of which pose severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order,” he said at the beginning of the first plenary session, before reporters were evicted. “The G20 must work together to confront these threats.” With Reuters, AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Theatre is Michael Paynter’s ‘idea of hell’ but he’s making an exception for John Farnham
World.content:
The acclaimed performer has a lot in common with the legendary Australian singer he plays in Whispering Jack. And it’s not just that they’ve both been Jesus.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One voice was better than the rest at this year’s AFL grand final, and it wasn’t Kylie Minogue’s. No shade on Kylie but the man who sang the national anthem a cappella had the best pipes on field. That’s not a controversial statement: there’s a rocking power to Michael Paynter’s voice and those who’ve heard it tend to become fans. Anyone, for instance, who saw him in the 2024/25 stage production of Jesus Christ Superstar, for which he received rave reviews and industry awards in the titular role of Jesus. Those, too, who know him as a much-loved part of the Australian music scene, including as a member of the Jimmy Barnes and Icehouse touring bands. And those who went to his The Great Australian Songbook concerts, which began in February as seven gigs and ended up as 30 concerts running right through to September, the venue sizes doubling as they went along. Barring the few songs for which a special guest joins him each night, it’s Paynter solo on stage, with a guitar and a piano, singing household hits such as Flame Trees, You’re the Voice, Even When I’m Sleeping and We Are Australian. So popular has it been that a return Songbook tour was recently announced for 2027, to include more than a dozen regional centres as well as every capital city. Singer, guitarist, pianist – Paynter does the lot, along with being an accomplished songwriter and music producer. But for most at the Melbourne Cricket Ground that last Saturday in September, or watching it on TV, his was not a familiar name. Not like Kylie or even G Flip, her support act. That’s changing fast, however, and will likely shift again when Paynter takes on the role of The Voice himself, John Farnham, in Whispering Jack: The John Farnham Musical. The Sydney Theatre Company will premiere the show on November 15 ahead of a likely national tour with commercial producer Michael Cassel Group and Gaynor Wheatley, the widow of Farnham’s late manager and best friend, Glenn Wheatley. There’s a certain synchronicity to Paynter playing Farnham. Paynter was born in 1986, the year Whispering Jack came out. They’ve both been Jesus in Superstar (Farnham in 1992) and have both done versions of the great Australian songbook (Farnham released a Songbook album in 2005). It’s more than that, though. They both know what it’s like to be the next big thing – then not. And just as Farnham’s second wave came at the age of 37, so Paynter, at 40, appears to be moving from a career supporting others into one in which it’s finally him owning centre stage.



Michael Paynter (Jesus) and Mahalia Barnes (Mary Magdalene) in Jesus Christ Superstar. Jeff Busby I’m meeting Michael Paynter at his favourite cafe in Oakleigh, in Melbourne’s south-east. He walks in punctually and I’m struck by three things I’d noticed at his Sydney Songbook concert back in April. The first: he’s ripped. Paynter is a gym junkie and it’s there in his physique, which he shows off on stage via tight black T-shirts and fitted pants that finish slightly above a set of clean white sneakers, typically worn with invisible socks. Second, he’s a friendly bloke, with more than a dash of the loveable dagginess Farnham was renowned for. Third, he’s a man of God, with a silver cross hanging on a chain around his neck. He wears it offstage and on. The cross makes sense when Paynter tells me he’s the son of pastors, who left their jobs as an art teacher (mum) and bank manager (dad) to set up a non-denominational church on Victoria’s Mornington Peninsula. That was in 1986; he was christened at their first service. Music was a regular part of life for the family, which included daughter Bethany, who also works for the church. “Dad has a great voice and mum’s a great piano player,” Paynter says. He started piano lessons at the age of five and by 12 had also picked up the guitar, mainly to impress girls. It was a happy upbringing, which he’s felt embarrassed about in the past. Not very rock ‘n’ roll, and he very much wanted to be rock ‘n’ roll. “I created a bunch of demons in my closet when I signed to a record label but they were of my own making, because I had a very normal, non-traumatic upbringing.” Loading Related Article Good Weekend She took over as his manager. Now Gaynor Wheatley is helping bring John Farnham’s story to the stage Paynter orders a cold brew, no milk, which I assume is to do with lactose being bad for the voice, which I’ve heard from singers before. “No,” he says with a laugh. “Where you eat and where you breathe are two different holes, so unless you’re lactose-intolerant and it causes problems … ” Most of the ritualistic things singers do “are up here”, he says, tapping his head. “It’s fine, I have them as well.” It’s simply that he really loves coffee. “It’s like whisky – if you have a good whisky don’t put it with coke or ice, just have a whisky.”



When Paynter finished school he enrolled in a double law/business degree at Victoria University. He’d won a statewide school music competition and was performing on the side, and when Mushroom Records founder Michael Gudinski asked him to play guitar for his teen daughter, who went by the stage name of Kate Alexa, he quit the degree to focus on music. Gudinski wasn’t the only bigwig to notice Paynter’s talent. So too did then Sony boss Denis Handlin, who put him on the kind of development deal labels offered budding singer-songwriters back then. “They don’t exist any more but it was kind of like, here’s $5000, come back in five months with five songs, and if they’re good, we’ll sign you and turn them into something.” He came back; they signed him. Paynter spent a decade with Sony, much of it living in Britain and the US, where he joined the songwriting teams for big names including the Black Eyed Peas and James Blunt, and toured with the likes of Seal and Miley Cyrus. “It didn’t make me arrogant – well actually that’s debatable – but it gave me an inner confidence to believe in what I do.” In 2010 he wrote the single Love the Fall, recording it with The Veronicas, who took it to number 19 on the ARIA charts. “Looking back [its success] was because it featured The Veronicas, I’m very aware of that,” he says. “But it was a great song and it opened a lot of doors for me.” Michael Paynter with a poster of John Farnham, after the Whispering Jack announcement in January. Steven Siewert At a certain point the music industry changed, however, and in 2011 Paynter and Sony parted ways. “To invest in a singer or a band and hang in there for the long haul was gone,” he says. “It was the quick buck, TV every night, 10 million eyeballs. It makes complete sense. So they moved to that model and let a lot of singers and bands go.” In his own version of “if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em”, in 2013 Paynter auditioned for the second Australian season of The Voice, where he got as far as the top four before bombing out. “I sang horribly,” he says of his final performance. “TV can be nerve-wracking at the best of times. There was a lot riding on it for me and I wasn’t my best self.” He was by now living back in Melbourne, in his late 20s, and keen to start a family with his wife, Keinzley, who he’s known since kindergarten. “That was the end of me wanting to be an artist,” he says. “I just didn’t want to do it any more. I lost the drive to be famous.”



Instead, he started a business with his friend Michael De Lorenzis to write, mix and record songs for other artists. MSquared ran for 15 years, snaring two ARIAs and three Golden Guitars, before the pair decided to close it last year. In tandem Paynter continued working as a session player – at weddings and pubs, for bands such as Bachelor Girl and Killing Heidi, and for a while, was tour manager for The Veronicas. In 2011 he started playing with Icehouse, then from 2020, with Jimmy Barnes’ band. You’d be lucky to have people speak about you the way people in this industry speak about John. Michael Paynter He and Keinzley had three young daughters and between family life, producing and gig work, he was fully occupied. The last thing he was thinking about was a musical. Then, in 2024, Mahalia Barnes was cast as Mary in a new production of Jesus Christ Superstar. They couldn’t find their Jesus. She knew Paynter through her dad, Jimmy. She knew he dug Jesus. She suggested him and he got the part. “I got two standing ovations a night, in the middle of the show,” says Paynter with incredulity. As Superstar was coming to an end, word started getting around that a Farnham musical was in the works. There’s always a tension in musicals: do you veer towards an actor who can sing or a singer who can act? With a character like Farnham it was a no-brainer: any musical would be stillborn if the lead didn’t have a knockout voice. People started suggesting Paynter, but he initially wasn’t keen. “There’s a lot about theatre I don’t like,” he says bluntly. “You’re doing the same thing, in the same place, at the same time, with the same people, in the same clothes, the same way, for a year. That’s my idea of hell.” The world he was used to was much more free-flowing. “Every stage is new, you’re on a plane every second day. Writing songs you’re in a new studio, with a new person, every time. There’s a lot of movement and that keeps me interested.” It didn’t help that he’d been working at MSquared while doing Jesus Christ Superstar, which meant 9am-5pm songwriting, recording and managing other artists, then jumping in the shower, scoffing down some food, and getting to the theatre for his evening shift.

World.title: Trump revives final midterm rallies after erupting over idea he was ‘sick’
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS midterms Trump revives final midterm rallies after erupting over idea he was ‘sick’ Michael Koziol October 31, 2026 — 5:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Atlanta: US President Donald Trump revived two midterm election rallies the day after cancelling them in an abrupt change of strategy at the end of a long campaign. Trump will now hold in-person rallies on Sunday (US time) in the midwestern states of Kansas and Iowa, where Republicans are fighting to hold seats in the US Senate. Trump tosses hats to a crowd at one of his rallies in Chillicothe, Ohio. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein “Rallies are BACK ON!” a White House official said on Friday. “President Trump loves his supporters, and in addition to nearly 20 ​tele-rallies, he will hold back-to-back rallies ​in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday.” The reversal came less than 24 hours after the Republican National Committee announced Trump’s scheduled rallies would not take place because the party was in a strong position in both those states, and the president would focus on telephone events.



Trump has held rallies nearly every day since the start of October, criss-crossing the country on his taxpayer-funded plane and appearing mostly in red states, or swing states such as Michigan, where Senate contests are especially close. On Thursday, the president unleashed on a reporter who asked whether the Kansas rally had been cancelled because he was “sick of travel”. He appeared to interpret the question as an indictment of his health. Donald Trump bristled at questions about his cancelled rally and told the reporter: ’You look like hell.” X/@CSPAN “You’re sick to ask that question,” Trump told Reuters reporter Jacob Bogage. “Look at this guy, he’s way out of shape. Look at how badly … You are disgusting, put yourself in shape, you look like hell.” Later, an official White House account, Rapid Response 47, posted screenshots taken from Bogage’s personal Instagram page that showed him tasting snacks in a car. The video had been from an unflattering low angle. “Sloppy!” the White House said.



Trump, 80, denied he had any issues keeping up with the travel schedule: “You’ve been following me for two weeks; I feel perfect.” The decision to resurrect the rallies comes as polls suggested Democrats were ahead in Kansas, though within the margin of error. A CNN/SSRS poll had the Republican incumbent Roger Marshall trailing Democrat Adam Hamilton 45-49, in a state that has not sent a Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years. Donald Trump dances at a campaign rally in South Carolina on Thursday. AP Photo/Scott Kinser Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the Senate, with 35 up for re-election this year. It is widely expected Democrats will gain control of the House of Representatives, where Republicans hold a slim majority. Meanwhile, Leo XIV became the first Pope to vote in a US election. The Vatican confirmed the American Pope cast a mail-in ballot in Chicago, where he was born, adding that he had always exercised his right to vote whenever he was eligible to do so.



Related Article US midterms ‘I feel betrayed’: Is the heartland about to turn on Trump and the Republicans? The final stages of the midterm election campaign have been dominated by discourse around Trump’s rally appearances and a bombshell New York Times story revealing the Democrats recruited a so-called “decoy” candidate in Alaska with the same name as the incumbent Republican senator. The Department of Justice is suing the state of Alaska to block certification of the election results in the event Republican Dan Sullivan loses, arguing voters will be confused by the appearance of “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr” on their ballot paper. The paper clearly distinguishes between Dan Sullivan the incumbent Republican and the unaffiliated challenger. Calling into a Kansas City radio station on Friday, Trump suggested voters in Alaska would not understand what the word “incumbent” meant. A sample election ballot is displayed in Anchorage, Alaska. AP



“You need about 190 IQ to figure out the ballot,” he said. “Most people don’t know in Alaska – in a lot of other states too – what does ‘incumbent’ mean? They don’t know what ‘incumbent’ means.” Alaska judge Sharon Gleason set the federal government a Friday afternoon (US time) deadline to respond to the state’s request to dismiss the legal challenge, with a reply deadline set for Saturday. The election is on Tuesday. In some recent rally appearances, Trump has sounded hoarse. He has also attracted attention for occasional vocal slip-ups and his focus on men’s bodies, especially the Republican senator from Ohio, Jon Husted. Loading But the president is doubling down on the routine. On Thursday, he posted a TikTok video praising Husted’s physique.
