World.title: This single word will leave you breathless – literally
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

This column has 530 words. Or some 2600 letters, since counting characters is our focus this week. Take titin, say. Not the Belgian journo who takes Snowy the dog on big adventures but a protein boosting a muscle’s elasticity.

Five letters. Two syllables. Titin may seem one more silhouette on the page, until the word performs its own Tardis trick, elasticising outward to reveal its alter ego of methionyl­threonyl­threonyl­glutaminyl­alanyl­prolyl­threonyl­phenylalanyl­threonyl­glutaminyl­prolyl­etc-etc. That’s 102 letters, and just one slice of titin’s polysyllabic heft of 189,819 letters. Give or take, that’s the Gettysburg Address times 167, a speech in which Abraham Lincoln diverted the course of America’s civil war by the time titin had put on its socks.

Mary Poppins’ 34-letter “supercalifragilisticexpialidocious” is nothing compared the full rendering of “titin”.

E. coli is equally windy. Extended fully, the bacterium brags 1909 letters. Chemists in general have an occupational bug for long words, placing a compound’s every element on show, much like a traveller disgorging their suitcase on the customs counter.

Mary Poppins, of course, provided the longest word most of us know. At 34 letters, supercalifragilisticexpialidocious was coined by Robert and Richard Sherman for the 1964 film. Dictionary sleuths have tried to derive the mouthful, sourcing each syllable to define the adjective as “atoning for being teachable via delicate beauty”. Not that meaning matters as much as the delight’s length.

World.title: Can the health system deliver parties' election promises?
World.content:
Hot on the heels of a hard-hitting flu season, healthcare has become one of the major election issues. As 7 November approaches, the parties are offering cheaper access, more medicines and new services - but can the health system actually deliver them? Health correspondent Kate Green reports.

Free visits to the doctor? Free dental care? Or a brand new cancer treatment centre?

Political parties have put forward a raft of ideas to improve the state of the system, from free care to funding boosts to new taxes ringfenced for health.

See a list of every political party's election policies on health here.

But according to Professor Frank Frizelle ONZM, surgeon and editor-in-chief of the New Zealand Medical Journal, policies and outcomes are not the same thing.

Free GP consultations would still require GPs, just as lowering the bowel screening age would require enough colonoscopy, pathology and treatment capacity, while funding more cancer drugs would require oncology capacity, he said.

He compared this year's election promises to patching holes rather than addressing the underlying problem.

"Everyone's thinking very short term with health and it's very hard to see how continuing to do minor adjustments is going to change the fundamental issue we have, which is that we've got an ageing population."

Professor Frank Frizelle. Michael Bradley

Health targets here to stay

The government's most recent health target results show the postcode lottery remains a barrier to care. Nationally, all five targets had improved on the year before, but in the Northland and Southern districts, more than 40 percent of patients were waiting longer than the target of four months for elective treatments.

Compared with the previous quarter, emergency department wait times improved in half of the country's health districts, while the other half went backwards.

Labour has said it would keep coalition government's health targets if elected.

Focus on primary care and early detection

Labour has promised three free doctor's appointments a year, funded by its new capital gains tax, as well as free prescriptions, maternity scans and cervical screening.

ACT has promised a $400 million funding boost aimed at retaining more GPs in New Zealand and attracting more from overseas.

The Greens want to provide free dental care.

NZ First is promising to focus on prevention by embedding good nutrition into the school curriculum, focusing on metabolic health to prevent chronic illness, funding research into how nutrition can prevent or treat mental illness and investing in hospital trials of how effective intravenous vitamin C pre- and post-surgery is for treating infection.

And Opportunity wants to work across the aisle to establish a 10-year health plan, increase health spending from the current 7.4 percent of GDP to 9 percent, and increase the proportion going to primary care.

Grey Power NZ Federation national president David Marshall. Supplied / Grey Power

David Marshall, national president of Grey Power, said access to primary care was important for seniors.

"If people are seen early, you prevent deterioration and getting into hospital and clogging up the system and poorer outcomes," he said.

While some Grey Power members didn't believe they needed free GP visits, Marshall said cost was a real barrier for others. Delaying treatment could mean their condition worsened, eventually requiring hospital care and adding to pressure there.

But he raised the same question as Frizelle: "Do we have the GPs available to service that?"

He also wanted more commitment from parties to supporting aged care.

"We really don't want older people having to be in hospital, which once again is very expensive," Marshall said. "It would be far better that they could be cared for in home or in residential care. But of course, there's not enough beds at the moment."

Malcolm Mulholland, chair of Patient Voice Aotearoa, said the Greens' dental policy could help a large number of people and argued it could save the country millions of dollars.

A dentist in Timaru had told him he was performing a huge number of teeth extractions, and characterised the state of children's dental care as "a total disintegration of services".

Medicines and cancer care

The National Party wants to redirect foreign aid money into funding for new medicines, and would continue to pursue its health targets.

ACT wants to build New Zealand's first dedicated national cancer centre, as well as allowing pharmacists to treat and manage more conditions.

The National-led government has already boosted Pharmac's budget and funded a series of new cancer drugs.

Patient Voice Aotearoa chair Malcolm Mulholland. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

But Mulholland described the increase as a "sugar hit".

"[The improvements] won't be obvious to the public, but they certainly will be by the end of next year, I would expect.

"The bit that we need the politicians to focus on is what they're responsible for, and that is the budget that Pharmac receives," he said. "Give us a plan by which we can catch up with the rest of the world, a plan that preferably would have multi-partisan support."

Frizelle said no matter who people normally voted for, health was a "significant issue" this election.

World.title: New arrangement for rugby in Samoa
World.content:
World Rugby has confirmed that the Samoa Association of Sports and National Olympic Committee SASNOC will now oversee the high-performance rugby programme in Samoa.

A statement issued on Friday said this was agreed by the Government of Samoa, Lakapi Samoa and the Samoa National Olympic Committee during meetings held in Apia on Thursday.

The meetings were attended by World Rugby chairman Brett Robinson.

SASNOC will work with an appointed stewardship group.

Lakapi Samoa billboard in Apia. RNZ Pacific / Talaia Mika

World Rugby said the group and SASNOC shall be responsible for all matters on and off the field relating to the national teams, including their preparation and participation in global elite competitions such as Men's Rugby World Cup 2027.

The stakeholders have agreed a process to ensure Samoa and its players continue competing at the sport's highest levels during a governance review.

The agreement follows productive meetings in Apia this week led by Robinson and Prime Minister of Samoa, Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Polataivao Fosi Schmidt and Lakapi Samoa.

"The agreed steps address concerns about Lakapi Samoa's governance and administration raised with World Rugby earlier this year by the Hon. Prime Minister on behalf of the Government," World Rugby said in a statement.

"Those concerns, and those of other rugby stakeholders, prompted immediate dialogue between all parties to resolve the issues and agree a way forward.

"All parties agreed that it was imperative that the union's high-performance programmes remain unaffected, with Samoa's national teams committed to participating in Men's Rugby World Cup 2027, the World Rugby Nations Cup, WXV Global Series Challenger and sevens programmes."

Part of the agreed steps to be taken includes the 'self-suspension' of Lakapi Samoa from the World Rugby Council.

"This self-suspension can only be lifted by a future request to the Executive Board of World Rugby and a subsequent recommendation to the World Rugby Council," World Rugby said.

"In any event, the self-suspension shall remain in place during the review processes referenced below."

Samoa Rugby Football Union launch on 31 July 2026. Youtube / Talamua Media

The appointment of a Samoan-led Independent Review Group, the membership of which shall be agreed by Lakapi Samoa and the Government of Samoa, to review all issues pertaining to the governance of Samoan rugby will also be done.

Plus a review of Lakapi Samoa's compliance with World Rugby's membership criteria by a World Rugby oversight committee.

All parties agreed that domestic rugby activities taking place in Samoa shall remain unaffected.

Government withdrew their support of Lakapi Samoa three months ago, with a new union set up by former Manu Samoa players.

World.title: Government shelves proposed system to 'transform' responses to family violence
World.content:
The Government has shelved a system that would have supported more "timely multi-agency responses" to family violence and alerted staff to "high-risk situations".

Documents released under the Official Information Act (OIA) obtained by RNZ says the proposed integrated case management project, which had already had $2m spent on it, was paused last year "as there was no practicable or sustainable way to fund, host and operate the proposed platform".

Officials said agencies would continue with the status quo in the interim, which had several risks, including agencies lacking a shared view of information needed for "effective triage and risk assessment" and "vulnerabilities with regard to data security and information sharing".

Minister for the Prevention of Family Violence and Sexual Violence Karen Chhour said while the technology component of the project was on pause, she had been assured non-technical elements of the "best practice operating model" for multi-agency responses continued to progress.

This included the high-risk protocol and information sharing guidance.

"The decision to pause Project Whetū has not resulted in any reduction to frontline services. This decision will be reviewed in the future and, if practical or sustainable way to host and operate the proposed platform can be found, the technology component of Project Whetū could be resumed.

"This is also subject to any directives from the Government Chief Digital Officer."

Labour's police spokesperson Ginny Andersen said the decision was "an absolute shocker".

"The Government is scrapping a project designed to help agencies identify people at risk of family violence - despite officials warning that without it, vital information cannot easily be shared.

"When agencies can't join the dots, people at risk can fall through the cracks. The consequences can be devastating. The Government should be strengthening the response to family violence. They need to explain why they are walking away."

Minister for the Prevention of Family Violence and Sexual Violence Karen Chhour RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Documents shed light on decision to pause proposed system

RNZ has obtained documents released by Chhour's office, which shed light on decision-making related to the proposed system.

The Centre for Family Violence and Sexual Violence Prevention earlier proposed a new technology solution, Project Whetū, to "transform how agencies share information safely and appropriately to support multi-agency family violence responses".

Project Whetū aimed to introduce a case management system that would support "more effective, coordinated and timely multi-agency responses to family violence".

It would also make children "more visible to help ensure they have appropriate support in place", improve data security and "alert staff to high-risk situations".

However, in December 2025, the executive board for the Elimination of Family Violence and Sexual Violence had decided to pause the project "as there was no practicable or sustainable way to fund, host and operate the proposed platform".

At that stage $2m had been spent over two years. The board approved about $5.2m to be returned to the Crown.

In the meantime, agencies would continue to use existing systems, the documents said.

"Officials are exploring various contingencies, including an Excel-based form. There are pros and cons to this; for now, it is the only affordable (i.e. no-cost) option."

Officials said there were risks with the status quo.

"Without a fit-for-purpose integrated case management system, agencies lack a shared view of the information needed for effective triage and risk assessment."

Agencies would also continue to rely mainly on manual processes, "which constrains efficiencies and reduces the potential return on investment".

There were also "vulnerabilities" in relation to data security and information sharing.

World.title: Fetu Samoa beat England to seal historic World Cup semi-final spot
World.content:
Fetu Samoa has made history, reaching its first Rugby League World Cup semi-final with a 24-6 win over England in Wollongong on Friday night.

Five tries to one in Samoa's favour guaranteed their spot alongside Australia in the last four next weekend.

They will meet New Zealand in the semi-finals, as the runner-up from Pool A.

Players and fans celebrated the historic moment as the final whistle went at the WIN Stadium, as England were denied making their third straight semi-final appearance.

Captain Evania Isa'ako said the job was not done yet and praised the team for the historic win.

"It's pretty cool to be honest," she said post-match.

"Just so proud of all the girls, They really showed up for one another and they just keep turning up. Thank you to everyone who turned up to support us, to watch us go and make history.

But the jobs is not done. You know you realty wanna play for the people and those standing in front of you."

She also paid tribute to head coach Frank Pritchard, who she said has done so much for the team and the game in Samoa.

Pritchard said he was proud of the team and pointed to starting well as the key for them.

"Very overwhelming. Yeah, it definitely hasn't sunk in yet but I think once again, it's changing with the team, and we speak about it," he said at the post-match press conference.

It was important for us to start strong in that second half, and you know we got the penalty, we worked our way down, and we scored the try.

So, it was just a very focused thing for us and we spoke about that all week, being about us, and I thought the team done it really well."

Co-captain Annetta Nuuausala said England gave them a tough time in the match.

"Honestly, it didn't feel dominant because they were like, running into them, was like running into a brick wall," she said.

"They really gave it to us in that first half. They just kept coming back, no matter how hard we were running or whatever structure we threw at them.

"They still kept coming at us, and they made it really hard for us."

First half dominance

Samoa laid the challenge with their siva tau and then rocked England in the first 35 minutes spell, leading 12-0 at half-time.

Winger, 18 year old Freedom Crichton Ropati scored three tries in the half, as Samoa dominated play with the wind behind them.

Playmaker Pauline Piliae-Rasabale missed her three conversion attempts.

England kicked off proceedings through Georgia Roche, as the two teams went into battle, looking for the win to push them into the semi-finals.

Fetu Samoa completed their first set of six, but England showed intensity on defence early as they threw some big hits.

However, Samoa kept their cool and Pliae-Rasabale switched the attack button on deep inside the English half, sending a high kick up towards England's Fran Goldthorp, who knocked the ball on, presenting Samoa with an early opportunity.

But Destiny Mino-Sinapati lost the ball over the line as she dived over in the corner.

Samoa's consistent pressure saw Ropati claiming her first try in the eighth minute, before she also got over the line in the same right hand corner in the 18th and 30th minutes.

They led 12-0 at half-time.

Christabelle Onesemo-Tuilaepa, Ivana Lolesio, Tavana Papalii and Annetta Nuuausala led their forward pack on attacks through the middle of the field.

Isa'ako said at half-time that the pressure was on, and England did not hold back.

"They matched us on physicality," Isa'ako said after the first half.

"We just need to go back and get better in the second half."

Wrapping up

England had the wind behind them in the second spell but Samoa claimed the first try of the second spell and wrapped up the game with two tries at the end of the second spell.

That first try came through Mercedez Taulelei-Siala, who got over in the corner after another impressive Samoan attack.

England claimed their try in the 42nd minute, with Evie Cousins reaching over the line to score, after failed Samoan attempts to stop her near the line.

Piliae-Rasabale kicked a penalty after England were penalised for stripping the ball in a tackle just outside the England 10 metre line before Fanua Rimoni dived over between the posts and under the crossbar to seal the deal for Samoa.

The conversion by Piliae-Rasabale added the extra two points as Samoa marched into the semi-final for the first time.

Meanwhile, Papua New Guinea Kumuls have ended their campaign at the world cup following their 34-12 loss to England last night.

PNG trailed 24-0 at half-time in the clash before they scored two of their own tries through Dudley Dotoi and Gairo Voro, which were both converted by retiring captain Rhyse Martin.

England scored six tries in the match

World.title: Country Life: Makahuri - from former boarding school to village
World.content:
A decade after Drew Mackenzie and Anthony Ryan bought a derelict Catholic convent on the Kāpiti Coast a village is taking shape.

The sign on the gate says, "people and dogs running free", but the project has not been without struggles.

Makahuri, in Te Horo, was once Marycrest - a boarding school for girls which closed in the early 1980s - leaving classrooms, a chapel, paddocks and dormitories to the pigeons and vandals until, in 2016, its new owners came along.

With people seeking accommodation and keen on a village lifestyle, the couple decided to invite others in, turning the buildings into homes and shared spaces, an idea developed in Denmark in the 1960s.

"If I could see this 10 years ago, would I have done it? I probably would have, you know, for all its battles," Mackenzie told Country Life.

Audio player for " It takes a village " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/country/2254389%2Fcountry-life-makahuri-from-former-boarding-school-to-village

It takes a village Country Life Download MP3 14m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

It's been a protracted process navigating regulations and council requirements, she said.

"We kept trying to say we're not a subdivision, that's not what we're about."

The 14.6-hectare property at Te Horo, south of Ōtaki, includes a hotch potch of former school buildings and a homestead, where Mackenzie and Ryan live, plus an ancient stand of native forest and paddocks which are being planted as part of the Ōtaki Carbon Forest Project.

The entryway to Makahuri RNZ/Sally Round

Drew checks out some of the new plantings on the property RNZ/Sally Round

The buildings had lain empty for seven years before the couple and their family moved in.

"We've replaced, we think, probably around 2000 windows since we got here. Most of the windows were broken. People have been coming in, ripping out the nice native timbers."

Work is ongoing as consents allow and residents include students, retirees, full-time workers and families - aged from under a year to 90.

The aim is to have about 14 households either buying their apartments under a body corporate system or renting, Mackenzie said.

"Makahuri is a sustainable, safe, creative and harmonious co-housing community. It is a place of beauty where the mauri, forest, land, people and animals are honoured and respected by all," its vision statement reads.

"People often have asked if we're a commune, which we're so not, and even 'community' has connotation that you're living in each other's pockets and we don't do that. We are a village.

"I think of villages of old and how they just lived in an area together and they knew each other and supported each other, and they didn't necessarily even get on all the time but they had each other's backs regardless and that's us, that's how we are. We're a village."

Berylla on the steps of her home RNZ/Sally Round

Berylla Jones moved in during the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020. She grew up on a farm and liked the idea of being in the country as well as village-style living.

"There's a diversity of people, so there's a diversity of ideas. There's like support around if you need support. When my partner died during Covid, it was really lovely to have villagers here to, you know, be here supporting."

Jones' quilts adorn the walls of the former chapel now used for community events, exercise classes and meetings.

The community garden at Makahuri RNZ/Sally Round

Residents pay a co-housing fee to run the vegetable garden. They pay for wheelbarrows of wood collected from the property as well as eggs from the chickens looked after by Makahuri's oldest resident.

"We have our own recycling station and John manages that. Anything you want fixed; you can take it to John. So, if you break a shovel handle, you just take it to John. He fixes it for you. And his wife, Blossom, who's 82, I think, she just feeds everybody and she's a fabulous gardener.

"She's one of our wise people of the village."

Jess, one of Makahuri's residents with her baby RNZ/Sally Round

Mackenzie said Makahuri had experienced significant tensions and difficult periods but has treated each problem as an opportunity to improve its clarity and processes.

"We've never got to the point that we looked like we were going to fall over but there have been times when there has been huge issues going on. But every one of them we've learnt from, every one of them we thought it's because we weren't clear or we didn't have a process and so with every point of tension we develop better as human beings and as a village."

World.title: South Auckland teacher uses rugby league stars to inspire Pacific kids to read
World.content:
With the 2026 Rugby League World Cup in full swing, a South Auckland teacher is highlighting some of the tournament's biggest stars to encourage Pacific kids to read.

David Riley, a former Tangaroa College teacher in Ōtara, has released a new series of books called Rugby League All Stars, focusing on players like Brian To'o, Jason Taumalolo, Isaiah Katoa, as well as the Samoan and Tongan national teams.

But his passion for the sport goes back much further than this recent tournament.

"That's cool that you went back to when I was born, because my dad's Australian, so he brought us up with rugby league. We played from the age of five, for the Manukau Magpies Rugby League Club ... it's in the DNA," Riley said.

However, the idea for the Rugby League All Stars series was born out of seeing the waves of Tongan fans pouring into Eden Park for last year's Pacific Championships game against the Kiwis.

Actor Beulah Koale reading the Brian To'o book with his twin boys. Supplied

"There were kids everywhere, dressed in red and flags and everything. The sipi tau started, and they all knew the words. I was just watching them, like really fascinated, seeing how they knew the words and they were chanting everything. I was thinking, man, there's a lot of literacy here that we can we can tap into. For Samoan children and Tongan children, I know how much they love their sport team, and they love their culture. I knew that we could use that to get them reading, and to inspire them," Riley said.

Riley has released other series related to Pasifika culture, as well as sports like rugby union and professional wrestling, and he adds that libraries are also yearning for these types of books.

"There's not a lot of written material for Pacific young people, so libraries and librarians are looking for content that they can give to Pacific children. I come from a teaching background, so I'm always concerned and caring for our kids' educational achievement and academic achievement at school, and a lot of that is to do with reading," said Mr Riley.

Riley hoped his stories can provide an alternative to the more negative content they might see on social media or TV.

"I think it's important to counter that and push back with stories that inspire and give hope for children about you know the future, about who they are, where they come from, and what the future can look like for them," said Mr Riley.

While he doesn't get much feedback from the kids themselves, librarians have shared some cool stories about how in demand these books have become.

"One librarian told me that three boys sneaked into the library before she even got to school to wait for her, so that they could get the books before their friends could. So I knew that our kids would feel this way about these books," said Mr Riley.

Looking ahead, with permission from Tonga Rugby League and Samoan Rugby League, he is also working on books about Toa Samoa's Siva Tau and Tonga's Sipi Tau - which are the traditional war dances or challenges the teams perform at the start of games.

"[It's about] finding connections between the words of the Siva Tau and life for the children. They can use some of the ideas in the Siva Tau, not only to do with playing a game against another team, but also how you can carry that same spirit into other areas of your life, such as school," Riley said.

World.title: Black Caps annihilate India with record total
World.content:
It was utter brutality from the Black Caps.

Down 3-0 in the T20 series, New Zealand responded with a record total at Eden Park to crush the Indians in emphatic fashion by 87 runs.

Led by a blazing Glenn Phillips century, Michael Bracewell inflicting further carnage with 65, New Zealand smashed their way to 259 for 7, their highest total in the format.

They were just as ruthless with the ball, never allowing India to get going after being bullied by their batsmen in the first three matches.

Jacob Duffy set the tone with two wickets in his first over, and the Indians quickly crumbled in their futile pursuit.

The win won't be enough to keep the Kiwis alive in the series, but will give them plenty of belief ahead of the one dayers starting Wednesday.

After a stuttering start, Phillips and Bracewell combined and sent the Indian bowlers flying to all corners of Eden Park, the pair plundering 16 sixes between them.

There were some early nerves as opener Finn Allen sliced one down to third man with Prince Yadav taking the catch but stepping over the boundary, however it proved moot as Mayank Yadav had also overstepped during his delivery.

New Zealand’s Finn Allen shows his frustration as he heads back to the dressing room. Andrew Cornaga / Photosport

The Prince made no such mistake two balls later though, when Tim Seifert slashed at one and got a thick outside edge, swallowed up by Yadav to put the Kiwis in some early strife.

Intermittent rain throughout the day resulted in a noticeably slow outfield, the Black Caps struggling to find the rope in the first powerplay.

The shackles were finally broken in the third as Daryl Mitchell sent Yadav into the stands with back to back sixes followed by consecutive bondaries.

However, Yadav got his man in the same over, trapping Mitchell in front for 24 off just nine.

Enter Phillips.

He and Allen continued to press in the powerplay, bringing up fifty in the fifth over with a Phillips six over backward square.

Having been kept somewhat quiet for most of the powerplay, Allen got in on the action with two massive sixes to bring up the fifty partnership.

But just as he looked to really explode, Allen holed out to deep cover off the bowling of Axar Patel.

Phillips continued his charge, bringing up the three figures for the hosts, but Bevon Jacobs was unable to hang around, sent back to the sheds for just seven.

Joined by Bracewell in the middle, Phillips notched his third fifty of the series, the pair racing to a 50 partnership from just 18 balls.

Blazing his way to 40 from 13, Bracewell was given a life in the fourteenth, sending one into the night sky only to be spilled by Naman Dhir.

New Zealand’s Nathan Smith and Daryl Mitchell combine to dismiss India’s Naman Dhir. Andrew Cornaga / Photosport

It would be a chance India would regret letting slip as Bracewell and Phillips put on a century stand in blistering style.

The pair pushed the run rate past 12 and the score past 200 with four overs still to play, their highest ever total in sight.

India finally broke the stand with Bracewell having blasted 65 off only 25 balls, but it didn't stem the flow of runs.

Bringing up his ton in style with another mammoth six over long off, Phillips steered the Black Caps closer to the record as Mitch Santner departed at the other end for five.

Phillips was eventually dismissed in the final over, leaving the ground to a rapturous ovation.

With a daunting total in front of them, India made a horror start to the chase, Duffy claiming the scalps of both Ishan Kishan and Sanju Sampson in his first over.

Abhishek Sharma and Shreyas Iyer kept the chase in check, bringing up the fifty but just as they were starting to build momentum, Matt Fisher took just his second international wicket after Sharma sent one straight to Santner.

The asking rate quickly ballooned to over 14, and India's woes were compounded when Adam Milne castled Sharma to have them reeling at 56/4.

Bringing himself on in the eighth, Santner struck with his very first ball, Nitish Kumar Reddy hitting one straight to Bracewell at cover.

The New Zealand skipper then took a sixth scalp for his side, his second in the same over with a brilliant caught and bowled to send Axar Patel packing.

India Tilak Varma during the 4th T20I cricket match between the New Zealand Black Caps and India held at Eden Park, Auckland, New Zealand, on Friday October 30th 2026. © photo: Blake Armstrong / www.photosport.nz Photosport / Blake Armstrong

With the result well and truly assured, India were meandering their way to the twentieth over, but there was more magic to come.

Needing a miracle, Nahman Dhir looked to go over the rope but found Mitchell at deep long on.

The momentum sent Mitchell towards the boundary, so he would fire it back in play, Nathan Smith taking a spectacular diving catch from his teammate.

Duffy went two in two after Arshdeep Singh hit one straight to Jacobs, but a frustrating period would follow.

Indian tailenders and Prince Yadav and Tilak Varma ensured there were no early showers with a stubborn stand of 37 from 42, prompting some "boring" chants from the crowd.

Varma was finally dismissed by Smith in the 19th, the partnership somewhat taking the gloss off the Black Caps dominance.

They would bat out the 20 overs, a subdued end after the earlier fireworks with most of the 39,000 fans having made their way home.

World.title: Joint's promising run in Japan ends with QF exit
World.content:
Maya Joint's encouraging run at the Pan Pacific Open in Japan has ended with a three-set quarterfinal loss on a day when world number one Elena Rybakina pulled out with an injury.

The Australian, ranked 94 in the world, had been impressive in earlier wins over sixth-seeded Romanian Sorana Cirstea and Spain's Cristina Bucsa to book her spot in the quarterfinals at the WTA 500 event against Kamilla Rakhimova.

The Uzbekistani won a tight first set 7-5, before Joint rebounded to claim the second by the same scoreline.

However, Rakhimova romped away in the final set to win 7-5, 5-7, 6-1 in Tokyo on Friday, local time.

Joint took the honours in first serves, landing 66 per cent compared with her opponent's 59 per cent, and serving five aces to Rakhimova's one.

However, the world number 66 was much more effective on her return, converting six of the 12 break points she set up, compared with the three Joint managed.

Despite the loss, the late-season Asian swing has been a welcome confidence boost for Joint.

Ranked a career-high number 28 in February, the Australian's year had been underwhelming until she made the final at last month's Korea Open in Seoul, where she lost to compatriot Kim Birrell.

The signs are certainly promising for the 20-year-old as she plans her assault on the Australian Open in January.

Rakhimova's victory set up a semifinal against Leylah Fernandez.

The Canadian had an armchair ride to the semis when world number one and reigning Australian and US Open champion Rybakina withdrew from their quarterfinal because of injury.

Rybakina said she could not play because of an undisclosed injury. She stepped onto the court in Tokyo and delivered the news to fans and ended by saying, "I hope to see you all next year."

She said she had been struggling for several days "with a little injury" and needs to be ready for next month's WTA Finals in Indian Wells, California.

AAP

World.title: Australia facing monster chase to win series after Mulder, Rickelton tons
World.content:
Australia will require 288 runs to win the third Test in Cape Town after centuries from Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder put South Africa back in favour.

After beginning day four at 4-140, Rickelton (101) and Mulder (115) combined to help South Africa post 387 in its second innings.

Mitchell Starc was once again Australia's best bowler, finishing with figures of 3-61 off 22 overs, while Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon added two wickets apiece.

If successful on day five, Australia will have recorded the second-highest successful run chase at Newlands behind their predecessors, who mowed down 334 with six wickets down in 2002.

Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder combined for a 154-run partnership to turn the tables on Australia on day four in Cape Town. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher)

South Africa began the day with a lead of just 40 runs with six wickets in hand having lost their skipper minutes before stumps yesterday.

Rickelton and Matthew Breetzke, two players who have shown an ability to score at rapid rates in other forms of the game, needed to curb their natural aggression.

They did so superbly, fending off vicious short deliveries from Australia's pacemen and snaking spinners from Nathan Lyon for much of the morning session.

Breetzke notched 43 off 121 deliveries before being the latest South African to be sucked into taking on a short delivery as he holed out, giving Pat Cummins his first wicket since the first Test.

Nathan Lyon could not reap the rewards of spin-friendly conditions on a frustrating day for Australia's bowlers. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

Breetzke's dismissal came prior to the second new ball and gave Australia fresh hope of wrapping up the Proteas innings in a hurry, as they did on day one.

However, it was not to be as Wiaan Mulder joined Rickelton at the crease and put on a partnership for the ages.

Mulder initially looked shaky, scoring just five off his first 30 deliveries while fending off the second new ball before he expanded his game after lunch.

The pair took the shine of the new ball through the middle session while simultaneously adding to South Africa's lead, adding 92 priceless runs.

Pat Cummins gave Australia the breakthrough in the opening session, with the wicket his first since the first Test of the series. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

With the ball getting softer, Australia turned to spin later in the day with Travis Head, Matt Renshaw and Marnus Labuschagne all getting a chance at the bowling crease.

After seemingly spending an eternity toiling through the 90s while being peppered by short-pitched deliveries, Rickelton brought up his century with a classy flick to the leg side off Josh Hazlewood, sparking a raucous applause around Newlands.

However, his excitement was short-lived after being run out by Mulder in the very next over following a horrible mix-up, ending a sensational 154- run partnership between the pair.

Rickelton's dismissal brought a host of wickets, with Marco Jansen holing out in the deep before Simon Harmer was bowled by Lyon after leaving a big-spinning delivery that pitched well outside the off stump.

Mulder looked set to be stranded when Gerald Coetzee was run out late in the day, but he farmed the strike expertly with South Africa's No.11, Kagiso Rabada, to register his fourth Test century in the dying overs of the day.

Mulder hit out after reaching his milestone and was caught in the deep going for his fifth six of the innings in the final over of the day.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all the action from day four as it happened.

World.title: Retiring Swan Rampe 'hurt' over Pullman Hotel saga
World.content:
Sydney stalwart Dane Rampe "selfishly" grappled with putting off retirement, feeling hurt and upset that the Pullman Hotel saga had derailed his final AFL season.

The 36-year-old defender, who has confirmed his playing career is over, had quietly settled on making this season his last and seemed on track to have one last crack at an elusive premiership after the Swans finished second on the ladder ahead of the finals.

But Sydney's premiership bid — as Swans chairman Andrew Pridham put it — was "torpedoed" after vice-captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice were stood down.

The five were suspended from round 24 and the club's two finals for what the Swans termed a "serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

Those AFL-endorsed club bans were separate from a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel, which is ongoing. No charges have been laid and there is no suggestion of wrongdoing on the part of the suspended players.

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Riley Bice were among the Swans players suspended by the club. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Rampe, who played in four losing grand finals (2014, '16, '22 and '24) across 289 games, confessed to his personal hurt at what happened.

The former Swans co-captain was emotional and held back tears as he announced his retirement on Friday in front of family, teammates and media.

"Deep down, I probably knew at this time last year, this was going to be my last year," Rampe said on Friday.

"Everything was going swimmingly … and then, I'm not going to lie, the events that happened at the back end of the season really muddied those waters.

"It really threw into disarray what I was thinking, what I hadn't probably admitted to myself yet.

"Selfishly, there was part of me that felt a little bit upset and hurt by what had happened.

"I was struggling to accept whether this was the way I was going to bow out.

"And then, coupled with that, was the place in which the club found itself. It didn't feel right. It didn't feel right leaving with where things are at."

Rampe said conversations with coach Dean Cox and football Leon Cameron had helped him achieve "clarity" surrounding his retirement.

He was re-drafted as a rookie this season alongside fellow defender Jake Lloyd, who has signed on for a 15th season.

Dane Rampe captained the Swans in a Grand Final defeat to Brisbane in 2024. (AAP: James Ross)

Cox "delicately" suggested that Rampe was struggling to meet the physical demands after 14 seasons in the system.

"I couldn't quite give the 100 per cent that made me Dane Rampe, the Swans player," Rampe said.

"I'm grateful for the way he [Cox] delicately posed that to me, because it was something I needed to hear.

"Given the emotions of the back end of the season, it was hard for me to see the forest for the trees."

A Swans fan who sprinted onto the SCG in 1999 after Tony Lockett broke the league's goal-kicking record, Rampe has been a heart-and-soul player since he was drafted as a rookie in 2012, aged 22.

He made his debut in 2013 and went on to co-captain the Swans with Josh Kennedy and Luke Parker from 2019 to 2023.

Rampe is a Bob Skilton Medallist (2019) as the club best and fairest and an All-Australian ('16), making him one of the club's greatest rookie-list success stories alongside childhood idol Brett Kirk.

When captain Callum Mills suffered an ACL injury last month in their semi-final win over Brisbane, it was only natural for the Swans to turn to Rampe.

Rampe would captain the Swans in what would be his final match, the club's preliminary final loss to Fremantle.

Dane Rampe reacts emotionally on the final siren of Sydney's first game following the Pullman Hotel incident. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

With nothing confirmed for his future besides a break from the AFL, Rampe said he leaves the club with confidence.

"I'm completely at peace with where the club sits," Rampe said.

"Does that mean that we're not going to be having robust conversations? Absolutely not.

"In fact, I hope to hear that they are having challenging conversations going forward, and that the media is reporting difficult conversations.

"That's a sign of a healthy club, a healthy culture, and I urge and implore the boys and the rest of the club to lean into that."

AAP

World.title: Player prepares for World Cup after career reshaped by injury
World.content:
There are many things to prepare for when playing a game of rugby league. How to break a line, gain an edge or pick a way through a defence.

You don't prepare for one unfortunate tackle to alter the course of your life forever.

In 2020, at the age of 18, while playing for the Narellan Jets in south-west Sydney, Bryce Crane was on the wrong end of a tackle and suffered permanent nerve damage and paralysis of his right arm.

Yet, there was only one thing on his mind.

"You don't really quite understand how much something means to you until it is ripped away," Crane said.

"It's weird to think about but I didn't think about my life, I just thought that I lost the game that I loved growing up playing."

For the love of the game

Crane was told not to worry about the sport. Now, he is preparing for a home World Cup as Australia's Physical Disability Rugby League (PDRL) star fullback.

Australia will host New Zealand and England in the three-team round-robin tournament which runs from October 30 to November 8 in Sydney.

Crane (left) says it will mean a lot to once again represent Australia at the tournament. (Getty Images: Ashley Allen)

"It's really exciting to get into the World Cup; we have had a few camps with the squad, so we are getting around knowing each other," Crane said.

It will be his second PDRL World Cup after he starred for Australia in the inaugural edition in 2022.

Despite Australia failing to win a game, Crane's performances earned him a spot in the Rugby League World Cup Dream Team, which also contained players from the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments.

He was the only PDRL player in the team, and was named alongside fellow Australian internationals Josh Addo-Carr, Cameron Murray and Tarryn Aiken.

Bryce Crane was a stand-out for Australia at the 2022 World Cup. (Getty Images: Ashley Allen)

In the eyes of his teammates though, he does not just contribute to the team through his talismanic play.

Luke Vella, who is also an NRL assistant coach at the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs, knows the hallmarks of a top-quality player.

"He is obviously very skilful and has a great ability to play the game, but he is very humble," Vella said.

"He is also very encouraging, there is times I know Bryce can make a break or make a tackle, but he puts others before himself quite often and encourages them and supports them along with their game."

Full circle moment

The final of the tournament will be held at the Sydney Football Stadium before one of the men's semifinals, the biggest stage the game has been played on so far.

Vella was injured at the ground while playing for the Bulldogs' under-20 side in 2014, and should Australia qualify for the decider, he will step onto that field for the first time in a playing role since then.

Luke Vella is part of the Australian PDRL team. (Supplied: Lainey Gaudron)

"It's funny, I haven't really thought about it too much to be honest," Vella said.

"Obviously the stadium got knocked down and rebuilt, it is a little bit different.

"I can't really describe what the emotions would be if we get there and I get the opportunity to play on the field again."

Vella's passion for the game quickly returned after his career-ending injury, and in 2019, he was named head coach of the Bulldogs' under-20s team, giving him a chance to push players to achieve dreams of making the NRL.

After coaching the team to the Jersey Flegg Cup in 2023, he earned his promotion to the first grade coaching ranks for the 2024 season, while balancing his return to playing.

He made his international debut for Australia against New Zealand in November 2024 in Auckland.

"When I got injured at 20, I fell back in love with it because it got taken away from me," Vella said.

"I love it because my thing for coaching is to develop players and help them achieve their goals, but then the competitive side, running around, throwing the ball around, a bit of contact too.

"All things rugby league, all come back to love."

For Crane and Vella, the pride in representing their country is palpable.

"At the end of the day, I'm not just representing myself, my family, my country, but I'm also representing people with all different types of disabilities," Crane said.

"I feel like that is a pretty cool thing to do."

This content was produced for the ABC's International Day of People with Disability coverage, which runs from November 19 to December 25, 2026.

The ABC is partnering with International Day of People with Disability to recognise the contributions and achievements of the 5.5 million Australians with disability.

World.title: Dream shakes off scheduling controversy to force WNBA Finals decider
World.content:
Izzy Borlase's dream of winning a WNBA championship ring with Atlanta remains alive and kicking after the Australian rookie helped the Dream drag the finals series into a winner-takes-all decider against the Golden State Valkyries in San Francisco.

Game seven in San Francisco on Sunday (AEDT) should be a Halloween spine-tingler, with 22-year-old Borlase dreaming of joining 11 previous Australian winners of WNBA championships.

Opals ace Borlase was one of only seven players picked by Atlanta coach Karl Smesko as the Dream powered its way to an emphatic series-levelling 80-69 victory in front of a noisy near sellout crowd.

The Dream brushed aside the irritation and indignity of having to play the pivotal game six at lunchtime, rescheduled to accommodate a regular season home game for men's counterparts the Atlanta Hawks.

Izzy Borlase was used sparingly as the Dream leaned on the starting five. (Getty Images: Kevin C. Cox)

Increased interest in the Dream's finals run saw a number of games shifted to the home of the NBA's Hawks, which can accommodate 17,000 people, but game six was initially scheduled to be played at the Dream's regular-season home arena, with a 3,500-seat capacity.

After an outcry about the sixth game of the Hawks' 82-game regular season taking precedence over the Dream's push for their first title, the contest was moved to the bigger venue but forced into a 12:30pm (local time) slot to allow the Hawks to face the Cavaliers in prime time.

Borlase played very much a support role in her 12 minutes of court action as Atlanta's powerful starting line-up took control in an opening blitz and never looked back after holding a 17--point advantage at the end of the first quarter.

The Dream was sparked by Allisha Gray (23 points), Rhyne Howard (21) and another double-double from star Angel Reese, who had 14 rebounds and six assists to go with her 15 points.

Atlanta, shooting hot, only ever looked remotely rattled in the final quarter as the visitors, seeking to seal the win that would have brought them the title for the first time in just their second season, got to within eight points going into the final minute.

But there was no cause for alarm as Gray sank a three-pointer under pressure to get the home crowd roaring.

This marks the first time the WNBA Finals has gone to a decider since 2019, when the Washington Mystics beat the Connecticut Sun 3-2 in a best-of-five series.

This season marks the second time the championship has been decided in a best-of-seven format, with last year's victory by the Las Vegas Aces over the Phoenix Mercury coming via a 4-0 sweep.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: For the fans who became heroes, Samoa vs Tonga is bigger than a grand final
World.content:
Ahead of their sold-out Rugby League World Cup match on Sunday, the new faces of the eternal rivalry between Tonga and Samoa didn't quite go straight from the stands onto the field, but they went pretty close.

Four years ago, when the two met in the last World Cup, Francis Manuleleua was hunched over in his bedroom in South Auckland, watching the game on his phone.

He was 18, with the rugby league world at his feet, and after Samoa held on for a pulsating 20-18 victory, he snatched up a flag and marched into the street because his life had changed forever.

Loading...

"Growing up I was always picked in the Kiwi teams, Under 16s and Under 18s and that, so there was a feeling of wanting to pull on that black jersey in either league or union," Manuleleua said.

"But after that 2022 World Cup, seeing all the boys play, how much it meant to them, that's when it changed for me and I thought to myself 'this is the jersey I'd want to put on if I ever get the opportunity'."

Across the Tasman, Sua Fa'alogo was part of the same celebratory throng, wherever the four winds could take Samoans from their islands.

The parades of the Samoan and Tongan fans have become legendary. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

The 23-year-old was born and raised in Samoa, in the village of Si'umu, and lived there until he was nine, when his parents moved to Melbourne to find a better life for him and his eight siblings.

Leka Halasima's story was similar: he was born in Tofoa, Tonga, before moving to New Zealand as a boy.

In 2024, a few months after his NRL debut and well before every league fan knew his name, he watched his two nations go head-to-head in the Pacific Championship, cheering on the Mate Ma'a in a 25-24 victory.

Halasima has gone from admiring his heroes to playing alongside them. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

"Then the next year I was playing with them," Halasima said.

Now the 21-year-old Warriors tyro is doing more than just playing, he is starring alongside the heroes of his childhood and taking forward what they started.

"For a young person like me, I've been a fan since that 2017 World Cup and to go from being in the stands cheering to playing alongside people like Jase (Jason Taumalolo), who I look up to, it's an honour. It's a privilege," Halasima said.

Fa'alogo, Manuleleua and Halasima are not just three of rugby league's brightest young stars; they are part of a new generation inheriting a relationship thousands of years in the making.

Samoa creates rugby league magic The passion of the Pacific shines through in Samoa's rugby league team, and the pride the people have is evident on the island.

The history and culture of Tonga and Samoa are proudly separate and distinct but also irrevocably intertwined by centuries of love and blood and faith, first back in the islands and now within the great Pasifika diaspora.

Today, that relationship plays out in all its colour and splendour on the rugby league field, in grand occasions that prove Tonga and Samoa are a people as much as they're a place.

That place can be wherever either nation plays on their own, but it happens the most when they face one another.

Tonga and Samoa can meet anywhere in the world and their people will find them. (Getty Images: Michael Steele )

It's been this way long enough that players like Manuleleua, Fa'alogo, and Halasima grew up on occasions like this and dreamed of being part of it.

"Since the draw came out, I've been thinking of this day. I'm pretty sure every islander around the world can't wait for it," Halasima said.

"This is pretty much finals footy, this is what it's all about."

Manuleleua played in the NRL grand final for Newcastle earlier this month in what was the most important night of his young life — until Sunday.

Tonga and Samoa renew rugby league's greatest international rivalry Between them they have a population smaller than Canberra, but when they meet on Monday morning for a shot at the semi-finals, Tonga and Samoa will be the talk of the rugby league world.

"This will probably be the biggest game I've ever been a part of it. A grand final is pretty big too, but the rivalry between Samoa and Tonga runs deeper than footy," Manuleleua said.

"A few of my mates are Tongan, and we know deep down we have that hatred for each other when it comes to coming up against them.

"As soon as we cross that white line there's no friends, but after those 80 minutes we'll get together, have a beer and everything will be all sweet."

These games can happen anywhere, because while the islands are always home, the Pasifika diaspora has taken them to the world, and another home can happen wherever Samoans or Tongans come together.

Last year's Samoa-Tonga game attracted more than 45,000 people. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Four years ago it happened in Warrington, 12 months ago it happened in Brisbane in front of 45,000 people in a game that felt like the State of Origin of the new century, and on Sunday it will happen in Parramatta.

Manuleleua's parents are coming over from Auckland but his siblings, he jokes, will have to make their own way.

Halasima will have his partner and newborn son there, as well as his parents, sisters, aunts, and uncles coming from New Zealand and up from Melbourne.

For Fa'alogo it will be an even more special day because his father, Eti, has never seen him play for Melbourne or Samoa in the flesh but he will be there on Sunday to watch his youngest become a part of history.

Sunday will mark a special occasion for Fa'alogo. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

"I can't wait. He's done so much for me," Fa'alogo said.

"I just want to give back to him for everything he did, for bringing me over and trying to give me the opportunity for a better life."

The game itself is a coin flip. Tonga is bigger, stronger and more battle-hardened; Samoa is faster and has more strike as proven by their big win last year.

The former is already locked into a semifinal spot, and the latter may well be by kick-off depending on the scoreline between England and Papua New Guinea, but this is a game that is bigger than a World Cup and larger than life.

The fresh faces feel the legacy of the history between the two nations even as they write its latest chapter, and they want to pass it down just as it was passed to them.

Earlier this year, Fa'alogo went back to Si'umu as part of a trip with the Storm.

He went to his old house and his old school and caught up with family.

Wherever he went, children followed. It has been that way ever since he made his NRL debut in 2023 and his Samoan debut a few months later, but Fa'alogo might not ever get used to it.

"I was shocked," Fa'alogo said.

"Back then I was one of them."

World.title: Australia's Cape Town desperation evident on another pulsating Test day
World.content:
If there was any doubt how much the Cape Town Test matters to Pat Cummins's Australian team, one only needed to clock the cooing pack of them careening towards Cameron Green and Mitchell Starc an hour into the evening session of day three at Newlands.

The catch Green claimed to send his teammates into raptures was straightforward enough, its genesis and aftermath a little more dramatic.

Proteas opener Marques Ackerman, set fair on 62 and attacking everything Australia threw at him, had tried to limbo away from a Starc bouncer that followed him like a heat-seeking missile. Not quite agile enough with his Matrix manoeuvre, Ackerman faintly edged the ball flush into his faceguard, from which it ballooned into the cordon.

Unsure of the deflection and with his ears still ringing from the ding on his grill, Ackerman walked over to his skipper Temba Bavuma to discuss a review of the umpire's call, perhaps as surprised as the Australians when Travis Head arrived on the scene to inquire after his health.

But, in all the chaos and confusion, the crucial 15 seconds had passed before Ackerman could signal for a review. He had to depart.

It has been that sort of series, really; so many periods of ascendancy abruptly terminated by moments of genius, madness and confusion, and so many subversions of the pattern recognition Test cricket followers can normally rely on to impose a sense of order on what they're looking at.

South Africa finished the so-called moving day at 4-140 and 40 runs ahead. It would have wanted to be further in front. It could easily have been far worse off.

Earlier, in the latter stages of its first innings of 429, Australia probably let an extra 100 runs go begging. It sets up a perfect scenario even for those Australian fans who are not normally night owls: a thrilling finish on Friday night into Saturday morning.

On a pulsating day that produced 243 runs and 10 wickets, there was a second Test century for the recalled Josh Inglis and 80 for Alex Carey, both of whom fell to the off-spin of Simon Harmer.

In a Test featuring plenty of runs, only Josh Inglis has reached triple figures. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

An obscurity to most Australians before this series, and tipped to be dropped after the first Test, Harmer was in the thick of everything again with four wickets, two catches, a busted finger and plenty of chatter.

Youngster Cooper Connolly, looking entirely at home at Test level, made a patient 29 from 83 deliveries and might have kicked on further with better support from Australia's tail; the loss of 6-59 to finish off Australia's first innings was, as Pat Cummins often phrases such things, not ideal.

Yet it was still a 100-run lead, and early in South Africa's second innings you got the sense the game was about to break right open for an early finish.

In quick succession, Aiden Markram, who has been a thorn in Australia's side, lazily slapped a loose one from Starc into the clutches of Head at mid-off, and David Bedingham, seemingly rattled by a Starc bouncer that cannoned into his chest, holed out with another inexplicable hook.

The Proteas were 2-31, still 69 runs behind, and the hyenas were circling.

Via the counter-attack of Ackerman, then in a slow and steady partnership between Temba Bavuma and Matthew Breetzke, South Africa began its rally. Yet there was one last twist in store with barely 15 minutes left in the day's play.

Having tortured Bavuma for a few hours with his sharp turn out of the footmarks, Nathan Lyon removed the Proteas skipper again, this time a dipping off break that snuck between bat and pad to castle the lunging batsman. Bavuma is not quite to Lyon what Daryll Cullinan once was to Shane Warne, but he is not far off.

Proteas captain Temba Bavuma posed a major threat to Australia. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

On the matter of hoodoos, much has been made in recent days of Cummins's record-breaking streak without a wicket.

It continued today, despite periods in which the Aussie skipper bowled with genuine pace and guile, although his desperation to break his drought was made clear by one ill-advised review. Even when it is 1.6 metre Bavuma in the firing line, it is always difficult to get an LBW call when it hits above the batsman's knee roll.

In truth, the odd brain fade was perfectly excusable due to the ratcheting up of the atmosphere as this game progressed.

Some testiness and conflict in this series was inevitable, but it has manifested in curious ways. Each team's most vocal player — Marnus Labuschagne for Australia, Matthew Breetzke for the Proteas — has been its worst performed.

Breetzke, in fact, finally started to come good late on day three, and will resume tomorrow believing he is the man to turn the game for his country.

Given the way these two teams have echoed each other's efforts in the past few weeks, perhaps that suggests one last tantalising and slightly mad prospect in the Australian chase: how about Marnus Labuschagne as the last-minute hero?

World.title: Quick hits: Marnus caught in ugly exchange after all-time send off
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne was involved in an ugly moment of DRS drama after giving a retaliatory send-off, as Temba Bavuma threw his wicket away in the shadows of stumps.

Here are the quick hits from day three of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. DRS drama and Labuschagne's ugly exchange

It was one of the most contentious moments of the series when, midway through the evening session, with South Africa 2-95 and still five runs behind, Mitchell Starc collected Marques Ackerman with a steepling, searing bouncer.

The South African lost his balance as the ball thudded into what looked to be a mixture of helmet and bat before flying to Cam Green behind the wicket.

The Australians went up and so did the umpire's finger.

Undoubtedly dazed from the contact, the batter regained his composure and met with partner Temba Bavuma.

Eventually, a referral was called for, but only as the DRS timer ticked to zero.

Ackerman called for the review as the timer hit zero. (Fox Cricket)

It was touch and go, but the officials deemed Ackerman had taken too long, despite the severity of the hit.

With the South Africans pleading their case to the umpires, the ever-vocal Marnus Labuschagne could be heard giving his own opinion over the stump mic.

"The timer's up, oh no, see you buddy!" Labuschagne said from his position at the other end of the wicket.

Meanwhile, Travis Head had made his way over to the South African camp.

"Heady, what are you doing mate? He's off!" Labuschagne could be heard saying.

Head, hands outstretched towards batter and umpire in what appeared to be a peace offering, turned back towards his team and replied.

"I'm just checking if he's alright," Head said.

Head made his way over to check on Ackerman. (Fox Cricket)

Reluctantly, Ackerman made his from the middle, but spent some time at the boundary in the futile hope of being called back.

Thankfully, the replays showed the ball had collected a thick edge before crashing into visor, meaning Ackerman was doomed to be out for 62 even if the review had been permitted.

The technology showed Ackerman was rightly given out. (Fox Cricket)

2. Bloodied Harmer keeps South Africa in the game

Simon Harmer, left, made the breakthrough in the first hour of day three. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

With an advantage to press home at the beginning of day three, the set Australian pair of Alex Carey and Josh Inglis would have been hoping for at least another full session of batting.

The conditions were perfect, the pitch was flat, and things looked very promising as Inglis reverse-swept his way to a hugely impressive second Test century.

However, neither wicketkeeper-batter would see the other side of the first drinks break, with off spinner Simon Harmer once again doing the damage.

Only moments after ripping a nail and bloodying his fingers while attempting a low catch with his non-bowling hand, Harmer had Inglis caught behind for 102.

Harmer received some treatment on a torn nail before dislodging the two set batters. (Fox Cricket)

It was a brilliant delivery; drifting away, spinning in and kissing the outside edge of the Western Australian's blade.

Four overs later, a similarly exquisite off break had Carey (80) nudging to Aiden Markram at slip, and Harmer, a fingernail down, had dragged his side back into the game.

Australia's tail proceeded to eke out a 100-run first-innings lead, eventually dismissed for 429.

3. Marnus gives it to Bedingham

Labuschagne was in quite a mood on day three.

Before the DRS drama in the evening session, the Queenslander took quite some pleasure in giving it back to Proteas batter David Bedingham.

On day two, Matthew Breetzke had joyously celebrated Labuschagne's five-ball duck by leaping over the pitch and shouting directly at the Australian.

And when Bedingham holed out to Josh Hazlewood during the middle session on day three, Labuschagne responded in similar fashion.

The Queenslander had his chest puffed out as he ran towards the South African, face red and fist pumping, screaming what you can only imagine was something entirely considered and reasonable.

Bedingham was out for 11 and South Africa's second innings was already beginning to teeter at 2-31.

4. A strange moment on the hill

It was an unlikely proposal. (Fox Cricket)

It was a strange morning on the hill.

During the first session, the broadcast cameras found a man holding a sign that read: "Ryan Rickelton, is your mum single?"

The middle-aged gentleman received a good amount of screen time, which he used to blow kisses and adjust his sunglasses in a performance that probably wouldn't have endeared him to anyone in the Rickelton family.

Rickelton, South Africa's wicketkeeper-batter, was stony-faced in response, before pursing his lips and shaking his head solemnly.

The commentators were lost for words at what was an uncomfortable moment for everyone involved — and especially, you'd imagine, for Ryan Rickelton's mother.

5. Bavuma throws it away in the shadows of stumps

Stumps were in sight for Bavuma and Breetzke.

The South African pair had so diligently rebuilt South Africa's innings after Ackerman's dismissal, and had just eight more balls to survive.

But with shadows lengthening at Newlands and with the pitch offering more and more for the slower bowlers, Nathan Lyon conjured a little bit of magic.

It was the perfect off spinner's delivery; drifting, turning sharply and bowling a swinging Bavuma clean through the gate.

However, it was a wildly inappropriate shot from the usually so-considered Bavuma, and the South African captain couldn't quite believe what had happened.

Bavuma was a picture of regret on his way from the middle. (Fox Cricket)

He grimaced and shook his head as he made is way from the middle for 35, with South Africa finishing the day on 4-140 and just 40 runs in front.

Tech.title: Google’s satellite AI server transmits its first response to Earth
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google’s AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post on Friday, Google says it successfully booted up the satellite’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), allowing the on-board Gemma 4 model to follow through on a prompt to create a haiku about being in space:

Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨

Google says it tried out other space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts as well. The test is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, an experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers in space. Google launched the satellite into orbit earlier this month.

“Next, we will continue with a series of tests to evaluate how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit,” Google says. “Verifying our TPUs can reliably execute workloads in space paves the way for our next milestone of twin interconnected satellites in 2027.”

Tech.title: Starbucks wants to use AI to show you a ‘personalized digital menu’ at the drive-thru
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Starbucks could eventually show you a personalized digital menu when you pull up to the drive-thru. During an earnings call on Thursday, Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol said the company is going to explore “experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless,” as spotted earlier by More Perfect Union.

It sounds similar to the technology that Taco Bell is experimenting with, which could change the layout, content, and visuals on a digital menu board “on a car-by-car basis.” McDonald’s also recently showed off an AI-powered feature it’s piloting at a handful of drive-thrus, allowing its “ArchIQ” chatbot to identify repeat customers and let them order their “usual.”

Starting in 2027, Starbucks will also begin testing background AI models at the drive-thru to help baristas “input orders more accurately and efficiently,” according to Niccol. The company also plans to integrate AI into the Starbucks app’s search and discovery features, and may allow “conversational and agentic” ordering in the future.

Starbucks has already started allowing customers to place orders through ChatGPT, and also rolled out an AI-powered Green Dot Assist that employees can use to ask questions about things like recipes and service standards.

It’s still not clear how soon we can expect to see personalized digital menu boards at Starbucks, but Niccol says it’s still “early,” adding that “we’ll test, learn, and scale what works.”

Tech.title: The delightfully messy state of Apple gadgets
